## 8. Framed bordism invariance {#framed-six-bordism-invariance}

We first prove the change across an actual stage of index-three handles, then reduce an arbitrary framed bordism between two-connected six-manifolds to two such stages. The reduction needs vanishing in relative degree two, not an assumption that the whole bordism is a homology equivalence.

### 8.1. A complete index-three stage

Let \(T\) be the trace obtained from \(M\times[0,1]\), with \(M\) as in Section 6, by attaching \(r\) handles \(D^3_{a_j}\times D^4_{b_j}\) of index three. Retain every radius \(a_j,b_j>0\), attaching map and original orientation. Suppose \(T\) has its specified stable framing extending that on \(M\). Write its outgoing boundary as \(P\) with its induced frame. The sphere-attaching maps have domain \(S^2_{a_j}\). Since \(M\) is two-connected they are nullhomotopic.

The pair \((T,M)\) has a relative CW model with precisely \(r\) cells of dimension three, and the reversed pair \((T,P)\) has precisely \(r\) cells of dimension four. These are the original core and cocore models from the handle-chain companion. The first description gives \(\pi_1T=\pi_2T=0\); the second shows that \(P\to T\) induces isomorphisms on \(\pi_1,\pi_2\). In the latter claim the relative groups through degree three vanish because all relative cells have dimension four. Thus \(P\) is also two-connected, and Section 6 applies to it.

Put \(H=H_3(M;\mathbb Z)\), \(K=H_3(T;\mathbb Z)\), and \(V=H_3(P;\mathbb Z)\). The complete relevant integral sequences are
\[
 \begin{split}
 0&\longrightarrow H\xrightarrow{\,j\,}K
               \xrightarrow{\,r_3\,}\mathbb Z^r\longrightarrow0,\\
 0&\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^r\xrightarrow{\,\delta\,}V
               \xrightarrow{\,p\,}K\longrightarrow0 .
 \end{split}
 \tag{8.1}
\]
For the first line, \(H_4(T,M)=0\) and \(H_2(M)=0\). For the second line, \(H_3(T,P)=0\) and \(H_4(T)=0\). The last vanishing follows from \(H_4(M)=H^2(M)=0\) and the first relative cell description. All these are the original relative homology groups, with the indicated zero terms accounted for. Both sequences split as sequences of abelian groups because their right-hand groups are free: \(H\) is free by (6.17), and the first sequence makes \(K\) free. In particular \(\delta\) has a primitive image \(L\) of rank \(r\), and reduction of both sequences modulo two remains exact.

The image under \(\delta\) of the \(j\)-th cocore generator is the actual belt sphere
\[
            B_j=\{0\}\times S^3_{b_j}\ \subset P.
 \tag{8.2}
\]
These spheres are disjoint, with zero mutual and self-intersections; a small normal push-off in the \(D^3_{a_j}\) factor proves the self-intersection assertion with the original radius retained. The reversed handle is an index-four surgery along this sphere, and the given framing of \(T\) extends across that actual handle. By (7.7),
\[
                         q_P(\rho B_j)=0.
 \tag{8.3}
\]
The reversed collar has the same negative incoming radial coordinate as Section 2 after the specified reversal of time. A constant reflection needed to express the reversed stable frame cancels in the based comparison (2.5); it introduces no extra parity. Since the pairing on \(L\) is zero, the proved quadratic identity then gives \(q_P=0\) on the whole image \(L_2\) of \(L\) modulo two.

We identify the reduction space, including its actual maps. For every original handle let \(\sigma_j\in\{+1,-1\}\) be the orientation sign of its given ordered parameter chart
\((u_1,u_2,u_3,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4)\)
relative to the orientation of \(T\). Give its core the given \(u\)-orientation and its belt the boundary orientation of the given \(v\)-disc. Then
\[
             \lambda_P(B_j,z)=\sigma_j\bigl(r_3p(z)\bigr)_j
                         \quad (z\in V).
 \tag{8.4}
\]
To check the sign and coefficient, represent the relative core by \(D^3_{a_j}\times\{v_*\}\) on the outgoing face and a chain in the old boundary capping its attaching sphere. The cap exists since \(H_2(M)=0\). At \(v_*=(b_j,0,0,0)\) the outward normal of \(T\) is \(+\partial_{v_1}\). Moving it past the three \(u\)-directions reverses orientation, so the outgoing boundary has orientation \(-\sigma_j\) times
\((u_1,u_2,u_3,v_2,v_3,v_4)\).
The ordered tangents “belt, core” are
\((v_2,v_3,v_4,u_1,u_2,u_3)\),
which are minus that displayed tuple. Their intersection sign is therefore \(\sigma_j\). They meet once; other handle cores miss this belt. Chains from \(M\) can be represented outside the attaching cores and have zero such intersection. Additivity and the exact first line of (8.1) prove (8.4) for every \(z\), retaining all original signs.

It follows that
\[
 L^\perp=p^{-1}(jH),\qquad
 \Xi:L^\perp/L\longrightarrow H,\qquad
                    \Xi(z+L)=j^{-1}p(z)
 \tag{8.5}
\]
is an isomorphism. It is well-defined since \(\ker p=L\). It is injective by the same equality and surjective because \(p\) is onto. These statements give both the actual map and its inverse: lift \(j(x)\) through \(p\); its class modulo \(L\) is independent of the lift.

The isomorphism preserves the full intersection pairing. Represent any finite chosen set of middle classes in \(M\) by immersed three-spheres as in Section 5 and move them off the finitely many attaching two-sphere cores. The avoidance inequality is \(3+2<6\). Their images have positive compact separation from those cores. The actual tube compression of the handle companions puts all attaching tubes inside that separation, retaining the original tube domains, radii and the ambient comparison diffeomorphism. Thus these cycles lie in the common exterior of \(M\) and \(P\). Their ordered tangent intersections and orientation agree there, so their integral pairings agree. Different lifts add belt classes, which pair to zero with \(L^\perp\) by definition. This proves the pairing assertion for (8.5).

The same common-exterior representatives prove equality of the quadratic functions under its reduction modulo two. The specified trace framing restricts along the product there to a homotopy of the original stable frames; (2.4)–(2.9) preserve the parity during that homotopy. The immersion and its double points are the same in the exterior. Formula (6.22) therefore identifies its two \(q\)-values. Adding an element of \(L_2\) does not change the value on \(L_2^\perp\), by (8.3) and the quadratic law. Consequently
\[
 \bar\Xi:(L_2^\perp/L_2,\bar q_P,\bar\lambda_P)
                  \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }
       (H_3(M;\mathbb F_2),q_M,\lambda_M)
 \tag{8.6}
\]
is an actual isomorphism of quadratic spaces. It is the reduction of (8.5) through the exact free sequences (8.1), not an unidentified comparison of isometry classes.

The dimensions differ by \(2r\). Apply the full Gauss-sum identity (4.16) to \(L_2\):
\[
                         G(q_P)=2^rG(q_M),\qquad
                         \operatorname{Arf}(q_P)
                              =\operatorname{Arf}(q_M).
 \tag{8.7}
\]
This proves invariance across the entire original index-three stage.

### 8.2. Making the interior two-connected with the stable frame retained

Let \(C^7\) be a compact framed bordism from two-connected closed \(M^6\) to two-connected closed \(N^6\). We may make its interior connected without changing its boundary. In the eight-dimensional product trace, attach an index-one handle along two seven-discs in distinct components of the upper interior face, away from the original boundary. Its new upper face is obtained by removing those two seven-balls and joining their six-spheres by a tube. The frame on each small attaching disc is homotopic to its centre value by contraction, with that homotopy implemented in its collar. The two centre frames join by a path in the appropriate connected component of invertible matrices; the orientations of the two attaching feet fix that component. Extend over the product one-handle, then restore the full prescribed disc frames using those collar homotopies. This gives the new upper face its stable frame and leaves both original boundary framings fixed.

Next make \(\pi_1C\) and \(\pi_2C\) zero by framed surgeries in the interior. Here are the exact existence and extension arguments. A finite handle CW model gives finitely many generators of \(\pi_1C\). Represent them by disjoint embedded loops: the coincidence and avoidance dimensions for finitely many curves are at most two, less than seven. Their actual oriented normal bundles have rank six and are trivial because an oriented bundle on \(S^1\) is obtained by identifying its end frames by an element of the connected \(SO(6)\).

For a surgery on an embedded \(S^k\subset C^7\), \(k=1,2\), compare the original stable frame on the attaching region with the parameter frame on \(D^{k+1}\times D^{7-k}\). The comparison is the same full radial splitting as (2.3)–(2.4), with \(z\in\mathbb R^{k+1}\), radial component \(\langle q,z\rangle\), and last coordinate \(-\langle q,z\rangle\). Its extension obstruction is in \(\pi_kSO(8+s)\). Changing the actual normal frame changes it by the inclusion from \(\pi_kSO(7-k)\), by the product calculation of (2.8). This is the same extension-over-the-core argument used in Section 2, with the original dimensions displayed.

For \(k=1\), the map
\[
                    \pi_1SO(6)\longrightarrow\pi_1SO(8+s)
 \tag{8.8}
\]
is an isomorphism. Each successive sphere bundle \(SO(j)\to SO(j+1)\to S^j\), \(j\ge6\), has zero adjacent sphere groups in degrees one and two, so its exact sequence proves this statement. Choose the normal-frame class which cancels the obstruction. The resulting framed surgery trace attaches an index-two handle in dimension eight; seen from the outgoing seven-manifold its dual handle has index six. Attaching the original two-handles kills the normal closure of the chosen loop generators in \(\pi_1\), and the outgoing inclusion preserves \(\pi_1\), since its relative cells have dimension six. Thus the new interior is simply connected.

Its \(\pi_2\) is finitely generated: Hurewicz identifies it with the finitely generated \(H_2\) of the compact manifold. Represent a finite set of generators by disjoint embedded two-spheres in the interior. The derivative rank-loss codimension exceeds two, the self-coincidence dimension is four, and \(4<7\); the same relative chart perturbation gives the embeddings and mutual disjointness.

Their oriented normal bundles have rank five. The stable frame of \(TC\), together with the actual radial trivialization \(TS^2\oplus\mathbb R\cong\mathbb R^3\), makes each normal bundle stably trivial. Its clutching class is in \(\pi_1SO(5)\); its stabilization is injective by the sphere-bundle argument just given, starting at \(j=5\). Hence the original clutching class is zero and the original rank-five bundle is trivial. For \(k=2\), the remaining handle obstruction is zero because
\[
                             \pi_2SO(8+s)=0.
 \tag{8.9}
\]
This follows from the covers of \(SO(3),SO(4),SO(5)\) in Section 1 and the successive sphere bundles; all their relevant degree-two groups vanish.

Attach the resulting framed index-three traces in dimension eight. Their outgoing dual handles have index five. The incoming cell attachment quotients \(\pi_2\) by the selected generators, as follows from the exact homotopy sequence of the relative three-cell attachment on a simply connected space. The outgoing inclusion is an isomorphism on \(\pi_1,\pi_2\), since its relative cells have dimension five. Thus the final \(C'\) is two-connected. All surgeries and their complete frame extensions took place in the interior, so the original boundary manifolds, boundary maps and stable frames are retained. Extra stable outward-normal coordinates produced by the traces are retained as appended coordinates; the stabilization invariance proved in Section 2 compares them with the original boundary frames.

### 8.3. Only indices three and four are needed

Take a finite relative Morse presentation of \(C'\), with its actual incoming and outgoing collars. The included zero/top removal applies because \(C'\) and both boundaries are connected. The included index-one removal applies because \(C'\) and both boundaries are simply connected; its proof explicitly assumes only those fundamental-group conditions. Apply it also to the reversed cobordism. This gives precisely the index range \(2,3,4,5\).

The long exact sequences of the two original pairs give
\[
                 H_2(C',M;\mathbb Z)=0,\qquad
                 H_2(C',N;\mathbb Z)=0,
 \tag{8.10}
\]
since \(H_2(C')=0\) and \(H_1(M)=H_1(N)=0\). After index-one removal the relative degree-two chain group has zero outgoing differential. The first equality in (8.10) therefore says that its degree-three boundary is onto. The included integral handle-chain proof constructs an integer section and an actual kernel basis, making that boundary \((I\ \ 0)\) by a recorded invertible upper-basis change. The higher-handle-slide companion realizes this change by the full original framed slides.

Use the included Whitney construction with sheet dimensions \((2,4)\) in the six-dimensional regular level. The lower level is the original simply connected \(M\). It removes opposite-sign intersection pairs and turns the displayed incidence coefficients into exactly one or zero geometric intersections. Sections 2–5 of *Actual Morse data for the modified framed handles* realize that presentation by actual Morse data, identify every intersection with its unique trajectory, prove escape and compact support, and cancel all the index-two handles with their selected index-three partners.

Only indices \(3,4,5\) remain. Reverse the original cobordism, retaining the reversal maps and every frame. Its indices are \(2,3,4\), and the second equality in (8.10) supplies the same surjectivity in relative degree two. The identical argument cancels the reversed index-two handles with reversed index-three handles. In the original direction these are indices five and four. No lower index is introduced. Consequently the final presentation of the same \(C'\), with both original boundary maps retained, has only
\[
                              \text{indices }3\text{ and }4.
 \tag{8.11}
\]
This derivation checks the precise hypotheses of the existing cancellation proofs. It uses no acyclicity in relative degrees three or four.

Order those two handle stages by the included rearrangement construction and call their common regular boundary \(P\). The first stage is exactly an index-three trace from \(M\) to \(P\), so (8.7) gives \(\operatorname{Arf}(q_P)=\operatorname{Arf}(q_M)\). The second stage, viewed in reverse, is exactly an index-three trace from \(N\) to \(P\). Its incoming boundary is two-connected, so the same proof gives \(\operatorname{Arf}(q_P)=\operatorname{Arf}(q_N)\). Stable frames under reversal are compared by the original collar isomorphisms; a constant coordinate reflection changes neither based parity nor the mod-two pairing. Hence
\[
                         \operatorname{Arf}(q_M)
                               =\operatorname{Arf}(q_N)
 \tag{8.12}
\]
for every framed bordism between the stated two-connected six-manifolds.

### 8.4. The homomorphism on the entire framed bordism group

Every class in \(\Omega^{\mathrm{fr}}_6\) has a two-connected representative. Join its finitely many connected components by framed index-one traces. Kill a finite set of loop generators by interior one-sphere surgery in dimension six, using rank-five normal bundles and the isomorphism \(\pi_1SO(5)\to\pi_1SO(7+s)\). After simple connectedness, kill finitely many \(\pi_2\) generators by two-sphere surgery. These spheres can be made disjoint and embedded since \(2+2<6\). Their rank-four normal bundles are trivial: stable triviality kills their clutching class because \(\pi_1SO(4)\to\pi_1SO(7+s)\) is an isomorphism, using the covers and sphere bundles of Section 1. Their frame-extension obstruction is \(\pi_2SO(7+s)=0\).

The traces now have dimension seven. The two-sphere surgery attaches index-three handles, and its outgoing dual handles have index four; their relative cells preserve \(\pi_1,\pi_2\) at the outgoing end. The one-sphere surgery has dual index five and preserves \(\pi_1\) there. These exact cell comparisons prove the claimed effect on the homotopy groups. Thus the result is two-connected and framed bordant to the given manifold.

Define its value to be the Arf invariant of (6.21) on any such representative. If two choices represent the same framed bordism class, a framed bordism between them exists by the definition of that group, and (8.12) proves their values equal. This is a well-defined function
\[
                  \kappa:\Omega^{\mathrm{fr}}_6\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2.
 \tag{8.13}
\]
For addition, take two two-connected representatives and connect their disjoint union by the same framed one-handle trace. The resulting connected sum has middle homology the direct sum of their original middle groups: apply the Mayer–Vietoris sequence across the joining five-sphere, whose homology in degrees two and three is zero. The ordered intersection pairing is the orthogonal sum, since cycles in the two punctured summands are disjoint. Every such class has a representative in its punctured summand, and (6.22) proves that its quadratic value is its original value. The full quadratic function is therefore the orthogonal sum. Equation (4.17) proves additivity of (8.13).

The zero class has the standard framed \(S^6=\partial D^7\) as a representative and has zero middle homology. Its value is zero. Reversing an oriented representative reverses its integral pairing and its orientation data, but the corresponding constant target and normal-coordinate reflections in (2.4) preserve the based parity by the stable conjugation proof following (5.5). Modulo two the reversed pairing equals the original pairing. Thus its value is unchanged, as required for a homomorphism to \(\mathbb F_2\). These arguments establish (8.13) on the whole original framed bordism group, not only on a collection of chosen two-connected representatives.

## 9. The original framed homotopy six-sphere has a framed nullbordism {#framed-six-original-nullbordism}

The included Pontryagin–Thom companion proves the actual map and both inverse bordism/homotopy constructions
\[
                  \operatorname{PT}:\Omega^{\mathrm{fr}}_6
                                       \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\pi_6(\mathbb S),
 \tag{9.1}
\]
with the original normal and tangent frame comparison and the right-appended suspension coordinates. For arbitrary stable tangent frames in this six-dimensional bordism group, the [general stable tangent-frame comparison](sphere-twists-and-the-original-smooth-six-sphere-comparison.md#twist-general-stable-framing) supplies the full original-involution homotopy without a complex-structure hypothesis, independently of the later sphere-recognition conclusion. Its (7.9)–(7.19) prove both inverse maps and the complete boundary-frame correction used here. The included integral stable comparison proves, with the original unit map to the two-completion and all other primary components retained, that
\[
                                   \pi_6(\mathbb S)\cong\mathbb Z/2.
 \tag{9.2}
\]
The product with the actual Lie framing (3.6) has \(\kappa=1\) by (6.24) and (8.13). Thus (8.13) is a nonzero homomorphism from the two-element group in (9.1)–(9.2) to \(\mathbb F_2\). It is consequently an isomorphism: its two elements have distinct images. In particular
\[
 [S^3\times S^3,\tau_{\mathrm{Lie}}]
       \quad\hbox{is the unique nonzero element of }
                                  \Omega^{\mathrm{fr}}_6.
 \tag{9.3}
\]
This conclusion now uses the proved bordism invariance; the earlier product example by itself did not establish it.

Let \(\Sigma\) be the original smooth homotopy six-sphere in lesson 7, with the actual stable tangent framing constructed in the spin-six companion. Its original integral homology gives \(H_3(\Sigma;\mathbb F_2)=0\). Hence its quadratic space is the zero space, its Gauss sum is \(1\), and its Arf invariant is zero by (4.8)–(4.9). Since (8.13) is an isomorphism,
\[
              [\Sigma,\tau_\Sigma]=0\quad\hbox{in }\Omega^{\mathrm{fr}}_6,
 \qquad
              \operatorname{PT}(\Sigma,\tau_\Sigma)=0
                                      \quad\hbox{in }\pi_6(\mathbb S).
 \tag{9.4}
\]
By the definition of framed bordism, or by the explicit inverse nullhomotopy construction in the Pontryagin–Thom companion, there is a compact smooth seven-manifold \(W\) with boundary the original \(\Sigma\) and a stable framing which restricts to the specified \(\tau_\Sigma\), after the stated appended coordinates. The boundary identification is part of this construction. Formula (9.4) has therefore supplied the actual existence of a framed nullbordism.

The conclusion is about that framed bordism and its retained boundary map. Its relative homology in degrees three and four has not been proved zero. The [sphere-twist and smooth-recognition proof](sphere-twists-and-the-original-smooth-six-sphere-comparison.md#twist-original-smooth-map) now constructs the new interior gluing with its full frame defect, cancels every actual handle and gives the orientation-preserving diffeomorphism to the original six-sphere, homotopic to its original degree-one map. A framed nullbordism alone does not replace that calculation.

More generally, for every closed two-connected framed six-manifold \(M\), the same proved isomorphisms give
\[
 \begin{split}
 M\text{ has a framed nullbordism}
   &\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \operatorname{Arf}(q_M)=0\\
   &\ \Longleftrightarrow\
       H_3(M;\mathbb F_2)\text{ has a }q_M\text{-zero Lagrangian}.
 \end{split}
 \tag{9.5}
\]
The first equivalence is (8.13) together with (9.1)–(9.3); the second is the full constructive algebraic argument (4.11). Two such framed manifolds represent the same framed bordism class exactly when their Arf values agree, because \(\kappa\) is injective. These are framed bordism statements with the specified stable frames. They do not assert that the underlying smooth manifolds are diffeomorphic.

### Exercise 1. The full local derivative and double-point change

For the original family (5.22), take \(t=9/25\). Determine its unordered double pair, the signed six-column determinant in the original sheet order, the local derivative degree at the unique singular parameter, and the resulting change of \(Q_\tau\). Retain the cubic term and every numerical coefficient.

**Solution.** The equal-output equations in Section 5.5 give the pair
\[
       \{(0,0,3/5),(0,0,-3/5)\}.
 \tag{10.1}
\]
In both images the third coordinate is \(9/25\), and the last coordinate is
\[
              (3/5)^3-(9/25)(3/5)=27/125-27/125=0,
 \tag{10.2}
\]
with the same equality after both signs are reversed. The first, second, fourth and fifth coordinates are zero. Thus the common image is \((0,0,9/25,0,0,0)\).

At the positive sheet, the three columns are
\[
 a_1=(1,0,0,3/5,0,0)^T,\quad
 a_2=(0,1,0,0,3/5,0)^T,\quad
 a_3=(0,0,6/5,0,0,18/25)^T.
 \tag{10.3}
\]
The negative sheet has
\[
 b_1=(1,0,0,-3/5,0,0)^T,\quad
 b_2=(0,1,0,0,-3/5,0)^T,\quad
 b_3=(0,0,-6/5,0,0,18/25)^T.
 \tag{10.4}
\]
The last entries are \(3(9/25)-9/25=18/25\), using the full derivative of the cubic. Subtract \(a_1,a_2\) from \(b_1,b_2\) and expand along the first two rows. The remaining determinant is
\[
 \left(\frac{-6}{5}\right)^2
   \det\begin{pmatrix}6/5&-6/5\\18/25&18/25\end{pmatrix}
    =\frac{36}{25}\frac{216}{125}
    =\frac{7776}{3125}
    =32(3/5)^5>0.
 \tag{10.5}
\]
Thus the double point is transverse with the positive sign in that specified order of sheet coordinates.

The singular derivative parameter is \((u,v,w,t)=(0,0,0,0)\). Equations (5.24)–(5.26) retain its four-component residual column \((2w,u,v,3w^2-t)\), with determinant \(-2\) at zero. The local degree is therefore \(-1\). For the actual local lift (5.11) its stable integer is \(-1\); another oriented normal frame adds the displayed even integer \(2n\) in (5.12). Hence its contribution to the change of \(\varepsilon_\tau\) is one. The family has no double point for \(t<0\) and exactly the one in (5.27) for \(t>0\); its change of \(\mu\) is also one. Therefore
\[
                        \Delta Q_\tau=1+1=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_2.
 \tag{10.6}
\]
This calculation accounts for the local end of the compact double curve and for the full framing comparison. It does not equate the two signed integer contributions: the cancellation is the stated equality in \(\mathbb F_2\).

### Exercise 2. Two belt classes, both original signs, and the full quotient

Take the actual integral lattice with ordered basis
\((A,B,p_1,t_1,p_2,t_2)\) and intersection matrix
\[
 J=
 \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}
 \oplus
 \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
 \oplus
 \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{10.7}
\]
On its reduction modulo two prescribe \(q(A)=q(B)=1\),
\(q(p_1)=q(p_2)=0\), \(q(t_1)=1\), \(q(t_2)=0\), and the quadratic law with the reduction of this exact matrix. Calculate the quadratic polynomial, the reduction by \(L=\mathbb Zp_1\oplus\mathbb Zp_2\), both fibre counts, and the Arf value. This is a specified integral algebraic example of the comparison (8.5); no geometric realization of these extra data is assumed.

**Solution.** Write the original vector as
\[
        z=xA+yB+u_1p_1+v_1t_1+u_2p_2+v_2t_2.
 \tag{10.8}
\]
The exact integral belt pairings are
\[
                     \lambda(p_1,z)=-v_1,\qquad
                     \lambda(p_2,z)=v_2.
 \tag{10.9}
\]
Thus \(L^\perp\) is precisely the sublattice \(v_1=v_2=0\). Its actual quotient map and inverse are
\[
 \begin{split}
  L^\perp/L&\longrightarrow\mathbb ZA\oplus\mathbb ZB,
       &z+L&\longmapsto xA+yB,\\
  \mathbb ZA\oplus\mathbb ZB&\longrightarrow L^\perp/L,
       &xA+yB&\longmapsto xA+yB+L.
 \end{split}
 \tag{10.10}
\]
The two original signs in (10.9) have been retained, although both reduce to the same nonzero sign in the coefficient field.

Iteration of the quadratic identity gives, with all coordinates now reduced modulo two,
\[
 q(z)=x+y+xy+v_1+u_1v_1+u_2v_2.
 \tag{10.11}
\]
In particular \(q\) vanishes on the original \(L/2L\). On its perpendicular quotient (10.10), the polynomial is exactly \(x+y+xy\). The three ordered two-coordinate Gauss factors in (10.11) are respectively \(-2,2,2\), by their four-term sums in (4.7). Therefore
\[
       G(q)=(-2)\cdot2\cdot2=-8
             =2^2\,G(\bar q),\qquad
       \operatorname{Arf}(q)=\operatorname{Arf}(\bar q)=1.
 \tag{10.12}
\]
There are \(2^6=64\) original vectors modulo two. Keeping both total and signed count gives
\[
                    \#q^{-1}(0)=\frac{64-8}{2}=28,\qquad
                    \#q^{-1}(1)=\frac{64+8}{2}=36.
 \tag{10.13}
\]
The zero-valued isotropic plane \(L/2L\) is not a Lagrangian: it has dimension two while half the full dimension is three. Equation (4.11) and the computed Arf value prove that no zero-valued Lagrangian exists. Thus adjoining these two zero-valued belt directions has retained the nonzero Arf invariant, exactly as the complete index-three comparison (8.7) requires.

## 1. The specified levels and the complement used to fill the disk {#receiving-whitney-levels}

The three receiving dimension triples are
\[
 (d,p,q)=(5,2,3),\quad(6,2,4),\quad(6,3,3),
 \qquad d=p+q.
 \tag{1.1}
\]
Let \(N\) be the original connected, oriented, simply connected closed \(d\)-manifold before a finite collection of disjoint framed index-\(p\) surgeries. Retain the original full attachments
\[
 \varphi_j:S^{p-1}_{r_j}\times D^{q+1}_{s_j}\longrightarrow N,
 \qquad r_j,s_j>0.
 \tag{1.2}
\]
Denote the resulting boundary by \(N'\) and its belt spheres by
\[
 B_j=\{0\}\times S^q_{s_j}.
 \tag{1.3}
\]
Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) be disjoint oriented embedded \(p\)-spheres in \(N'\), with their original framed attaching maps retained, and transverse to every \(B_j\). Choose opposite-sign intersection points \(a,b\) of a particular \(A=A_i\) and \(B=B_j\).

The original complement map is
\[
 P:N'\setminus\bigcup_j B_j
    \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }
    N\setminus\bigcup_jL_j,\qquad
 L_j=\varphi_j(S^{p-1}_{r_j}\times\{0\}).
 \tag{1.4}
\]
It is the simultaneous disjoint-region map of the [belt-complement chapter](belt-sphere-complements-and-the-whitney-disk.md#belt-complement-map), with every original radial function, cutoff integral and seam map included. Its positive-face formula, before the retained rounding comparisons, is
\[
 (u,v)\longmapsto
 \varphi_j\left(\frac{r_j}{\|u\|}u,
               \frac{F_j(\|u\|)}{s_j}v\right),
 \quad u\ne0,\quad\|v\|=s_j.
 \tag{1.5}
\]
All components of its derivative are given in that chapter's equation (1.13a).

The complement in (1.4) is simply connected. Indeed loops and their based null-homotopies in \(N\) can be perturbed relative their prescribed collars off the finitely many \(L_j\). The exact inequalities are
\[
 1+(p-1)<d,\qquad 2+(p-1)<d
 \tag{1.6}
\]
in each of (1.1). To see why they suffice, use finite chart perturbations whose value parameters span the normal space to \(L_j\) at each possible intersection. For a transverse parameter the inverse-image dimensions are the left sides of (1.6) minus \(d\), both negative. Sard's theorem gives such a parameter, fixed near the collars that already avoid the cores. Relative smoothing gives the required initial smooth representatives. This is exactly the finite-parameter construction already proved in Sections 2-3 of the belt-complement chapter, now with the displayed dimensions. The original inclusion induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups; (1.4) carries this assertion to the belt complement.

Construct embedded arcs \(\alpha,\beta\) from \(a\) to \(b\), respectively in \(A,B\), with interiors missing all intersection points. Both spheres have dimension at least two. Coordinate paths, finite detours around the forbidden points, removal of loops and smoothing relative endpoint germs give these arcs, as in the earlier disk proof, Section 7.1. They are disjoint from one another except at the two endpoints, since their interior crossings would be forbidden intersections of \(A\) and \(B\).

At an endpoint \(c\in\{a,b\}\), use actual parametrizations
\[
 a_c(x,u)\in A,\quad u\in\mathbb R^{p-1},
 \qquad b_c(y,v)\in B,\quad v\in\mathbb R^{q-1}.
\]
Their first axes give the chosen arcs, directed away from that endpoint, with the specified original parameters. In a target chart \(\psi\), define
\[
 \mathcal H_c(x,u,y,v)=
 \psi^{-1}\bigl(\psi(a_c(x,u))+\psi(b_c(y,v))-\psi(c)\bigr).
 \tag{1.7}
\]
Its derivative at zero is the direct sum of the two transverse sheet tangent maps, hence invertible. It gives a full chart on a smaller original neighbourhood and satisfies the exact identities
\[
 \mathcal H_c(x,u,0,0)=a_c(x,u),\qquad
 \mathcal H_c(0,0,y,v)=b_c(y,v).
 \tag{1.8}
\]
The prescribed disk quadrant is \(\mathcal H_c(x,0,y,0)\), \(x,y\geq0\). Its interior avoids both sheets. The endpoint neighbourhoods can be made disjoint and avoid every other sphere.

Along \(\alpha\), extend the endpoint \(y\)-direction to a transverse vector field; its normal quotient has rank \(q\geq3\). Along \(\beta\), extend the endpoint \(x\)-direction; its normal quotient has rank \(p\geq2\). The spaces of nonzero vectors in these ranks are connected. Trivialize each quotient over the interval by the already proved projector transport, join the prescribed endpoint vectors through nonzero vectors with their end germs fixed, and interpolate the tangent components separately. Extend the fields to neighbourhoods, retaining the exact endpoint coordinate fields. Their small positive-time flows give the two strips, agreeing exactly with the endpoint quadrants. Their derivatives have rank two at time zero. The compactness and local-inverse argument in Section 7.2 of the belt-complement chapter gives a uniform width on which the strips and quadrants form an embedded corner collar. Their inward sides avoid every sphere: the local defining functions have leading term \(t\nu(s)\), with \(\nu(s)\ne0\), and a uniform \(O(t^2)\) remainder; the other sheets have positive compact separation away from the endpoint charts.

Keep the same complete rounding curve with its positive width \(\epsilon\), original smooth step \(\chi\), and \(\kappa(t)=\chi(3t-1)\):
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 x(t)&=\frac{\epsilon}{2}+2\epsilon\int_0^t\kappa(s)\,ds,\\
 y(t)&=\frac{\epsilon}{2}+2\epsilon\int_t^1\kappa(1-s)\,ds,\\
 (x',y')&=2\epsilon(\kappa(t),-\kappa(1-t)),\\
 \kappa(t)+\kappa(1-t)&=1,\qquad
 \int_0^1\kappa(t)\,dt=\frac12 .
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{1.9}
\]
Thus its endpoints are \((\epsilon/2,3\epsilon/2)\) and \((3\epsilon/2,\epsilon/2)\); its exact vertical and horizontal germs join the strip edges at width \(\epsilon/2\). This gives the original compact corner annulus \(C_0\), with smooth inner boundary \(\gamma\), and preserves both outer corner charts.

The inner curve is in the simply connected belt complement (1.4), so bounds a continuous disk there. Prescribe its entire inward filling collar by extending \(C_0\) smoothly a little across \(\gamma\), away from its existing interior, using the actual transverse collar field. Parametrize that filling collar by a round disk \(D_h^2\), retaining \(h>0\). The relative embedded-disk proof from Section 5 of the belt-complement chapter applies with the following explicit dimension checks. For immersions of a two-dimensional disk into a \(d\)-manifold, the rank-one stratum of two-column derivative matrices has codimension \(d-1>2\), and the rank-zero stratum has codimension \(2d>2\). The far-pair coincidence domain has dimension four, less than \(d\). For avoidance of the additional sheets and the retained annulus,
\[
 2+p<d,\qquad 2+2<d .
 \tag{1.10}
\]
Their boundary and corner strata have no larger dimensions. Value-and-first-derivative chart perturbations give transversality to the rank strata; independent value perturbations at two separated points give transversality to the diagonal. Compact near-diagonal injectivity of the resulting immersion remains under a sufficiently small \(C^1\) perturbation. Sard then eliminates every listed locus. Keep the full prescribed collar fixed, and take the perturbation small enough to remain in the open belt complement. These are all the estimates used by the earlier relative construction, and they hold for every triple (1.1).

The resulting embedded filling meets \(C_0\) only along its prescribed boundary and agrees with its whole continued collar there. Glue them to obtain a disk \(D\) with the two original outer corners. Its interior avoids every \(A_\ell,B_j\). The domain has the original quadrant charts, strip charts and round filling chart; their common collar agrees with all derivatives. In particular no assertion about the smooth extension of an arbitrary higher-dimensional sphere diffeomorphism has entered the disk construction.

## 2. The original orientation and normal blocks {#receiving-whitney-normal-blocks}

Both arc parameters run from \(a\) to \(b\). Write \(a'=\alpha'\), \(b'=\beta'\), and choose full tangent frames \(U=(u_1,\ldots,u_{p-1})\), \(V=(v_1,\ldots,v_{q-1})\) along the respective arcs so that \((a',U)\), \((b',V)\) have the original sheet orientations. Their endpoint germs are the original coordinate frames with these signs; interval frame transport extends them. Retain
\[
 \sigma_a=\operatorname{sgn}_{TN'}(a'_a,U_a,b'_a,V_a),\qquad
 \sigma_b=\operatorname{sgn}_{TN'}(a'_b,U_b,b'_b,V_b)
          =-\sigma_a.
 \tag{2.1}
\]
Orient \(D\) so its boundary follows \(\alpha\) forward and \(\beta\) backward. At \(a\) its tangent orientation is \((a'_a,b'_a)\). At \(b\) its quadrant coordinates point backwards along both arcs, and its disk orientation is the negative of their coordinate orientation; equivalently it is the negative of \((a'_b,b'_b)\). Moving \(b'\) past \(p-1\) columns gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{sgn}_{TN'}(TD_a,U_a,V_a)
       &=(-1)^{p-1}\sigma_a,\\
 \operatorname{sgn}_{TN'}(TD_b,U_b,V_b)
       &=-(-1)^{p-1}\sigma_b
        =(-1)^{p-1}\sigma_a .
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{2.2}
\]
This common factor is retained.

For any original metric matrix \(G\), let \(V_0\) be the two-column disk tangent matrix and \(W=(U,V)\) the \((d-2)\)-column extra-sheet matrix. The exact normal projections and Gram matrix are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 W^\perp&=W-V_0(V_0^{\mathsf T}GV_0)^{-1}V_0^{\mathsf T}GW,\\
 (W^\perp)^{\mathsf T}GW^\perp
 &=W^{\mathsf T}GW
   -W^{\mathsf T}GV_0(V_0^{\mathsf T}GV_0)^{-1}V_0^{\mathsf T}GW .
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{2.3}
\]
The Gram matrix is positive definite: a zero value would put a nonzero linear combination of \(W\) into the span of \(V_0\), contradicting the invertibility of the corner chart. The column operation taking \((V_0,W)\) to \((V_0,W^\perp)\) has determinant one, so preserves both signs (2.2). These projections give an exact frame on each whole endpoint quadrant.

Along the \(A\)-arc, its \(p-1\) projected extra tangent vectors are independent because the disk tangent plane meets \(TA\) exactly in the arc line. Positive completions by \(q-1\) vectors form a connected space: in a quotient frame the complementary block is in \(GL^+(q-1,\mathbb R)\), and its components along the first block are arbitrary. The group \(GL^+(r,\mathbb R)\) is connected by its exact positive triangular factor and a succession of rotations for its orthogonal factor. Hence completions can be chosen smoothly along the interval, retaining both entire corner germs. Along the \(B\)-arc apply the same argument with its fixed \(q-1\) projected tangent vectors and the remaining \(p-1\) vectors. The determinant factor (2.2) puts both endpoint choices in the same positive component.

To extend these frames through the strips while preserving the exact corner frames \(e_C\), start with the normal-bundle projection connection \(P_\perp\,d\). On the corner patches change it to
\[
 \nabla^C s
 =P_\perp\,ds-
   (P_\perp\,de_C)(e_C^{\mathsf T}e_C)^{-1}e_C^{\mathsf T}s .
 \tag{2.4}
\]
This displayed expression uses an auxiliary Euclidean realization of the bundle, as in the original projector construction; the original metric normal projections remain (2.3). Direct substitution gives \(\nabla^C(e_C\xi)=e_C\,d\xi\). Cut off this connection correction to the disjoint corner patches, equal to it on the whole joining germs. Transport the boundary frames along each strip width. Linear ODE uniqueness makes the transported frames agree with \(e_C\) on the overlaps, and invertible transport preserves their ranks. This yields a full frame on \(C_0\), adapted to the \(A\) block on one outer arc and to the \(B\) block on the other. Extend it a little over the filling collar in the same way.

At \(d=5\) the rank-three extension and its controlled sign change are proved in the earlier chapter, Section 6.6. At \(d=6\) the rank is four. We now prove that extension with every original frame coefficient retained.

## 3. Rank-four frames and the exact rotation obstruction {#receiving-rank-four-frame}

Use the real quaternions \(\mathbb H\) with their original ordered basis \((1,i,j,k)\), multiplication \(ij=k,jk=i,ki=j\), reversed products with minus signs, and \(i^2=j^2=k^2=-1\). Their associative matrix realization, conjugation and full norm identity are proved in [lesson 11](almost-complex-structures-and-integrability.md), Section 2. No alteration of the receiving disk coordinates is made by this auxiliary algebra.

For unit quaternions define
\[
 \rho:S^3\times S^3\longrightarrow SO(4),\qquad
 \rho(a,b)(x)=a x b^{-1}.
 \tag{3.1}
\]
Norm multiplicativity proves orthogonality. Its determinant is \(+1\), since the domain is connected and the identity pair acts as the identity. It is a homomorphism: the two left multipliers multiply in order, and the right multipliers do too after taking the inverse. If it acts trivially, substitution \(x=1\) gives \(a=b\), and then \(a\) commutes with \(i,j,k\). Comparing its four coefficients gives zero imaginary part. Thus
\[
 \ker\rho=\{(1,1),(-1,-1)\}.
 \tag{3.2}
\]
The derivative at the identity sends imaginary \(u,v\) to the skew map \(x\mapsto ux-xv\). A zero such map gives \(u=v\), which commutes with all quaternions and is imaginary, hence \(u=v=0\). Both tangent spaces have dimension six, so this derivative is an isomorphism. Translation gives local inverses everywhere. The image is open and, by compactness of \(S^3\times S^3\), closed. The group \(SO(4)\) is connected: send a first unit column to the first standard vector by a rotation in their two-plane, continue on its orthogonal complement, and end with the orientation-preserving one-dimensional identity; varying each rotation angle to zero gives a path. Therefore \(\rho\) is onto.

This is a two-sheet covering. For an image point take disjoint inverse-function neighbourhoods of its two preimages (3.2). A smaller image neighbourhood has no other inverse images: otherwise compactness gives a limiting third preimage, contrary to (3.2). Intersect the two inverse images with that smaller neighbourhood. These are its two disjoint local sheets. This proves the covering assertion without a classification of compact Lie groups.

Each \(S^3\) is simply connected. Smooth a loop through the original Euclidean embedding and radial retraction. Its smooth image has measure zero in the three-dimensional sphere, by Sard in coordinate charts, so misses a point. Stereographic projection from that point identifies its image with a loop in \(\mathbb R^3\), and affine contraction gives a disk. The initial smoothing is homotopic to the loop by the same retraction construction. Thus the product \(S^3\times S^3\) is simply connected too.

Lift a loop \(Q\) in \(SO(4)\), choosing its initial point. Its final point is either that initial point or its product by \((-1,-1)\). Write this endpoint sign as \(\epsilon(Q)\in\{1,-1\}\). Then
\[
 Q\text{ extends over a disk}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \epsilon(Q)=1.
 \tag{3.3}
\]
Necessity follows by lifting a disk, whose domain is simply connected; the lift closes on its boundary. For sufficiency, a closed lift has two quaternion loops, each contracting by the preceding construction. Their product filling followed by \(\rho\) fills \(Q\). Homotopies of loops preserve the sign: lift the homotopy with its starting points varying continuously; the endpoint difference has values in the discrete kernel (3.2) and hence is constant. Changing the initial lift multiplies both ends by the same central kernel element and also leaves the sign unchanged.

There is an exact full rotation with negative sign. Put
\[
 a(\theta)=\cos(\theta/2)+i\sin(\theta/2),\qquad
 b(\theta)=\cos(\theta/2)-i\sin(\theta/2),
 \quad 0\leq\theta\leq2\pi.
 \tag{3.4}
\]
Since \(b^{-1}=a\), multiplication gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \rho(a,b)(1)&=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta,\\
 \rho(a,b)(i)&=-\sin\theta+i\cos\theta,\\
 \rho(a,b)(j)&=j,\qquad \rho(a,b)(k)=k .
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{3.5}
\]
For example \(a j=j\overline a\) proves \(a j a=j\); the same identity holds for \(k\). This is one full positive rotation in the ordered \((1,i)\)-plane, fixing its orthogonal complement. Its lift ends at \((-1,-1)\). Conjugation by an oriented orthogonal comparison carries it to any specified oriented coordinate two-plane and preserves this central endpoint. Its inverse has the same negative sign.

Now let \(e\) be the original smooth oriented frame of the rank-four disk normal bundle prescribed on a whole filling collar. The projector transport used in Section 6.1 of the belt-complement chapter supplies an auxiliary oriented orthonormal frame \(n\) on the complete round filling disk \(D_h^2\). That proof uses the projection identity \(P_\perp^2=P_\perp\) and a linear ODE along radial segments; it is valid in every rank, with four initial independent vectors here. Express the prescribed full frame as
\[
 e=nR,\qquad R:D_h^2\text{ collar}\longrightarrow GL^+(4,\mathbb R).
 \tag{3.6}
\]
Here \(R\) is the exact matrix of all original coefficients.

Apply Gram-Schmidt with each positive length retained. For its columns \(r_j\), define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 w_j&=r_j-\sum_{a<j}\langle q_a,r_j\rangle q_a,\\
 t_{jj}&=\|w_j\|>0,\qquad q_j=w_j/t_{jj},\\
 t_{aj}&=\langle q_a,r_j\rangle\ (a<j),\qquad t_{aj}=0\ (a>j).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{3.7}
\]
Every \(w_j\) is nonzero by independence of the original columns. Thus
\[
 R=QT,\qquad Q\in SO(4),\quad
 T\text{ upper triangular with }t_{jj}>0.
 \tag{3.8}
\]
This is an exact factorization; no entry of \(T\) is discarded. All factors depend smoothly on the collar coordinates.

The original frame extends, retaining its entire prescribed collar, precisely when the loop \(Q|_{\partial D_h^2}\) has sign \(+1\). If a full \(R\) extends, (3.7) applied to it extends \(Q\), proving necessity. For sufficiency, lift the prescribed whole collar map \(Q\) through (3.1). A closed boundary lift makes its annular lift single-valued: extend radially by path lifting, and use the same endpoint sign on every radial circle. Choose an inner collar circle. Its two lifted quaternion loops bound disks by the argument for (3.3). Put a product collar on these fillings and join it to the given collar using its actual radial parameter dependence; the smooth relative approximation and radial retraction, fixed on a smaller whole prescribed collar, give a smooth \(S^3\times S^3\)-valued disk extension. Its projection is an extension \(\widetilde Q\) equal to every value and derivative of the original \(Q\) on that smaller collar.

Extend the triangular factor just as explicitly. First choose \(r_0<h\) within the given collar. A smooth radial map \(r\mapsto\tau(r)\), equal to \(r\) near the boundary and constant \(r_0\) farther inside that collar, keeps its argument within the given domain. Composing each prescribed entry with \((\theta,\tau(r))\) gives an extension that is constant in the inward radial direction before leaving the collar. Choose a further radial cutoff \(\lambda\), one there and zero on a neighbourhood of the disk centre. For \(a<j\) set
\[
 \widetilde t_{aj}(r,\theta)=\lambda(r)t_{aj}(\tau(r),\theta),
 \qquad
 \widetilde t_{jj}(r,\theta)
   =\exp\bigl(\lambda(r)\log t_{jj}(\tau(r),\theta)\bigr).
 \tag{3.9}
\]
Where \(\tau\) is no longer needed, retain its constant value \(r_0\). The expressions are constant \(0\) off the diagonal and \(1\) on it near the centre, hence smooth there despite polar coordinates. All diagonal entries stay positive, and all original entries and their derivatives remain on the prescribed outer collar. Then
\[
 \widetilde e=n\,\widetilde Q\,\widetilde T
 \tag{3.10}
\]
is the required full extending frame. It retains every original Gram and triangular factor on the original collar.

Finally, the sign can be changed while preserving the adapted outer boundary conditions of Section 2. On a closed subarc of the \(A\)-arc, away from both corners, keep its first \(p-1\) frame vectors fixed and rotate two of the last \(q-1\) vectors by an angle from \(0\) to \(2\pi\), constant near the subarc endpoints. Such two vectors exist since \(q\geq3\). Use the same angle along the corresponding whole strip width, so the rotation is identity on the strip's end germs and extends by identity to the rest of \(C_0\). It preserves the \(A\) tangent block exactly and does not change the \(B\)-arc at all.

To check its sign for a nonorthogonal original frame, keep the comparison homotopy
\[
 R_s=Q\bigl((1-s)T+sI\bigr),\qquad 0\leq s\leq1.
 \tag{3.11}
\]
Every upper triangular diagonal entry is positive, so this is a homotopy through invertible matrices retaining the endpoints as stated. The loop sign is constant under it. Apply (3.11) also to \(R_s T_{\rm rot}\). At \(s=1\) the two orthogonal factors have lifts whose endpoints multiply, and (3.4)-(3.5) give the negative factor. Therefore
\[
 \epsilon(RT_{\rm rot})=-\epsilon(R).
 \tag{3.12}
\]
This is an exact comparison for the original full \(R\), not a replacement of it by \(Q\).

If the initial filling sign is negative, make this supported rotation once. Its restriction to the inner circle traverses one full rotation; reversing the circle direction has the same negative endpoint sign. The new sign is positive. Apply (3.10) and glue to the unchanged corner annulus using the complete common collar. This constructs the adapted full frame over the actual disk with both original corners, in both new \(d=6\) cases. Its adjustment changes only an auxiliary disk frame. The original handle framings are transported later by the actual ambient diffeomorphism.

## 4. The exact supported move in both normal blocks {#receiving-whitney-flow}

Write \(r=d-2=(p-1)+(q-1)\), and use the auxiliary model coordinates
\[
 (x,y,z_A,z_B)\in
 \mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^{p-1}\times\mathbb R^{q-1}.
 \tag{4.1}
\]
The original two-dimensional disk-to-model comparison is constructed in Sections 3-4 of the [supported-move chapter](whitney-move-with-controlled-support.md#move-original-disk). It is a comparison of two-dimensional corner disks and their full collars, so its formulas have no ambient-rank dependence. Retain its arbitrary positive \(R\), both original corner germs, its polar radius and its complete collar-extension map. In this model put
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \phi(x)&=R^2-x^2,\\
 D_R&=\{(x,y,0,0):-R\leq x\leq R,\ 0\leq y\leq\phi(x)\},\\
 A_0&=\{(x,\phi(x),z_A,0)\},\qquad
 B_0=\{(x,0,0,z_B)\}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.2}
\]
Let \(\psi_D:D_R\to D\) be that complete original disk comparison. Its normal rank here is \(r\), with \(r=3\) or \(4\).

### 4.1. The full coordinates sending both model sheets to the originals

Use the finite coordinate embedding \(\iota\) and its tubular retraction \(\mathfrak r\) from the original disk proof. With the complete extending frame \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\), define
\[
 \mathcal E(w,z)=\mathfrak r\left(
   \iota\psi_D(w)+
   \sum_{\nu=1}^r z_\nu D\iota_{\psi_D(w)}e_\nu(\psi_D(w))
 \right).
 \tag{4.3}
\]
On the zero section its derivative is
\[
 D\mathcal E_{(w,0)}(\xi,\eta)
    =D\psi_D(\xi)+\sum_{\nu=1}^r\eta_\nu e_\nu .
 \tag{4.4}
\]
It is invertible because the disk tangent space and its full normal frame are complementary.

Extend the surface and frame slightly beyond the original boundary in their exact local quadrant and strip charts. On a smaller corner neighbourhood keep the original corner extension exclusively. Away from these smaller sets, combine their Euclidean \(\iota\)-images by a partition of unity and apply \(\mathfrak r\). The extensions agree on the disk, so their values and every derivative there agree: the terms differentiating the weights sum to zero. Project the extended frame into the normal bundle of the extended surface, retaining its exact original values on the disk. Independence and rank persist on a smaller neighbourhood.

The inverse function theorem and compactness give one open neighbourhood of the compact zero section on which (4.3) is an embedding. If arbitrarily small such neighbourhoods had equal-image pairs, limits would lie on the zero section; its injectivity makes their limits equal, and its local inverse then excludes the pairs. Thus (4.3) gives actual ambient coordinates, including outside both corners.

Let \(K_c\) be the exact map from the model corner chart to the original transverse chart (1.7), at \(c=a,b\), incorporating the prescribed disk comparison. The map \(g_c=\mathcal E^{-1}K_c\) fixes the zero section. Its normal quotient derivative is identity, because the frame there was the projection of those same original corner fields. Its tangential derivative can contain a full \(2\)-by-\(r\) shear \(A_c(w)\). Integral Taylor expansion gives
\[
 g_c(w,z)=
 \left(w+A_c(w)z+\sum_{\mu,\nu=1}^r z_\mu z_\nu B_{\mu\nu}(w,z),
       z+\sum_{\mu,\nu=1}^r z_\mu z_\nu C_{\mu\nu}(w,z)\right).
 \tag{4.5}
\]
Each vector coefficient is retained. For the transverse dilation
\(\Delta_s(w,z)=(w,sz)\), the exact conjugate extends smoothly to \(s=0\):
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 g_{c,s}(w,z)=\bigg(&w+sA_c(w)z+
           s^2\sum_{\mu,\nu}z_\mu z_\nu B_{\mu\nu}(w,sz),\\
                  &z+s\sum_{\mu,\nu}z_\mu z_\nu C_{\mu\nu}(w,sz)\bigg),\\
 Dg_{c,s}|_{z=0}
   &=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&sA_c\\0&I_r\end{pmatrix}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.6}
\]
For \(s>0\) it is \(\Delta_s^{-1}g_c\Delta_s\); at \(s=0\) it is identity. The last determinant is one. Compactness and the parameter-dependent inverse function theorem give uniform diffeomorphism germs for all \(s\in[0,1]\). Cut off their velocity \(\partial_s g_{c,s}\circ g_{c,s}^{-1}\), equal to it on all trajectories from a smaller required corner neighbourhood. Its flow \(G_c\) agrees there at time one with the entire \(g_c\), not just its derivative. The velocity vanishes on the disk and has zero normal quotient derivative there; the cutoff preserves these facts. Choose the two corner supports disjoint.

Now \(\mathcal E_1=\mathcal E G_aG_b\) agrees with both complete \(K_c\), fixes the prescribed disk map and retains its full normal quotient frame. Along the interior \(A\)-arc use base coordinates \((s,t)\), with that arc at \(t=0\). The original sheet is the unique graph
\[
 (s,h_A(s,z_A),z_A,k_B(s,z_A)).
 \tag{4.7}
\]
The graph functions vanish at \(z_A=0\), and \(D_{z_A}k_B(s,0)=0\), because the first \(p-1\) normal frame vectors span the projected \(A\) directions. The full derivative \(D_{z_A}h_A(s,0)\) is retained. The inverse function theorem gives this graph uniformly along a compact interior arc. Near the corners every graph function vanishes as a germ because those complete sheet charts already match.

The full graph shear and its vector field are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 (s,t,z_A,z_B)&\longmapsto
      (s,t+h_A(s,z_A),z_A,z_B+k_B(s,z_A)),\\
 X_A&=h_A(s,z_A)\partial_t+
       \sum_{\nu=1}^{q-1}(k_B)_\nu(s,z_A)\partial_{(z_B)_\nu}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.8}
\]
Its inverse subtracts the same functions, whose arguments remain fixed. Its model-sheet trajectories are
\[
 (s,\tau h_A(s,z_A),z_A,\tau k_B(s,z_A)),\qquad 0\leq\tau\leq1.
 \tag{4.9}
\]
For a sufficiently small closed transverse disk these trajectories are compactly contained in the required arc neighbourhood. A cutoff equal to one near their union and zero outside a larger neighbourhood therefore gives a global supported flow \(G_A\) agreeing exactly with (4.8) there. It fixes the disk; its normal quotient derivative is identity, because \(Dk_B(s,0)=0\). Its full tangent shear \(Dh_A\) remains.

Along the interior \(B\)-arc the exact graph and shear are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &(s,h_B(s,z_B),k_A(s,z_B),z_B),\qquad
       D_{z_B}k_A(s,0)=0,\\
 &(s,t,z_A,z_B)\longmapsto
       (s,t+h_B(s,z_B),z_A+k_A(s,z_B),z_B).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.10}
\]
The same explicit trajectory cutoff gives \(G_B\), with its complete tangent derivatives retained. Its support and that of \(G_A\) are disjoint, since the closed interior arc portions are disjoint and both corrections vanish near the corners. Consequently
\[
 \Psi=\mathcal E_1G_AG_B
 \tag{4.11}
\]
maps both whole model sheet germs to the original ones along the entire disk.

There are no additional sheet branches in a sufficiently small open neighbourhood \(U\) of \(D_R\). Otherwise extra-branch points tending to the compact disk would limit either to its interior, which avoids both sheets, or to its boundary, where the complete graph and corner charts describe the whole embedded sheet. Both are impossible. The other sphere cores are compact and miss \(D\), including its boundary, so decrease \(U\) to avoid them too. We have proved the full equalities
\[
 \Psi^{-1}(A)\cap U=A_0\cap U,\qquad
 \Psi^{-1}(B)\cap U=B_0\cap U,
 \tag{4.12}
\]
with no assertion limited to tangent spaces.

### 4.2. Every cutoff and the exact pair cancellation

Choose positive parameters \(d_0,b_0\), retaining the original \(R\). These are auxiliary support parameters; the ambient dimension is still the integer \(d\). Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 u(x)&=4\phi(x)/d_0+2,&
 \mu(x)&=\chi(u(x)),&
 \delta(x)&=\mu(x)(\phi(x)+d_0),\\
 L(y)&=(y+2d_0)/d_0,&
 H(x,y)&=(\phi(x)+d_0-y)/d_0,&
 \eta(x,y)&=\chi(L(y))\chi(H(x,y)),\\
 Z(z)&=2-\frac{2}{b_0^2}\sum_{\nu=1}^{r}z_\nu^2,&
 \zeta(z)&=\chi(Z(z)),&
 v(x,y,z)&=\delta(x)\eta(x,y)\zeta(z).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.13}
\]
The field is \(-v\partial_y\). Its support is contained in
\[
 K_{d_0,b_0}=
 \left\{x^2\leq R^2+d_0/2,\quad
 -2d_0\leq y\leq R^2-x^2+d_0,\quad
 \sum_{\nu=1}^{r}z_\nu^2\leq b_0^2\right\}.
 \tag{4.14}
\]
As \(d_0,b_0\) decrease to zero, any limiting point in these compact sets lies in \(D_R\). Therefore positive choices exist with \(K_{d_0,b_0}\subset U\), by the compact subsequence argument of the earlier supported move. Its complete flow is
\[
 \mathcal H_t(x,y,z)=(x,Y_t(x,y,z),z),\qquad
 \dot Y_t=-v(x,Y_t,z),\qquad Y_0=y.
 \tag{4.15}
\]
Compact support gives existence for all time; uniqueness gives inverse \(\mathcal H_{-t}\).

On \(A_0\), the full exact formula is
\[
 \mathcal H_t(x,\phi(x),z_A,0)
  =(x,\phi(x)-t\delta(x)\zeta(z_A,0),z_A,0),
 \quad0\leq t\leq1.
 \tag{4.16}
\]
Indeed \(\delta\geq0\), and where it is nonzero the entire vertical segment lies between \(-d_0\) and \(\phi(x)\): its endpoint is
\((1-\mu)\phi-\mu d_0\geq-d_0\).
Both factors of \(\eta\) are identically one there. Substitution proves (4.16); where \(\delta=0\) it is the constant solution.

Its intersection with the fixed comparison sheet \(B_0\) requires \(z_A=z_B=0\). If \(\phi<0\), the vertical coordinate remains negative. If \(\phi\geq0\), then \(\mu=1\), and the exact equation is
\[
 (1-t)(R^2-x^2)-td_0=0.
 \tag{4.17}
\]
The two solutions before cancellation and its unique time are
\[
 x_\pm(t)=\pm\sqrt{R^2-\frac{td_0}{1-t}},\qquad
 0\leq t<t_*=\frac{R^2}{R^2+d_0}.
 \tag{4.18}
\]
At \(t=t_*\) they meet at \(x=0\); for \(t>t_*\) none remains. The cutoff transition has \(\phi<0\), so contributes no extra intersection.

Orient \(A_0\) by \((x,z_A)\), \(B_0\) by \((x,z_B)\), and the ambient coordinates by \((x,y,z_A,z_B)\). Subtract the first \(A\)-tangent column from the first \(B\)-tangent column. This yields \(-f_t'(x)\partial_y\), where \(f_t(x)=(1-t)(R^2-x^2)-td_0\). Moving that column past the \(p-1\) \(A\)-normal columns gives the complete intersection determinant
\[
 \det(TA_t,TB_0)=(-1)^p f_t'(x)
             =(-1)^p[-2(1-t)x].
 \tag{4.19}
\]
Thus the \(p=3\) case has the opposite model convention from the earlier \(p=2\) case. The two signs remain opposite. At the meeting point the retained derivatives are
\[
 \partial_x^2 f_{t_*}(0)=-\frac{2d_0}{R^2+d_0}\ne0,\qquad
 \partial_t f_t(0)=-(R^2+d_0)\ne0.
 \tag{4.20}
\]
The original sheet signs multiply (4.19) by the determinant sign of \(\Psi\) and the two fixed signs comparing the model sheet parameters to their original orientations. This retains exactly the original pair (2.1).

### 4.3. The full derivative, original framings and cobordism map

Every cutoff derivative remains in
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \delta'(x)&=-2x\left[\chi(u)+
             \frac{4(\phi+d_0)}{d_0}\chi'(u)\right],\\
 \eta_x&=-\frac{2x}{d_0}\chi(L)\chi'(H),\\
 \eta_y&=\frac{\chi'(L)\chi(H)-\chi(L)\chi'(H)}{d_0},\\
 \zeta_{z_\nu}&=-\frac{4z_\nu}{b_0^2}\chi'(Z),\\
 v_x&=\delta'\eta\zeta+\delta\eta_x\zeta,\quad
 v_y=\delta\eta_y\zeta,\quad
 v_{z_\nu}=\delta\eta\zeta_{z_\nu}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.21}
\]
Put
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 J_t&=\exp\left(-\int_0^t v_y(x,Y_s,z)\,ds\right)>0,\\
 \partial_yY_t&=J_t,\qquad
 \partial_xY_t=-J_t\int_0^t\frac{v_x(x,Y_s,z)}{J_s}\,ds,\\
 \partial_{z_\nu}Y_t&=-J_t\int_0^t
                   \frac{v_{z_\nu}(x,Y_s,z)}{J_s}\,ds .
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.22}
\]
Differentiating (4.15) and then dividing by \(J_t\) proves each formula with its zero initial derivative. The full matrix is
\[
 D\mathcal H_t=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0\\
 \partial_xY_t&J_t&D_zY_t\\
 0&0&I_r
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \det D\mathcal H_t=J_t .
 \tag{4.23}
\]
All \(r\) mixed normal derivatives are included.

Push the vector field through \(\Psi\) and extend it by zero. Its global ambient isotopy \(H_t\) equals \(\Psi\mathcal H_t\Psi^{-1}\) on the support, with
\[
 DH_t|_{\Psi(w)}
   =D\Psi|_{\mathcal H_t(w)}D\mathcal H_t|_wD\Psi^{-1}|_{\Psi(w)}.
 \tag{4.24}
\]
Its determinant is
\[
 \det DH_t|_{\Psi(w)}
  =\frac{\det D\Psi|_{\mathcal H_t(w)}}{\det D\Psi|_w}\,J_t>0 .
 \tag{4.25}
\]
Both evaluations of the original coordinate derivative and their quotient remain. The signs agree because these points are joined by a trajectory in its coordinate domain.

Equations (4.12) and (4.16)-(4.20) show that \(H_1(A)\) loses exactly the selected two intersections with the fixed comparison \(B\), and creates none. All other sphere cores miss the support and are fixed on a neighbourhood. An injective ambient map fixing such a core cannot introduce a new intersection with it. The selected belt is the comparison set; the ambient isotopy need not fix that belt pointwise.

For every original whole attaching tube \(\varphi_\ell\) at this level, use
\[
 \varphi_{\ell,t}=H_t\varphi_\ell,\qquad
 D\varphi_{\ell,t}|_\xi
   =DH_t|_{\varphi_\ell(\xi)}D\varphi_\ell|_\xi .
 \tag{4.26}
\]
This carries the entire collection, retaining every domain, radius and mutual disjointness. The other framed cores remain unchanged because the ambient map is identity on their neighbourhoods, even if the outer parts of their thick tubes meet its support.

In the actual inward collar \(c:N'\times[0,L)\to W\) of the preceding cobordism, choose \(\beta=1\) near zero and zero near \(L\), and extend by
\[
 \widehat H_t(c(z,\rho))=c(H_{t\beta(\rho)}(z),\rho).
 \tag{4.27}
\]
The inverse uses \(H_{t\beta(\rho)}^{-1}\) at that same radius. Its full product-collar derivative is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 DH_{t\beta(\rho)}
   &t\beta'(\rho)\,\left.\partial_sH_s\right|_{s=t\beta(\rho)}\\
 0&1
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{4.28}
\]
Compose with the original collar derivatives. It fixes the incoming collar and agrees with the full outgoing gluing germs. Together with identity on each original parameter handle, it gives the exact diffeomorphism from the old attachments to those in (4.26). Transport every later attaching and collar map by this same map. For its final composite \(F\), retain \(G_{\rm new}=G_{\rm old}F^{-1}\) and the complete metric transformation \(DF^{-{\mathsf T}}g_{\rm old}DF^{-1}\), as in the higher-index slide chapter.

This proves the supported framed Whitney move in all three cases (1.1). Iteration terminates for any fixed pair of sphere systems: each move decreases the finite total number of intersection points by two, changes no intersection outside the selected support, and preserves all algebraic coefficients because the removed signs are opposite. Therefore every coefficient can be represented by exactly its absolute value of points, all of its sign. Sections 2–5 of the [actual Morse realization and middle-cancellation companion](realizing-framed-handles-and-middle-cancellation.md#middle-six-seven-reduction) now prove that actual-function and trajectory comparison before invoking Morse cancellation.

statement_as_printed: ### Exercise 1. A nonorthogonal rank-four frame and its corrected extension sign
complete_source_text:
### Exercise 1. A nonorthogonal rank-four frame and its corrected extension sign

In an auxiliary oriented normal frame retain the complete original matrix
\[
 R(\theta)=Q(\theta)T,\qquad
 Q(\theta)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,\operatorname{Rot}(\theta)),
 \quad
 T=\begin{pmatrix}
 2&1&4&-2\\0&3&1&5\\0&0&5&0\\0&0&0&5
 \end{pmatrix},
 \quad0\leq\theta\leq2\pi .
 \tag{5.1}
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Rot}(\theta)\) has columns \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) and \((-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)\). Decide whether this frame extends over a disk, and compute a correction fixing its first two original vectors and every Gram contribution.

Its determinant is \(2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot5=150>0\). With quaternion coordinates \((1,i,j,k)\), the matrix \(Q\) is conjugation by \(\cos(\theta/2)+i\sin(\theta/2)\). Both entries of its pair lift equal this quaternion; they end at \((-1,-1)\). Thus \(\epsilon(R)=-1\) and the original frame does not extend.

Right-multiply the full matrix by \(Q(\theta)\). This rotates its last two original vectors and fixes its first two exactly. Put \(c=\cos\theta,s=\sin\theta\). The corrected matrix, without discarding \(T\), is
\[
 R'(\theta)=Q(\theta)TQ(\theta)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 2&1&4c-2s&-4s-2c\\
 0&3&c+5s&-s+5c\\
 0&0&5\cos(2\theta)&-5\sin(2\theta)\\
 0&0&5\sin(2\theta)&5\cos(2\theta)
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{5.2}
\]
Its determinant is still \(150\). Equation (3.12) gives
\(\epsilon(R')=(-1)(-1)=1\), so the exact full frame extends by (3.9)-(3.10). The original and corrected Gram matrices are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 R^{\mathsf T}R&=T^{\mathsf T}T=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 4&2&8&-4\\
 2&10&7&13\\
 8&7&42&-3\\
 -4&13&-3&54
 \end{pmatrix},\\
 (R')^{\mathsf T}R'&=Q(\theta)^{\mathsf T}
       (T^{\mathsf T}T)Q(\theta).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{5.3}
\]
Thus all mixed Gram terms are present. The correction did not turn the original frame into an orthonormal one. For the supported arc construction replace \(\theta\) by \(2\pi\lambda(s)\), where \(\lambda\) is the actual smooth step from zero to one, constant on neighbourhoods of the subarc endpoints. It then agrees with the identity with every derivative on those endpoint germs.

statement_as_printed: ### Exercise 2. The three-dimensional sheet sign in a six-dimensional level
complete_source_text: ### Exercise 2. The three-dimensional sheet sign in a six-dimensional level Take the model \((d,p,q)=(6,3,3)\) with \(R=3\), \(d_0=2\), and the full cutoff (4.13) on a neighbourhood containing its compact support. Retain \(b_0>0\). Calculate the two core intersections at time \(t=\tfrac12\), their original model determinant signs, and the cancellation time. At the core \(z_A=z_B=0\), \(\zeta=1\). In the region where intersections are possible \(\mu=1\), and \(\eta\) is one on the whole trajectory. Thus \[ t_*=\frac{9}{11},\qquad x_\pm(1/2)=\pm\sqrt{9-2}=\pm\sqrt7. \tag{5.4} \] The slope of the moved sheet there is \[ -2(1-\tfrac12)x=-x. \tag{5.5} \] The ordered tangent determinant includes \((-1)^p=-1\), so (4.19) gives \(x\): it is negative at \(-\sqrt7\) and positive at \(+\sqrt7\). The earlier five-dimensional \((p,q)=(2,3)\) convention would give the opposite signs and cannot be substituted. Along these core tracks all first derivatives of the flat cutoff factors \(\eta,\zeta\) vanish. Hence (4.22) gives \(J_t=1\), \(D_zY_t=0\), and \(\partial_xY_t=2tx\) for the derivative at fixed original \(y\). The derivative along the original curved sheet is the full chain-rule expression \[ \partial_xY_t+\partial_yY_t\,\phi'(x) =2tx-2x=-2(1-t)x. \tag{5.6} \] This verifies (5.5) without omitting the derivative of the original sheet. At cancellation the exact second and time derivatives are \[ \partial_x^2 f_{t_*}(0)=-\frac4{11},\qquad \partial_t f_t(0)=-11. \tag{5.7} \] They are both nonzero, so the unique event is the stated pair tangency. In the cutoff transition \(\phi<0\), the vertical flow is nonincreasing and cannot create another intersection. The plots show the exact core equation from Exercise 2 on the displayed original interval. Their signs include the full ordered-tangent determinant (4.19). Every omitted drawing direction remains in (4.21)-(4.26). The lower panel records the full frame comparison (3.8)-(3.12); it does not discard the triangular or Gram factors.

## 1. The original stages and the moving handle {#higher-slide-stages}

Use the ordered presentation and notation of [the integral handle-chain chapter](integral-handle-chains-and-signed-incidences.md#handle-filtration). Let \(2\leq k\leq n-2\). Assume the boundary \(N=\partial_+A_{k-1}\) is connected. The application has \(n=6\) or \(7\). Choose different index-\(k\) labels \(i,j\); \(i\) is moving and \(j\) is the target. Their original domains remain
\[
 H_\nu=D^k_{r_\nu}\times D^{n-k}_{s_\nu},
 \qquad
 \varphi_\nu:S^{k-1}_{r_\nu}\times D^{n-k}_{s_\nu}\longrightarrow N,
 \qquad r_\nu,s_\nu>0.
 \tag{1.1}
\]
Every displayed core orientation is its ordered original \(u\)-orientation. The sphere orientation is its outward boundary orientation. No radius or framing is replaced.

Attach all the index-\(k\) handles other than \(i\) first, and write
\[
 A=A_{k-1},\qquad
 B=A\cup\bigcup_{\nu\ne i}H_\nu,\qquad
 S=\partial_+B,\qquad
 \mathcal B_\nu=\{0\}\times S^{n-k-1}_{s_\nu}\subset S .
 \tag{1.2}
\]
These attachments have disjoint original thick images. Their interchange therefore uses exactly the disjoint-attachment comparison already constructed in the [arrangement chapter](rearranging-the-original-framed-handles.md). In particular \(A_k=B\cup H_i\) is the original \(k\)-stage with its original maps.

The complement diffeomorphism, applied on the disjoint handle regions, is
\[
 P:S\setminus\bigcup_{\nu\ne i}\mathcal B_\nu
   \longrightarrow
 N\setminus\bigcup_{\nu\ne i}L_\nu,\qquad
 L_\nu=\varphi_\nu(S^{k-1}_{r_\nu}\times\{0\}).
 \tag{1.3}
\]
On the \(\nu\)-th original positive face it is
\[
 P(u,v)=
 \varphi_\nu\left(\frac{r_\nu}{\|u\|}u,
                  \frac{F_\nu(\|u\|)}{s_\nu}v\right),
 \qquad u\ne0,\quad \|v\|=s_\nu .
 \tag{1.4}
\]
Here \(F_\nu\), all its cutoff and seam terms, and the full rounding comparisons are those of [the belt-complement proof](belt-sphere-complements-and-the-whitney-disk.md), Section 1, and the arrangement chapter, Section 1. It is the identity on the common exterior. Its derivative includes the derivative of both radial factors, \(D\varphi_\nu\), and both rounding derivatives, exactly as in that proof; these factors will be composed, not absorbed into a new framing.

The right side of (1.3) is connected. Indeed, a path in connected \(N\) can be perturbed relative its endpoint collars off the finite \((k-1)\)-dimensional cores: the possible intersection dimension is
\[
 1+(k-1)-(n-1)=k-n+1<0.
 \tag{1.5}
\]
The finite chart-value perturbation and Sard argument in the belt-complement proof give this relative perturbation. Consequently the left side of (1.3) is connected too. The moving full tube starts in the common exterior, since its original thick attaching image is disjoint from every other thick image.

## 2. The one-crossing ambient isotopy {#higher-slide-crossing}

In the target's positive face choose original coordinates
\[
 (x,\zeta)\in\mathbb R^k\times\mathbb R^{n-k-1},
 \qquad
 (x,\zeta)\longmapsto (x,y(\zeta)),
 \quad y(0)=y_*\in S^{n-k-1}_{s_j}.
 \tag{2.1}
\]
The belt equation is \(x=0\). Choose \(\ell,\varepsilon,d_0>0\) so that the closure of the box
\[
 \|x'\|<2\ell,\qquad |x_k|<3\varepsilon,\qquad
 \|\zeta\|<d_0,\qquad x'=(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}),
 \tag{2.2}
\]
lies in this face and misses every other belt. Arrange a small positively oriented patch of the moving attaching sphere as
\[
 v\longmapsto(v,-\sigma\varepsilon,0),
 \qquad \|v\|\leq\ell,\qquad \sigma\in\{1,-1\}.
 \tag{2.3}
\]
Here positive refers to the original boundary orientation of \(S^{k-1}_{r_i}\).

We give the actual ambient construction of this arrangement. In the connected complement in (1.3), choose a path from the selected moving patch to the proposed endpoint, with its interior disjoint from the moving sphere. The relative avoidance dimension for this extra exclusion is again (1.5). The path can be made embedded: the dimension of two path parameters is two, strictly less than \(n-1\geq3\); perturb the values independently near two separated source points, and use compact local injectivity near the diagonal. Keep short endpoint germs fixed.

Prescribe a product chart around the initial embedded patch and the exact product chart (2.3) at the final patch. Choose the path transverse to the patch in these end charts and straight on its end germs. Extend a transverse frame along the interval. Its \((k-1)\) designated vectors carry the positively oriented patch coordinates. There is at least one other transverse direction, since \(n-k-1\geq1\); choosing its endpoint sign if necessary makes the two full transverse frames belong to the same component of the invertible-frame space. A smooth frame along the interval with the specified endpoints then exists. One direct construction is to retain each Gram matrix, deform its positive square root along the convex cone of positive matrices, and join the resulting orthogonal frames by successive rotations in coordinate two-planes. The determinant signs agree by the chosen remaining vector. Restoring the retained square roots gives the required frames with their exact endpoint values.

Choose an auxiliary connection flat in the two prescribed end charts, by a partition of unity on its coefficients. The normal exponential map along the path gives
\[
 J(s,w)=\exp_{c(s)}\left(\sum_{\mu=1}^{n-2}w_\mu E_\mu(s)\right).
 \tag{2.4}
\]
For a sufficiently small fixed transverse radius this is an embedding. The derivative is invertible on its zero section. Failure of injectivity for every smaller radius would give two limiting points of the embedded path with equal image; if their parameters differ this contradicts its injectivity, and if they agree it contradicts a local inverse chart. This proves the assertion, including a uniform radius by compactness. The flat end connections and constant end frames give exactly the prescribed product germs.

A vector field in this chart equal to \(\partial_s\) on the full track of a smaller patch, with a smooth cutoff supported in a larger compact corridor, transports the patch by \((s,w)\mapsto(s+t,w)\) on that track. The corridor misses all the belts. The field extends by zero and its flow is a diffeomorphism. It carries the entire original attaching tube by its full derivative. At the endpoint the rest of the moved sphere misses a sufficiently small crossing box: the endpoint sphere is embedded, and the complement of a slightly larger parameter patch is compact and disjoint from the selected point. Take the box inside this separation neighbourhood. If necessary first shrink the selected image patch by an ambient coordinate dilation with cutoff; its original parameter map is carried by that dilation and is never deleted. Thus the whole operation arranges (2.3) and has no belt crossing.

Choose \(\chi:\mathbb R^{k-1}\to[0,1]\), equal to one on \(\|v\|\leq\ell/3\) and zero on \(\|v\|\geq2\ell/3\). Choose \(\eta(x_k,\zeta)\), equal to one on a neighbourhood of \([-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\times\{0\}\) and supported strictly inside the last two factors of (2.2). The exact crossing field is
\[
 Y_\sigma
   =2\sigma\varepsilon\,\chi(x')\eta(x_k,\zeta)\,\partial_{x_k}.
 \tag{2.5}
\]
Its flow \(I_t\), extended by the identity outside the box, satisfies
\[
 I_t(v,-\sigma\varepsilon,0)
  =(v,-\sigma\varepsilon+2\sigma\varepsilon t\chi(v),0),
 \quad 0\leq t\leq1.
 \tag{2.6}
\]
The displayed track remains where \(\eta=1\), so substitution into the differential equation proves this formula. Only the point \((v,t)=(0,\tfrac12)\) meets the target belt. No other part of the sphere meets any belt, by the preceding separation and the support. The normal derivative with the ordered trace parameters \((v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1},t)\) is
\[
 D x=
 \begin{pmatrix}I_{k-1}&0\\0&2\sigma\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}
 \quad\text{at that crossing}.
 \tag{2.7}
\]
Its determinant sign is exactly \(\sigma\).

On the inner track neighbourhood, where \(\eta\) is identically one, the complete derivative is
\[
 D I_t=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 I_{k-1}&0&0\\
 2\sigma\varepsilon t\,D\chi&I_1&0\\
 0&0&I_{n-k-1}
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{2.8}
\]
On the rest of the whole tube the derivative is the unique solution of
\[
 \frac{d}{dt}D I_t=(D Y_\sigma)_{I_t}D I_t,\qquad D I_0=I,
 \quad
 D Y_\sigma=2\sigma\varepsilon\,\partial_{x_k}
       \otimes(\eta\,d\chi+\chi\,d\eta).
 \tag{2.9}
\]
Both cutoff contributions remain. These equations transport every original normal vector, including any component tangent to the core.

At the endpoint the moving core is disjoint from every belt. The ambient tube compression proved in the arrangement chapter, Section 2, therefore makes its entire original thick attaching image disjoint from them: choose a neighbourhood of the compact core missing the closed belts and compress the image into it. That compression fixes the core and retains its whole original parameter domain. Pull the whole compressed tube through \(P\). It is a compact subset of \(N\setminus\bigcup L_\nu\). In each original target tube its normal distance from \(L_\nu\) has a positive lower bound on the part needing motion. Apply the exact outward radial flow of the arrangement chapter, Section 3, with support in a small extension of that tube and with endpoint radius greater than \(s_\nu\). The original tubes and their small extensions can be chosen disjoint. Thus these finitely many flows move the whole moving image into the common exterior.

These return flows fix a neighbourhood of each \(L_\nu\). Their conjugates by (1.3) extend by the identity across the belts and have no belt crossing. Their derivatives are exactly
\[
 D(P^{-1})_{\mathcal R(P(z))}
       \,D\mathcal R_{P(z)}\,DP_z,
 \tag{2.10}
\]
where \(\mathcal R\) is the actual product of the disjoint radial flows, with each original radius and cutoff retained in its construction. Time-reparametrize the patch transport, crossing, compression and return flows to be constant near their endpoints and concatenate them. This gives an ambient isotopy \(T_t:S\to S\), from the identity, whose final whole moving tube is again in the common exterior. Its core trace has precisely the one transverse crossing (2.7).
