## 2. The actual coalgebra and its cofree comodules {#cooperation-actual-coalgebra}

Let \(u:k\to\Gamma\) be induced by \(1_H\wedge\eta\), and let \(\epsilon:\Gamma\to k\) be induced by \(\mu\). The original degree-zero calculation gives
\[
 \Gamma_n=0\quad(n<0),\qquad \Gamma_0=k\,1,
 \qquad\epsilon u=1_k.
 \tag{2.1}
\]
Every \(\Gamma_n\) is finite-dimensional, by Sections 10–11 of the Adams chapter. Define the cooperation and the coaction by the actual maps
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Delta&=Q_H^{-1}\,\pi_*(1_H\wedge\eta\wedge1_H):
       \Gamma\longrightarrow\Gamma\otimes\Gamma,\\
 \rho_X&=Q_X^{-1}\,M(\eta\wedge1_X):
       M(X)\longrightarrow\Gamma\otimes M(X).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{2.2}
\]
The unit in both lines is inserted between the original coefficient factor and the remaining original spectrum. Using the other cross product \(P_X\) in (2.2) would give a different coordinate formula. Equation (1.7) is the explicit comparison that prevents that mistake.

We verify every coalgebra and comodule identity. The iterated version of \(Q_X\) on
\(\Gamma\otimes\Gamma\otimes M(X)\) starts with
\[
 (H_1\wedge H_2)\wedge(H_3\wedge H_4)\wedge(H_5\wedge X)
 \longrightarrow H_1\wedge\mu(H_2,H_3)\wedge\mu(H_4,H_5)\wedge X.
 \tag{2.3}
\]
The parentheses in its two successive constructions give the same stable map by the associativity of \(\mu\). Under this isomorphism both
\((\Delta\otimes1)\rho_X\) and \((1\otimes\rho_X)\rho_X\) are the map on homotopy groups which inserts two consecutive original units into \(H\wedge X\). This proves coassociativity. Taking \(X=H\) proves coassociativity of \(\Delta\). Applying \(\epsilon\) in the first tensor factor of (1.5) composes with multiplication of the first two resulting \(H\)-factors. Applied to (2.2), this multiplies an original factor by the inserted unit and gives its identity. Thus
\[
 (\epsilon\otimes1)\rho_X=1_{M(X)},\qquad
 (\epsilon\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\epsilon)\Delta=1_\Gamma.
 \tag{2.4}
\]
For the second coalgebra identity in (2.4), multiply the last two \(H\)-factors of \(H\wedge H\wedge H\); the same unit identity applies. Inserting a unit into \(u(1)\) and using (1.5) also gives \(\Delta u(1)=u(1)\otimes u(1)\). These are all the coalgebra axioms with the indicated coaugmentation and counit.

For a map of spectra \(f:X\to Y\), naturality of (1.5) and of the inserted unit proves
\[
 \rho_YM(f)=(1\otimes M(f))\rho_X.
 \tag{2.5}
\]
Consequently each \(M(f)\) is a map of the actual left \(\Gamma\)-comodules just constructed.

The isomorphism \(Q_X\) identifies the coaction on \(M(H\wedge X)\) with the cofree one:
\[
 \rho_{H\wedge X}Q_X
   =(1\otimes Q_X)(\Delta\otimes1).
 \tag{2.6}
\]
To check (2.6), start with the four labelled factors of (1.5). On its left side the inserted unit sits after \(H_1\), before \(\mu(H_2,H_3)\). On its right side, (2.2) inserts that unit between the first pair, and (2.3) subsequently multiplies \(H_2\) and \(H_3\). These are the same map, with the same factor order. Thus (2.6) does not require a splitting theorem for arbitrary \(H\)-modules.

Here is the extension property of a cofree comodule, with both maps. For a graded comodule \((N,\rho_N)\) and a graded vector space \(V\), the mutually inverse assignments are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma}(N,\Gamma\otimes V)
   &\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_k(N,V),
       &f&\longmapsto(\epsilon\otimes1)f,\\
 \operatorname{Hom}_k(N,V)
   &\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\Gamma}(N,\Gamma\otimes V),
       &g&\longmapsto(1\otimes g)\rho_N.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{2.7}
\]
The second map is a comodule map by coassociativity. Their two compositions are identities by the counit axiom and the defining equation for a comodule map. If \(N'\subset N\) is a graded subcomodule and a comodule map \(f':N'\to\Gamma\otimes V\) is given, first extend the linear map \((\epsilon\otimes1)f'\) to \(N\): choose a basis in each degree of \(N'\), extend it to one of \(N\), and assign zero to the added basis vectors. The second assignment in (2.7) then gives an actual comodule extension. This is the injectivity property used below, together with an explicit construction of the extension.

## 3. An exact resolution made from the original tower {#cooperation-original-resolution}

The full original fibre sequence, smashed on the right with \(F_s\), is
\[
 F_{s+1}\xrightarrow{\alpha\wedge1}F_s
 \xrightarrow{\eta\wedge1}W_s
 \xrightarrow{\partial\wedge1}\Sigma F_{s+1}.
 \tag{3.1}
\]
Its homology map from \(M(F_s)\) to \(M(W_s)\), expressed using \(Q_{F_s}\), is exactly \(\rho_{F_s}\). Equation (2.4) proves that it is injective. The same assertion in the next degree makes the preceding map in its long exact sequence zero. Therefore that original long exact sequence gives, in every degree, the short exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow M(F_s)
 \xrightarrow{\rho_{F_s}}\Gamma\otimes M(F_s)
 \xrightarrow{b_s}\Sigma M(F_{s+1})\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{3.2}
\]
Here \(b_s\) is the original connecting map in (3.1), with the suspension comparison of the homology groups included. The suspension comparison moves the original suspension coordinate past the coefficient factor. Its graded signs are \((-1)^j\) on a coefficient of degree \(j\), hence are \(1\) in this exact coefficient field. Thus (3.2) is a sequence of graded comodules with the grading shift shown. No splitting as comodules has been asserted; (2.4) supplies a splitting only after forgetting the coaction.

For explicit indices, define
\[
 V^s_t=M(F_s)_{t-s},\qquad
 I^s_t=M(W_s)_{t-s},\qquad
 I^s\cong\Gamma\otimes V^s.
 \tag{3.3}
\]
The cofree identification in (3.3) is \(Q_{F_s}\), including the original suspension maps. Write \(v_s:V^s\to I^s\) and \(b_s:I^s\to V^{s+1}\) for (3.2) after this shift. Then
\[
 D^s=v_{s+1}b_s:I^s\longrightarrow I^{s+1},
 \qquad D^{s+1}D^s=0.
 \tag{3.4}
\]
The last identity follows from \(b_{s+1}v_{s+1}=0\). Moreover \(b_s\) is surjective and \(v_{s+1}\) is injective, so
\[
 \ker D^s=\operatorname{im}v_s
           =\operatorname{im}D^{s-1}\quad(s\geq1).
 \tag{3.5}
\]
At \(s=0\), the kernel is \(v_0(V^0)=u(k)\). We have proved the exact augmented resolution
\[
 0\longrightarrow k\xrightarrow{u}I^0
 \xrightarrow{D^0}I^1\xrightarrow{D^1}I^2\longrightarrow\cdots,
 \tag{3.6}
\]
and every term is cofree by (2.6). This is a construction for the actual original tower.

To recover its first spectral-sequence differential, let
\[
 \delta_s:W_s\xrightarrow{\partial\wedge1}\Sigma F_{s+1}
                 \xrightarrow{\Sigma(\eta\wedge1)}\Sigma W_{s+1}.
 \tag{3.7}
\]
The fibre/cofibre square for \(F_{s+1}\to F_s\to\mathbb S\) identifies (3.7) with the connecting composite between the consecutive layers of the tower \(C_s\). In the mapping-cylinder proof of (1.5) in the Adams chapter, the first map collapses the middle cylinder onto its suspended first fibre, and the second is its quotient to the next layer. These are precisely the two maps of (3.7). A reversal of a connecting-map orientation multiplies the resulting group map by \(-1\); its image in \(k\) is again \(1\). Thus the original \(d_1\) on \(E_1^{s,t}=\pi_{t-s}W_s\) is the map induced by (3.7), with no convention-dependent coefficient remaining in \(\mathbb F_2\).

For a graded comodule \(N\), write
\[
 \operatorname{Prim}(N)_t
 =\{z\in N_t:\rho_N(z)=1\otimes z\}.
 \tag{3.8}
\]
This is the space of degree-\(t\) comodule maps from \(k\) with trivial coaction to \(N\). Equation (2.7) gives
\[
 \operatorname{Prim}(\Gamma\otimes V)_t=1\otimes V_t.
 \tag{3.9}
\]
In (3.3), the corresponding actual inclusion and evaluation maps are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \lambda_s:\pi_{t-s}(H\wedge F_s)&\longrightarrow I^s_t,
       &z&\longmapsto\pi_*(\eta\wedge1_{H\wedge F_s})(z),\\
 \operatorname{ev}_s:I^s_t&\longrightarrow\pi_{t-s}(H\wedge F_s),
       &y&\longmapsto\pi_*(\mu\wedge1_{F_s})(y).
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{3.10}
\]
Indeed (1.5) sends \(1\otimes z\) to the first map in (3.10); applying \(\epsilon\) to its first tensor factor is the second map. The unit identity gives \(\operatorname{ev}_s\lambda_s=1\). Its restriction to primitives is the inverse of \(\lambda_s\), by (3.9). Naturality of the unit with respect to (3.7), including its suspension comparison, gives
\[
 D^s\lambda_s=\lambda_{s+1}d_1.
 \tag{3.11}
\]
Equations (3.10)–(3.11) identify the actual first-page complex, with its specified maps, as
\[
 (E_1^{*,t},d_1)\cong\operatorname{Prim}(I^\bullet)_t.
 \tag{3.12}
\]

## 4. A second exact resolution, with every endpoint retained {#cooperation-full-contraction}

Retain the full coalgebra \(\Gamma\), its coaugmentation and its counit. Define the two actual linear projections
\[
 \bar\Gamma=\ker\epsilon,\qquad q=1_\Gamma-u\epsilon,
 \qquad a=u\epsilon(a)+q(a).
 \tag{4.1}
\]
Thus \(\Gamma=k1\oplus\bar\Gamma\), and the quotient by \(k1\) maps isomorphically to \(\bar\Gamma\) by \([a]\mapsto q(a)\), with inverse the quotient map. For \(a\in\bar\Gamma\), write its entire coproduct as
\[
 \Delta a=1\otimes a+a\otimes1+\bar\Delta a,
 \qquad \bar\Delta=(q\otimes q)\Delta|_{\bar\Gamma}.
 \tag{4.2}
\]
Equation (4.2) follows by applying both counits and (4.1), and retains both unit terms. Applying \(q\) in all three factors of the coassociativity identity for \(\Delta\) proves the coassociativity identity for \(\bar\Delta\).

Put
\[
 J^s=\Gamma\otimes\bar\Gamma^{\otimes s}\quad(s\geq0),
 \tag{4.3}
\]
with coaction \(\Delta\) on the first factor. Use bars to display the ordered last factors. With every sum interpreted linearly, define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 d_J\bigl(g\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]\bigr)
 &=\sum g_{(1)}\otimes[q(g_{(2)})|a_1|\cdots|a_s]\\
 &\quad+\sum_{i=1}^{s}\sum
 g\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_i'|a_i''|\cdots|a_s],
 \qquad\bar\Delta a_i=\sum a_i'\otimes a_i''.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.4}
\]
The general alternating coefficient of the second sum at position \(i\) is \((-1)^i\); its value here is \(1\). The first sum in (4.4) uses the full \(\Delta g\). In particular it includes its contribution with first factor \(1\). The term with second factor \(1\) maps to zero by \(q(1)=0\), a fact specified by (4.1), rather than an omitted contribution.

The differential is a comodule map: coassociativity checks the first sum in (4.4), and the other sums leave its cofree first factor in place. Its square is zero. More explicitly, terms which split two different bar positions occur twice, in the two possible orders. The two terms which split one position twice coincide by coassociativity of \(\bar\Delta\). The terms involving the leading first sum twice agree with the terms which apply that first sum and then split its new bar factor, by coassociativity of \(\Delta\) with the projection \(q\) on its last factors. Their coefficient is \(1+1=0\) in the original field. This exhausts every term in the square. Also \(d_Ju=0\).

Here is a complete contraction of the augmented underlying vector-space complex. Define
\[
 h_0(g)=\epsilon(g),\qquad
 h_s\bigl(g\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]\bigr)
   =\epsilon(g)a_1\otimes[a_2|\cdots|a_s]\quad(s\geq1).
 \tag{4.5}
\]
For \(s=0\), \(h_1d_J(g)=q(g)\), since \(\sum\epsilon(g_{(1)})q(g_{(2)})=q(g)\). Hence \(u h_0+h_1d_J=1\) by (4.1). For \(s\geq1\), the contribution of the leading term of \(h_{s+1}d_J\) is \(q(g)\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]\). Its term splitting \(a_1\) is
\(\epsilon(g)\sum a_1'\otimes[a_1''|a_2|\cdots|a_s]\).
The leading term of \(d_Jh_s\), using the whole of (4.2), is
\[
 \epsilon(g)\,1\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]
 +\epsilon(g)\sum a_1'\otimes[a_1''|a_2|\cdots|a_s].
 \tag{4.6}
\]
The second term in (4.6) cancels the displayed splitting term. Every splitting of a later \(a_i\) also occurs once in each composite and cancels. The two terms left are \(q(g)\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]\) and \(u\epsilon(g)\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]\), whose sum is the original element by (4.1). Therefore
\[
 d_Jh_s+h_{s+1}d_J=1_{J^s},
 \tag{4.7}
\]
with the just-specified augmented interpretation in degree zero. This proves the exactness of
\[
 0\longrightarrow k\xrightarrow{u}J^0\xrightarrow{d_J}J^1
       \xrightarrow{d_J}J^2\longrightarrow\cdots.
 \tag{4.8}
\]
Every term is cofree. The contraction is a vector-space contraction; it is not asserted to preserve the coaction.

Using (3.9), primitives of (4.3) have the form \(1\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]\). The first sum of (4.4) is then zero, because the full coproduct is \(1\otimes1\) and \(q(1)=0\). Consequently their complex is exactly
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 C^{s,t}(\Gamma)&=(\bar\Gamma^{\otimes s})_t,
        &C^{0,t}(\Gamma)&=\begin{cases}k&t=0,\\0&t\ne0,\end{cases}\\
 d_C[a_1|\cdots|a_s]
   &=\sum_{i=1}^s\sum[a_1|\cdots|a_i'|a_i''|\cdots|a_s].
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{4.9}
\]
The earlier explicit maps and contraction prove why this bar complex may be used. It has not been substituted for the original tower by a change of notation.

## 5. Actual comparison maps and both homotopies {#cooperation-chain-comparison}

We construct chain maps
\[
 A:I^\bullet\longrightarrow J^\bullet,
 \qquad B:J^\bullet\longrightarrow I^\bullet
 \tag{5.1}
\]
which are identities on the augmented \(k\). Start with \(A^0=B^0=1_\Gamma\), using \(F_0=\mathbb S\). Suppose \(A^j\) is defined through degree \(n\) and respects the differentials through degree \(n-1\). On the graded subcomodule \(\operatorname{im}D^n\subset I^{n+1}\), define
\[
 \psi(D^n x)=d_JA^n x.
 \tag{5.2}
\]
If \(D^nx=0\), exactness of (3.6) gives \(x=D^{n-1}y\), with the augmented case for \(n=0\). The right side of (5.2) is then \(d_J^2A^{n-1}y=0\). Thus \(\psi\) is well-defined and is a comodule map. Since \(J^{n+1}=\Gamma\otimes\bar\Gamma^{\otimes(n+1)}\), use the explicit extension in (2.7): extend \((\epsilon\otimes1)\psi\) degree by degree to a linear map \(\widetilde\psi:I^{n+1}\to\bar\Gamma^{\otimes(n+1)}\), assigning zero on a chosen complementary basis, and put
\[
 A^{n+1}=(1\otimes\widetilde\psi)\rho_{I^{n+1}}.
 \tag{5.3}
\]
Its restriction is \(\psi\), so it satisfies the next chain identity. This defines every map \(A^n\). Interchanging the two exact resolutions and using the cofree expression \(I^{n+1}\cong\Gamma\otimes V^{n+1}\) defines every \(B^n\) by the identical extension rule. These constructions are degree preserving and apply to the actual comodules, not to a presumed polynomial coalgebra. Their finite-dimensional graded pieces admit the indicated basis extensions by ordinary row reduction.

For completeness, we construct the homotopies, including their extension maps. Put \(E=BA-1_I\); it is a cochain map which is zero on the augmentation. Set \(H^0=0\). Suppose \(H^j:I^j\to I^{j-1}\) has been chosen through \(j=n\) and
\(E^{n-1}=D^{n-2}H^{n-1}+H^nD^{n-1}\).
The map
\[
 R^n=E^n-D^{n-1}H^n
 \tag{5.4}
\]
vanishes on \(\ker D^n\). For a vector \(D^{n-1}y\) in that kernel, the chain-map identity for \(E\) and the preceding homotopy identity give
\[
 R^nD^{n-1}
  =D^{n-1}E^{n-1}-D^{n-1}H^nD^{n-1}=0.
 \tag{5.5}
\]
The augmented case follows from \(E^0u=0\). Define the comodule map \(\theta:\operatorname{im}D^n\to I^n\) by \(\theta(D^nx)=R^nx\). Equation (5.5) proves it is well-defined. Its target is cofree, so extend it to \(H^{n+1}:I^{n+1}\to I^n\) by (2.7), just as in (5.3). It satisfies \(H^{n+1}D^n=R^n\). Induction proves
\[
 BA-1_I=DH+HD.
 \tag{5.6}
\]
Repeating this construction for \(AB-1_J\) gives a homotopy \(K\) with
\[
 AB-1_J=d_JK+Kd_J.
 \tag{5.7}
\]
All the maps used in (5.6)–(5.7) preserve coactions. Applying primitives therefore gives both actual chain homotopies. Equations (3.10) and (4.9) turn (5.1) into mutually inverse chain-homotopy equivalences between the original first-page complex and the displayed cobar complex. In particular,
\[
 E_2^{s,t}\cong H^{s,t}\bigl(C^{\bullet,*}(\Gamma),d_C\bigr)
 \tag{5.8}
\]
for the actual original mod-two tower and the actual cooperation coalgebra (2.2).

The maps at the cochain level depend on the stated complementary bases. This does not conceal an ambiguity in (5.8). The difference of any two comparison maps which agree on the augmentation is a chain map zero there. The very construction (5.4)–(5.7), with the two different maps in place of the composite and the identity, constructs a homotopy between them. Thus the induced map on cohomology is independent of those choices. For maps between two such constructions, the two naturality composites agree on the augmentation; applying the same argument proves their equality on cohomology. This proves the claimed comparison and its naturality, rather than merely matching vector-space dimensions.

![The two original cross-product maps and the exact cofree-resolution comparison.](../assets/actual-cooperation.svg)

The upper arrows retain all four labelled input factors. The lower comparison is the pair of chain maps and both homotopies proved in Section 5; the degree limits are proved in Section 7. The reproducible source is `draw_actual_cooperation.py`.

## 6. The original degree-zero classes and a constraint in degree two {#cooperation-original-diagonal}

The arithmetic chapter, (7.10)–(7.13), already proves, for the original ordered factors at \(p=2\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \pi_0F_s&=(2\mathbb Z)^{\otimes s},
 &e_s&=2\otimes\cdots\otimes2,
 &(q_s)_*e_s&=2^s,\\
 \pi_0C_s&=\mathbb Z/2^{s+1},
 &E_\infty^{s,s}&=2^s\mathbb Z_2/2^{s+1}\mathbb Z_2.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{6.1}
\]
The empty tensor is the original \(1\in\mathbb Z\). We keep every factor \(2\) and the original transition maps; the last group is one-dimensional over \(k\).

The degree-zero Hurewicz comparison in the Adams chapter gives
\[
 E_1^{s,s}=M(F_s)_0
      =k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}(2\mathbb Z)^{\otimes s}
      =k\{\bar1\otimes e_s\}.
 \tag{6.2}
\]
Every later page is a subquotient of this one-dimensional space. Its limiting subquotient in (6.1) is nonzero. A zero intermediate page would force every subsequent page and the limiting subquotient to be zero. Hence
\[
 E_r^{s,s}=k\quad\text{for every }s\geq0\text{ and }r\geq1,
 \tag{6.3}
\]
and no differential entering or leaving any of these one-dimensional groups is nonzero. This conclusion uses the proved tower convergence and actual stage extensions; it assumes no classification of operations.

For \(s=0\), the degree-one part of (3.2), together with (2.1), identifies the original connecting map as an isomorphism
\[
 b_0:\Gamma_1\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }M(B)_0
    =k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}2\mathbb Z.
 \tag{6.4}
\]
Let \(x\in\Gamma_1\) be its unique element mapping to \(\bar1\otimes2\). Thus \(\Gamma_1=kx\), with its generator tied to the original integer \(2\). Grading and (2.4) force its whole coproduct to be
\[
 \Delta x=1\otimes x+x\otimes1.
 \tag{6.5}
\]
For \(y\in\Gamma_2\), (2.1) and (4.2) allow only
\[
 \Delta y=1\otimes y+y\otimes1+c(y)x\otimes x,
 \qquad c(y)\in k.
 \tag{6.6}
\]
In the actual cobar complex, \(C^{2,2}=k[x|x]\) and \(C^{3,2}=0\). Its incoming differential from \(C^{1,2}=\Gamma_2\) sends \([y]\) to \(c(y)[x|x]\). If any \(c(y)\) were nonzero, then \(H^{2,2}(C)=0\). Equations (5.8) and (6.3) prove this is impossible. Therefore
\[
 c(y)=0\text{ for every }y\in\Gamma_2,
 \qquad \Delta y=1\otimes y+y\otimes1.
 \tag{6.7}
\]
This is a proved statement about the entire degree-two subspace, without an unproved assertion about its dimension. For every \(s\), the only words of total degree \(s\) and length \(s\) are multiples of \([x|\cdots|x]\). Their differentials are zero by (6.5). A word of length \(s-1\) and total degree \(s\) contains exactly one factor of degree two and every other factor of degree one; its differential is zero by (6.5) and (6.7). Thus
\[
 H^{s,s}(C)=k\{[x|\cdots|x]\},
 \tag{6.8}
\]
including the empty word for \(s=0\). This gives the explicit cobar representatives of the actual nonzero line. Since both sides of (5.8) on that line have exactly one nonzero element, its original generator \(\bar1\otimes e_s\) maps to the class shown in (6.8).

## 7. The exact degree range for the receiving degree-six calculation {#cooperation-degree-range}

We continue to use the full \(\Gamma\) and every term of its coproduct. Because \(\bar\Gamma_n=0\) for \(n\leq0\), a homogeneous word of length \(s\geq1\) and total degree \(s+n\) satisfies
\[
 \sum_{i=1}^s(|a_i|-1)=n,
 \qquad 1\leq |a_i|\leq n+1.
 \tag{7.1}
\]
For stem six, the cohomology at position \((s,s+6)\) is calculated from exactly three groups and two of the original differentials:
\[
 C^{s-1,s+6}(\Gamma)\xrightarrow{d_C}
 C^{s,s+6}(\Gamma)\xrightarrow{d_C}
 C^{s+1,s+6}(\Gamma).
 \tag{7.2}
\]
For the incoming group of positive length, (7.1) has excess \(7\), so every factor has degree at most \(8\). For the middle group it has excess \(6\), giving degree at most \(7\). For the outgoing group it has excess \(5\), giving degree at most \(6\). The zero-length groups are exactly those in (4.9); negative lengths are zero. Hence every group and every matrix entry in (7.2), at every length \(s\), is determined by
\[
 \Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\ldots,\Gamma_8,
 \quad\text{and the full maps}\quad
 \Delta:\Gamma_d\longrightarrow
       \bigoplus_{i+j=d}\Gamma_i\otimes\Gamma_j
       \quad(0\leq d\leq8).
 \tag{7.3}
\]
No positive-degree term outside this range can enter (7.2): its factor would already contribute excess at least \(8\), exceeding all three displayed excesses. The unit terms in each map of (7.3) remain the two terms of (4.2), with their exact projection to (4.9). This is a support theorem for the full original calculation, and does not discard a factor or assert that a finite quotient is the original cooperation algebra.

The same argument for stem five gives factor bounds \(7,6,5\) in its incoming, middle and outgoing groups respectively. Thus the degree-six result and the degree-five differential targets both use the same actual range (7.3). The word length is still unbounded; this proof does not replace an all-length calculation by finitely many tested lengths.

There is also an exact map for a possible coproduct convention change. Let \(\Gamma^{\mathrm{cop}}\) have the original vector space, coaugmentation and counit and coproduct \(\tau\Delta\). At the actual prime two, define
\[
 R_s:C^{s,t}(\Gamma)\longrightarrow C^{s,t}(\Gamma^{\mathrm{cop}}),
 \qquad [a_1|\cdots|a_s]\longmapsto[a_s|\cdots|a_1].
 \tag{7.4}
\]
Reversing a term which splits \(a_i\) reverses both the position of that factor and the order of its two coproduct factors. Those are exactly the terms obtained by splitting the corresponding position using \(\tau\bar\Delta\). Their coefficients are the same in \(k\). Thus \(R_{s+1}d_C=d_CR_s\), and \(R_s^2=1\). Equation (7.4) proves a chain isomorphism, preserves both gradings, and fixes the representatives (6.8). It supplies a verified comparison if a source uses the opposite coproduct; it does not by itself identify either coalgebra with a source presentation.

### Exercise 8.1 The exact effect of choosing the other cross product

For the actual spectrum \(X\), compute \(P_X^{-1}M(\eta\wedge1_X)\). Compare its value on the nonzero original \(x\in\Gamma_1\), with \(X=H\), to the actual coproduct. Supply the invertible map between the two coordinate presentations.

**Solution.** Naturality of the full field cross product gives
\[
 P_X^{-1}M(\eta\wedge1_X)(m)=1\otimes m.
 \tag{8.1}
\]
Indeed write \(X=\mathbb S\wedge X\) and apply the cross product to the maps \(\eta:\mathbb S\to H\) and \(1_X\). The unit \(1\in M(\mathbb S)_0=k\) maps to \(1\in\Gamma_0\), and the other factor is the original \(m\). For \(X=H\) and \(m=x\), (8.1) is \(1\otimes x\). The actual \(Q_H\) presentation instead gives \(1\otimes x+x\otimes1\), by (6.5). Their difference is the nonzero tensor \(x\otimes1\). In particular the first expression cannot be the claimed coalgebra coproduct with both counits: applying \(1\otimes\epsilon\) to it gives zero, whereas that counit axiom would give \(x\).

The full connecting isomorphism, from the \(P\) coordinates to the \(Q\) coordinates, is
\[
 U_X=Q_X^{-1}P_X
     =(\chi\otimes1)P_X^{-1}T_XP_X,
 \qquad
 U_X^{-1}=P_X^{-1}T_XP_X(\chi\otimes1).
 \tag{8.2}
\]
The inverse identity follows from \(T_X^2=1\), \(\chi^2=1\), and the adjacent cancellations of \(P_X\) with \(P_X^{-1}\). This map retains the two original symmetries. Equations (2.2) and (8.1) prove
\[
 U_X(1\otimes m)=\rho_X(m),\qquad
 U_H(1\otimes x)=1\otimes x+x\otimes1.
 \tag{8.3}
\]
Thus the two presentations have an explicit invertible comparison, and the extra endpoint in the actual cooperation is accounted for.

### Exercise 8.2 A noncocommutative example with the full contraction

Consider the algebraic example \(G=k[x,y]\), with \(|x|=1\), \(|y|=3\), counit zero on both generators, and full coproducts
\[
 \Delta x=1\otimes x+x\otimes1,\qquad
 \Delta y=1\otimes y+x^2\otimes x+y\otimes1.
 \tag{8.4}
\]
Extend \(\Delta\) as an algebra map. Prove coassociativity, evaluate both sides of the contraction identity on \(v=1\otimes[y]\in J^1(G)\), and compute the effect of the reversal (7.4). This is an explicit algebraic example; an identification of \(G\) with the actual spectrum's cooperation algebra is not assumed.

**Solution.** Expanding the square of the first formula in (8.4) keeps the two mixed terms, whose coefficient is \(2=0\) in \(k\), and gives
\[
 \Delta(x^2)=1\otimes x^2+x^2\otimes1.
 \tag{8.5}
\]
Coassociativity on \(x\) follows by inserting the two units. On \(y\), both iterated coproducts give all six terms
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 1\otimes1\otimes y
 +1\otimes x^2\otimes x
 +x^2\otimes1\otimes x
 +1\otimes y\otimes1
 +x^2\otimes x\otimes1
 +y\otimes1\otimes1.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{8.6}
\]
Since both iterated coproducts are algebra maps, agreement on the two generators proves agreement on every polynomial. Both counit identities follow on the generators and then on all products. The term \(x^2\otimes x\) in (8.4) is not unchanged by interchange of factors, so the coproduct is not cocommutative.

Equations (4.4)–(4.5), with all endpoint terms of (8.4) included, give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 d_Jv&=1\otimes[x^2|x],
 &h_2d_Jv&=x^2\otimes[x],\\
 h_1v&=y,
 &d_Jh_1v&=1\otimes[y]+x^2\otimes[x].
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{8.7}
\]
The two identical terms \(x^2\otimes[x]\) have coefficient \(2=0\); their sum leaves exactly \(v\), proving \((d_Jh_1+h_2d_J)v=v\). In the primitive cobar complex, the calculation is \(d_C[y]=[x^2|x]\). The opposite coproduct gives \(d_C^{\mathrm{cop}}[y]=[x|x^2]\). Reversal sends the first displayed boundary to the second, as required by (7.4), while leaving the original one-letter word \([y]\) fixed.

complete_source_text: ## 1. The original Hopf algebra and the entire differential Work first over \(\mathbb F _2\). Define \[ H=\mathbb F _2[\zeta _1,\zeta _2,\ldots],\qquad |\zeta _i|=2^i-1,\qquad \zeta _0=1, \tag{1.1} \] with counit \(\epsilon(\zeta_i)=0\) for \(i>0\), and with the multiplicative coproduct \[ \Delta\zeta_i =\sum_{k=0}^{i}\zeta_{i-k}^{\,2^k}\otimes\zeta_k =\zeta_i\otimes1+1\otimes\zeta_i+ \sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\zeta_{i-k}^{\,2^k}\otimes\zeta_k . \tag{1.2} \] Both endpoint terms in the first sum are displayed in the second expression. The counit identities follow from them. Coassociativity follows on each generator because both iterated coproducts are the same full sum \[ \sum_{\substack{a,b,c\geq0\\a+b+c=i}} \zeta_a^{\,2^{b+c}}\otimes \zeta_b^{\,2^c}\otimes\zeta_c . \tag{1.3} \] Multiplicativity then proves it on every polynomial. No restriction to the first few generators is made in the definition. Put \(\overline H=\ker\epsilon\). A word of length \(s\) and internal degree \(t\) is denoted by \[ [m_1|\cdots|m_s]\in C^{s,t}(H) =(\overline H^{\otimes s})_t,\qquad \sum_{\nu=1}^{s}|m_\nu|=t . \tag{1.4} \] Here \(C^{0,0}=\mathbb F _2\), and the other length-zero components are zero. Write \[ \overline\Delta m=\Delta m-m\otimes1-1\otimes m. \tag{1.5} \] The two removed terms in (1.5) are exactly the displayed counit terms of the full coproduct. The differential is \[ d[m_1|\cdots|m_s] =\sum_{\nu=1}^{s}\ \sum_{\overline\Delta m_\nu =\sum a\otimes b} [m_1|\cdots|m_{\nu-1}|a|b|m_{\nu+1}|\cdots|m_s]. \tag{1.6} \] All coefficients are in \(\mathbb F _2\). It has bidegree \((1,0)\); hence it decreases the difference \(t-s\) by one. The equality \(d^2=0\) follows directly. Splittings at two different positions occur in both possible orders and cancel. The two orders of splitting one position agree by (1.3) and likewise cancel. Concatenation makes this a differential algebra. We will calculate \[ \mathcal H^{s,t}(H) =\frac{\ker(d:C^{s,t}\longrightarrow C^{s+1,t})} {\operatorname{im}(d:C^{s-1,t}\longrightarrow C^{s,t})}. \tag{1.7} \] **Theorem 1.1.** For the full Hopf algebra (1.1)–(1.2), \[ \mathcal H^{s,s+6}(H)= \begin{cases} \mathbb F _2\{[\zeta_1^4|\zeta_1^4]\},&s=2,\\ 0,&s\ne2. \end{cases} \tag{1.8} \] In particular the assertion includes arbitrarily large \(s\). The proof occupies Sections 2–5. Section 6 proves the corresponding vanishing at every odd prime. ## 2. A bounded filtration on every original internal degree For a nonnegative integer \(e\), let \(\alpha(e)\) be its number of nonzero binary digits. Define the weight of an original monomial and of an original word by \[ W\!\left(\prod_{i\geq1}\zeta_i^{e_i}\right) =\sum_{i\geq1}(2i-1)\alpha(e_i),\qquad W([m_1|\cdots|m_s])=\sum_{\nu=1}^{s}W(m_\nu). \tag{2.1} \] Let \(F_wC^{s,t}\) be the span of words of weight at most \(w\). This defines subspaces of the original complex; it does not change its monomials or differential. Binary carrying can only lower \(\alpha(e)+\alpha(f)\) when passing to \(\alpha(e+f)\). Consequently the weight of a product is no larger than the sum of the weights. In (1.2) applied to \(\zeta_i^{2^j}\), the two endpoint terms have weight \(2i-1\), while each interior term has weight \[ (2(i-k)-1)+(2k-1)=2i-2. \tag{2.2} \] It follows by multiplication that every term of \(\Delta m\) has total tensor weight at most \(W(m)\). Thus \(dF_w\subset F_w\). For a monomial of degree \(t\), its weight is at most its degree, since \[ 2i-1\leq2^i-1,\qquad \alpha(e_i)\leq e_i. \tag{2.3} \] Every nonunit monomial has degree at least one. Therefore, for fixed \(t\), \[ C^{s,t}=0\quad(s>t),\qquad 0=F_{-1}C^{s,t}\subset F_0C^{s,t}\subset\cdots \subset F_tC^{s,t}=C^{s,t}, \tag{2.4} \] and every space in (2.4) is finite dimensional. There is no infinite-filtration convergence assumption in the argument below. Here is the finite filtered-complex construction that we use. First take cohomology of the part of \(d\) preserving weight. A representative of weight \(w\) that survives this operation can be corrected by terms of weight \(w-1\). Its next obstruction is the component of its differential in weight \(w-1\). Iterating, the \(r\)-th obstruction decreases weight by \(r\), increases length by one and retains internal degree. At each step quotient by the obstructions already obtained from length \(s-1\). These are exactly changes of a representative by a boundary, with its highest nonzero weight treated first. To verify that this procedure computes (1.7), perform ordinary elimination in a basis ordered by weight, pairing each nonzero differential with its highest remaining target weight. Each pair is an acyclic two-dimensional summand and can be removed by the corresponding triangular basis change. The unpaired vectors are cocycles modulo boundaries. At a fixed \(t\), only finitely many pairs and weights occur by (2.4). Thus the procedure terminates and the surviving weight-graded vector space is the associated graded vector space of (1.7). A zero associated graded component is a zero cohomology group. A single one-dimensional component gives a one-dimensional cohomology group, with no additive extension over \(\mathbb F _2\). This also proves the convergence statement used here. We denote its pages by \(E_1,E_2,\ldots\), with \(E_1\) the cohomology of the weight-preserving differential and \(d_r\) the obstruction decreasing \(W\) by \(r\). ### The first page, with all generators retained In the associated graded Hopf algebra the elements \[ e_{ij}=\operatorname{gr}(\zeta_i^{2^j}),\qquad i>0,\ j\geq0, \tag{2.5} \] are primitive. They have square zero, since the square in the original algebra has weight \(2i-1\), strictly less than \(2(2i-1)\). Products of distinct binary factors give a basis. The associated graded Hopf algebra is therefore the tensor product of the primitive exterior algebras on all \(e_{ij}\), with \[ |e_{ij}|=2^j(2^i-1),\qquad W(e_{ij})=2i-1. \tag{2.6} \] The word “exterior” here includes its exact characteristic-two relation \(e_{ij}^2=0\). For completeness, the cobar cohomology of this coalgebra is polynomial. For one primitive exterior generator, the dual algebra is \(\mathbb F _2[u]/(u^2)\). The free resolution having one copy of this algebra in every nonnegative resolution degree, with every positive differential multiplication by \(u\), is exact: the kernel and image of multiplication by \(u\) are both the span of \(u\). Its degree-zero cokernel is \(\mathbb F _2\). Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}(-,\mathbb F _2)\) gives one zero-differential generator in every degree. The shift by one place in the free resolution represents its degree-one extension, and the successive shifts show that every power is nonzero. For finitely many generators, tensor these resolutions over the field. Exactness follows by decomposing each underlying vector-space complex into its degree-zero homology and two-term contractible pairs; tensoring a contractible pair remains contractible. The same degree-shift maps identify the cohomology ring as the polynomial algebra on one class for each generator. For the infinite tensor product, each fixed internal degree uses finitely many generators, so this argument applies degree by degree. Equivalently these are the cobar classes of the primitive factors: the bar resolution of the finite-degree dual algebra and the cobar complex are dual in each internal degree. The bar resolution is free and exact: its augmented complex contracts by moving the augmentation-ideal part of the leading algebra factor into the first bar slot; the multiplication term restores that part and the remaining terms cancel in pairs. The scalar part is restored by the augmentation term. Thus the resolution calculation computes the same cohomology. It follows that \[ E_1=\mathbb F _2[h_{ij}:i>0,\ j\geq0],\qquad (s,t,W)(h_{ij})=(1,2^j(2^i-1),2i-1). \tag{2.7} \] The weight drop (2.2), without discarding its summands, gives \[ d_1h_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}h_{i-k,j+k}h_{k,j}. \tag{2.8} \] The product order in a tensor representative is the order in (1.2); the product on \(E_1\) is commutative by the resolution computation. The differential on every polynomial follows by the Leibniz rule. ## 3. The first differential at every length The following letters retain an exact dictionary with the generators of (2.7): \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr} \text{letter}&x&y&a&z&b&c&w\\ \hline \text{generator}&h_{10}&h_{11}&h_{20}&h_{12}&h_{21}&h_{30}&h_{13}\\ t&1&2&3&4&6&7&8\\ t-s&0&1&2&3&5&6&7\\ W&1&1&3&1&3&5&1 \end{array} \tag{3.1} \] They are the only generators with \(t-s\leq7\). Every other generator has \(t-s\geq11\). Since all generator differences are nonnegative, an omitted generator cannot occur in any polynomial with difference at most seven. The unrestricted exponent of \(x\) is retained by working over \[ R=\mathbb F _2[x]. \tag{3.2} \] In this region (2.8) reads \[ d_1a=xy,\qquad d_1b=yz,\qquad d_1c=xb+az,\qquad d_1x=d_1y=d_1z=d_1w=0. \tag{3.3} \] Put \(B=a^2\) and \(u=xb+az\). Both are \(d_1\)-cycles. To show every kernel and image needed at difference six, here are the complete \(R\)-bases in differences five, six and seven: \[ \begin{array}{c|l} 5&y^5,\ y^3a,\ ya^2,\ y^2z,\ az,\ b\\ 6&y^6,\ y^4a,\ y^2a^2,\ a^3,\ y^3z,\ yaz,\ z^2,\ yb,\ c\\ 7&y^7,\ y^5a,\ y^3a^2,\ ya^3,\ y^4z,\ y^2az,\ a^2z,\ yz^2,\ y^2b,\ ab,\ yc,\ w . \end{array} \tag{3.4} \] Exhaustiveness follows by solving \[ e_y+2e_a+3e_z+5e_b+6e_c+7e_w=k,\qquad e_\bullet\geq0, \tag{3.5} \] for \(k=5,6,7\); \(x\) has difference zero and is already retained in \(R\). All nonzero differentials on these bases are \[ \begin{array}{c|l} 5& y^3a\mapsto xy^4,\quad az\mapsto xyz,\quad b\mapsto yz\\ 6& y^4a\mapsto xy^5,\quad a^3\mapsto xyB,\quad yaz\mapsto xy^2z,\quad yb\mapsto y^2z,\quad c\mapsto u\\ 7& y^5a\mapsto xy^6,\quad ya^3\mapsto xy^2B,\quad y^2az\mapsto xy^3z,\quad y^2b\mapsto y^3z,\quad ab\mapsto yu,\quad yc\mapsto yu . \end{array} \tag{3.6} \] Every basis element not listed has zero differential. Comparing coefficients over the integral domain \(R\) now gives \[ \begin{aligned} \ker(d_1|_5)&=R\{y^5,yB,y^2z,u\},\\ \operatorname{im}(d_1|_6)&=R\{xy^5,xyB,y^2z,u\},\\ \ker(d_1|_6)&=R\{y^6,y^2B,y^3z,z^2,yu\},\\ \operatorname{im}(d_1|_7)&=R\{xy^6,xy^2B,y^3z,yu\}. \end{aligned} \tag{3.7} \] For example, the coefficients of \(yaz\) and \(yb\) in a cycle must be in the ratio \(1:x\), which gives \(yu\). The independent \(b\) and \(az\) terms in the image of \(c\) force its coefficient to vanish in a difference-six cycle. The other displayed equalities follow one coefficient at a time from (3.6). Consequently \[ \begin{aligned} (E_2)_{t-s=5} &=(R/(x))\{y^5,yB\},\\ (E_2)_{t-s=6} &=(R/(x))\{y^6,y^2B\}\ \oplus\ R\{z^2\}. \end{aligned} \tag{3.8} \] These are module identities covering every power of \(x\), not a finite list of lengths. We also need two difference-seven cycles: \[ y^3B,\qquad v=ab+yc. \tag{3.9} \] The second is a cycle because \(d_1(ab)=yu=d_1(yc)\). Both classes are nonzero on \(E_2\). To verify this without assuming a table, set \(x=z=w=0\) in the polynomial algebra on (3.1). The induced differential on \(\mathbb F _2[y,a,b,c]\) is zero, whereas the images \(y^3a^2\) and \(ab+yc\) are nonzero. This detects that neither is a boundary. Boundaries into difference seven come from difference eight, where the same seven generators still suffice; the next omitted generator has difference eleven. Thus the projection argument covers every possible incoming boundary. Every monomial on \(E_1\) has \(W\equiv s\pmod2\), because all generator weights are odd. The same is true on \(E_2\). A differential increasing \(s\) by one and dropping weight by two cannot connect two such bidegrees. Therefore \(d_2=0\). The next possible differential is \(d_3\), which we now compute from the entire original cobar differential. ## 4. Two complete correcting cochains For the formulas in this section only, write \[ P=\zeta_1,\qquad Q=\zeta_2,\qquad T=\zeta_3. \tag{4.1} \] These letters do not change the original variables. The full coproducts are \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta P&=P\otimes1+1\otimes P,\\ \Delta Q&=Q\otimes1+P^2\otimes P+1\otimes Q,\\ \Delta T&=T\otimes1+Q^2\otimes P+P^4\otimes Q+1\otimes T. \end{aligned} \tag{4.2} \] Define the following seven-term cochain of length two and internal degree six: \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal B={}&[Q|Q]+[Q|P^3]+[P|P^2Q]+[P|P^5]\\ &+[PQ|P^2]+[P^3|Q]+[P^3|P^3]. \end{aligned} \tag{4.3} \] The only weight-six term is \([Q|Q]\). In the displayed order the seven weights are \(6,5,5,3,5,5,4\). Expanding (1.6) using (4.2) gives \[ d\mathcal B=[P^2|P^2|P^2]+[P|P|P^4]. \tag{4.4} \] Here is the complete term-by-term expansion; it also records every cancellation: \[ \begin{array}{c|l} [Q|Q]&[Q|P^2|P]+[P^2|P|Q]\\ [Q|P^3]&[Q|P|P^2]+[Q|P^2|P]+[P^2|P|P^3]\\ [P|P^2Q]&[P|Q|P^2]+[P|P^2|Q]+[P|P^2|P^3]+[P|P^4|P]\\ [P|P^5]&[P|P|P^4]+[P|P^4|P]\\ [PQ|P^2]&[Q|P|P^2]+[P|Q|P^2]+[P^2|P^2|P^2]+[P^3|P|P^2]\\ [P^3|Q]&[P|P^2|Q]+[P^2|P|Q]+[P^3|P^2|P]\\ [P^3|P^3]&[P|P^2|P^3]+[P^2|P|P^3]+[P^3|P|P^2]+[P^3|P^2|P]. \end{array} \tag{4.5} \] Each word except the two in (4.4) occurs twice. The weight drops from six to three. The leading class of \(\mathcal B\) is \(B=a^2\), so \[ d_3B=y^3+x^2z. \tag{4.6} \] For the second calculation use the complete eight-term cochain of length two and internal degree nine \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal V={}&[Q|Q^2]+[Q|P^6]+[P^2|T]+[P^2|PQ^2]\\ &+[P^2|P^4Q]+[P^2|P^7] +[P^2Q|P^4]+[P^5|P^4]. \end{aligned} \tag{4.7} \] Its weights in that order are \(6,5,6,5,5,4,5,3\). Its two highest-weight terms represent \(ab+yc=v\). Direct expansion gives \[ d\mathcal V=[P|P^4|P^4]. \tag{4.8} \] Again the entire expansion is included: \[ \begin{array}{c|l} [Q|Q^2]&[Q|P^4|P^2]+[P^2|P|Q^2]\\ [Q|P^6]&[Q|P^2|P^4]+[Q|P^4|P^2]+[P^2|P|P^6]\\ [P^2|T]&[P^2|Q^2|P]+[P^2|P^4|Q]\\ [P^2|PQ^2]&[P^2|Q^2|P]+[P^2|P|Q^2]+[P^2|P^4|P^3]+[P^2|P^5|P^2]\\ [P^2|P^4Q]&[P^2|Q|P^4]+[P^2|P^2|P^5]+[P^2|P^4|Q]+[P^2|P^6|P]\\ [P^2|P^7]&[P^2|P|P^6]+[P^2|P^2|P^5]+[P^2|P^3|P^4] +[P^2|P^4|P^3]+[P^2|P^5|P^2]+[P^2|P^6|P]\\ [P^2Q|P^4]&[Q|P^2|P^4]+[P^2|Q|P^4]+[P^2|P^3|P^4]+[P^4|P|P^4]\\ [P^5|P^4]&[P|P^4|P^4]+[P^4|P|P^4]. \end{array} \tag{4.9} \] Every word except (4.8) occurs twice. The resulting differential is \[ d_3v=xz^2. \tag{4.10} \] Equations (4.3) and (4.7) give the actual cobar preimages, so the calculation is reproducible without an external differential table. ### Exact comparison with the source's indices In Isaksen's source, the four indices are May filtration, stem, Adams filtration and motivic weight. Only its classical calculation is used here. If its first index is \(m\) and its Adams filtration is our word length \(s\), then the two retained filtrations satisfy \[ W=2m-s,\qquad m=\frac{W+s}{2} \tag{4.11} \] on the polynomial generators and their products. Thus a differential dropping \(W\) by three and increasing \(s\) by one lowers \(m\) by one. Our \(d_3\) is the differential denoted \(d_2\) in that source. Equations (4.6) and (4.10) recover its classical formulas for \(b_{20}\) and \(h_0(1)\). The original \(W\), the source's \(m\), the length \(s\) and every term of the cochain calculation remain identifiable. No motivic \(\tau\)-factor is silently transferred into the classical complex. ## 5. All other degree-six classes vanish The primitive words \([P]\), \([P^2]\) and \([P^4]\) are exact cocycles in the original complex. Consequently their page classes \(x,y,z\) have zero differential on every page on which they are present. Using (3.8), (4.6), the Leibniz rule and the relation \(yz=0\) on \(E_2\), we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} d_3(y^2B)&=y^5+x^2y^2z=y^5\ne0,\\ d_3(y^3B)&=y^6+x^2y^3z=y^6,\\ d_3v&=xz^2. \end{aligned} \tag{5.1} \] The first line removes the entire class \(y^2B\), which is already annihilated by \(x\). The second line makes \(y^6\) a boundary; that class too is annihilated by \(x\). The third line and all its \(x\)-multiples make \(xz^2,x^2z^2,\ldots\) boundaries. Every candidate in (3.8) has therefore been accounted for. After this differential the difference-six part has dimension at most one, represented by \(z^2\) at \[ (s,t,W)=(2,8,2). \tag{5.2} \] It remains to prove that this one class survives. Its representative \([P^4|P^4]\) has differential zero by (4.2), so it has no outgoing obstruction. A possible incoming differential would have source of length one and internal degree eight. On the entire \(E_1\)-page, the equation \[ 2^j(2^i-1)=8,\qquad i>0,\ j\geq0, \tag{5.3} \] has the unique solution \(i=1,j=3\). The resulting source is \(w=h_{13}\), of weight one. Any incoming \(d_r\) into weight two would need source weight \(2+r>2\). Such a source is absent already on \(E_1\), and passing to later subquotients cannot create it. The class is also nonzero on \(E_1\), where it is the polynomial square of \(h_{12}\). Thus it survives. The finite convergence proof in Section 2 yields exactly (1.8). In particular the conclusion covers all lengths because (3.7)–(3.8) were proved over the entire ring \(\mathbb F _2[x]\). There is a useful stronger piece of information in the explicit calculation: \[ [P]\,[P^4|P^4]=d\mathcal V \tag{5.4} \] is an equality of actual cochains, not merely an equality of associated-graded classes. The product by \([P]\) vanishes with the specific homotopy witness (4.7).

title: Theorem 6.1 (all-length odd-prime algebraic vanishing)
intended_section: Classical prerequisites appendix, in the dependency order of the retained course
statement_as_printed: ## 6. The odd-prime calculation with its signs
complete_source_text: ## 6. The odd-prime calculation with its signs For an odd prime \(p\), define the graded-commutative Hopf algebra \[ \begin{aligned} H_p&=\mathbb F _p[\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots] \otimes\Lambda(\tau_0,\tau_1,\ldots),\\ |\xi_i|&=2(p^i-1),\qquad |\tau_i|=2p^i-1,\qquad \xi_0=1,\\ \Delta\xi_i&=\sum_{k=0}^{i}\xi_{i-k}^{p^k}\otimes\xi_k,\\ \Delta\tau_i&=\tau_i\otimes1+ \sum_{k=0}^{i}\xi_{i-k}^{p^k}\otimes\tau_k . \end{aligned} \tag{6.1} \] The tensor-product multiplication uses its graded sign. The \(\xi_i\) have even degree and the \(\tau_i\) have odd degree. The counit kills every positive-degree generator. Thus the last sum contains \(1\otimes\tau_i\), and both counit terms are retained. Coassociativity for the \(\xi_i\) follows by the same three-index sum as (1.3), with \(2\) replaced by \(p\). For \(\tau_i\), both iterated coproducts are \[ \tau_i\otimes1\otimes1 +\sum_{k=0}^{i}\xi_{i-k}^{p^k}\otimes\tau_k\otimes1 +\sum_{a+b+c=i} \xi_a^{p^{b+c}}\otimes\xi_b^{p^c}\otimes\tau_c . \tag{6.2} \] The graded exterior relations are respected because the coproduct is graded-commutative and every odd element has square zero when \(2\) is invertible. In the cobar complex a slot \([m]\) has total degree \(|m|-1\). With the same counit subtraction (1.5), fix the sign convention \[ d[m]=\sum_{\overline\Delta m=\sum a\otimes b} (-1)^{|a|}[a|b],\qquad d(UV)=d(U)V+(-1)^{|U|_{\rm tot}}U\,d(V). \tag{6.3} \] The differential still increases word length and preserves internal degree. For a triple \(a,b,c\) in an iterated coproduct, the two ways of splitting have coefficients \((-1)^{|b|}\) and \(-(-1)^{|b|}\). They cancel. Splittings in different slots cancel by the displayed derivation sign. Hence \(d^2=0\) with precisely this convention. **Theorem 6.1.** For every odd prime, \[ \mathcal H^{s,s+6}(H_p)=0\quad\hbox{for all }s\geq0. \tag{6.4} \] **Proof for \(p\geq5\).** The only positive-degree monomial of degree at most seven is \(\tau_0\), of degree one. Indeed the smallest other generator is \(\xi_1\), of degree \(2(p-1)\geq8\), and \(\tau_0^2=0\). Every slot contributes \(|m|-1\geq0\) to the difference of its word. A word of difference six could use only monomials of degree at most seven, so every slot would have to be \(\tau_0\); its difference would then be zero. There are no such words. Thus the original cochain group itself is zero in the degree under consideration. **Proof for \(p=3\).** Write \(T_0=\tau_0\) and \(X=\xi_1\), preserving their degrees \(1\) and \(4\). The complete list of nonunit monomials of degree at most seven is \[ T_0,\quad X,\quad T_0X,\quad\tau_1,\quad T_0\tau_1, \qquad\hbox{of degrees }1,4,5,5,6. \tag{6.5} \] The corresponding slot differences are \(0,3,4,4,5\). Hence every original word of difference six consists of exactly two slots \(X\) and any number of slots \(T_0\): \[ [T_0]^{a}[X][T_0]^{b}[X][T_0]^{c}, \qquad a,b,c\geq0. \tag{6.6} \] The notation \([T_0]^a\) denotes concatenation of \(a\) slots; the exterior-algebra power \(T_0^a\) is zero only when the exponent is at least two. Both \(T_0\) and \(X\) are primitive. Therefore every word (6.6) is a cocycle. The exact coproducts of the two incoming monomials give, with all signs from (6.3), \[ \begin{aligned} \overline\Delta(T_0X)&=T_0\otimes X+X\otimes T_0,\\ d[T_0X]&=-[T_0|X]+[X|T_0],\\ \overline\Delta(X^2)&=2X\otimes X,\\ d[X^2]&=2[X|X]. \end{aligned} \tag{6.7} \] For any cocycle words \(U,V\), these identities imply \[ U[X][T_0]V-U[T_0][X]V =(-1)^{|U|_{\rm tot}}d\bigl(U[T_0X]V\bigr). \tag{6.8} \] Repeatedly apply (6.8) to move every \(T_0\) slot to the left, retaining its signed preimage at each interchange. This is a finite operation: each interchange decreases the number of pairs with an \(X\) to the left of a \(T_0\). Thus (6.6) is homologous to \[ [T_0]^{a+b+c}[X|X] =d\left(\frac12[T_0]^{a+b+c}[X^2]\right). \tag{6.9} \] Here \(1/2=2\) in \(\mathbb F _3\), and the prefix has total degree zero, so no additional sign is suppressed. Adding the explicitly signed interchange preimages from (6.8) to the cochain on the right of (6.9) supplies a preimage of the original word. Every cocycle in the component is a linear combination of these words. Therefore every one is a boundary, for every length \(s\), proving (6.4).

complete_source_text:
### Exercise 1. A boundary at arbitrarily high word length

For each integer \(r\geq1\), produce an original cochain whose differential is
\[
 [P]^r[P^4|P^4]\in C^{r+2,r+8}(H).
 \tag{7.1}
\]
List its entire set of terms, rather than referring only to the page relation.

**Solution.** Since \(d[P]=0\), equation (4.8) gives the required preimage
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal V_r=[P]^{r-1}\bigl(&[Q|Q^2]+[Q|P^6]+[P^2|T]
             +[P^2|PQ^2]\\
             &+[P^2|P^4Q]+[P^2|P^7]
             +[P^2Q|P^4]+[P^5|P^4]\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.2}
\]
It has length \(r+1\) and internal degree \((r-1)+9=r+8\). Its highest weight is \((r-1)+6=r+5\). Formula (1.6) and the complete cancellation table (4.9) give
\[
 d\mathcal V_r=[P]^{r-1}[P|P^4|P^4]
              =[P]^r[P^4|P^4].
 \tag{7.3}
\]
This works for every \(r\); no bound on word length is used.

An odd-prime preimage with the sign visible At \(p=3\), find a complete preimage of \([X|T_0|X]\). **Solution.** In this case (6.3) gives \(|[X]|_{\rm tot}=3\) and \(|[T_0]|_{\rm tot}=0\). A suitable length-two cochain is \[ Z=[T_0X|X]+\frac12[T_0|X^2]. \tag{7.4} \] Indeed \[ \begin{aligned} d[T_0X|X]&=-[T_0|X|X]+[X|T_0|X],\\ d\!\left(\frac12[T_0|X^2]\right) &=\frac12\cdot2[T_0|X|X]=[T_0|X|X]. \end{aligned} \tag{7.5} \] Their sum is exactly the required word. The coefficient \(1/2\), the negative term and its cancellation are all essential parts of the original differential. The diagram retains every power of the length-one class through the full module R in Section 3. Its arrows are the exact differentials (5.1), with every length, internal degree and weight displayed. The explicit cochains (4.3) and (4.7) prove the arrows. The weight argument (5.3) proves survival; Section 6 proves the odd-prime vanishing with its original signs. The source filtration comparison is (4.11). This depicts the algebraic calculation. The geometric framed-manifold correspondence is proved in its linked companion; the linked actual-cooperation and integral companions now prove its comparison with the stable group, and the [original geometric framing proof](the-original-six-dimensional-framing-invariant.md#framed-six-original-nullbordism) calculates the original manifold’s value.

## 1. The complete truncated-polynomial bar algebra {#odd-original-bar}

Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(k=\mathbb F_p\), and let \(T=k[e]/(e^p)\), with original even internal degree \(d\geq0\). The augmentation is \(e\mapsto0\). Every nonzero letter \(e^i\), \(1\leq i<p\), has even internal degree, so its suspended degree \(id+1\) is odd. Use the [full bar differential (2.2)](the-actual-mod-two-cooperation-comparison-through-degree-eight.md#actual-eight-bar-comparison), evaluated in this original coefficient field. Define the exact words
\[
 U_n=[e^{p-1}|e|\cdots|e^{p-1}|e]\quad(n\text{ displayed pairs}),
 \qquad V_n=[e|e^{p-1}|e|\cdots|e^{p-1}|e],
\]
where \(U_0=[]\) and \(V_0=[e]\). Every interior multiplication is a product with exponent \(p\), so its value is zero in \(T\). Thus these are cycles in the reduced bar. Their original bidegrees (length, internal degree) are \((2n,npd)\) and \((2n+1,(np+1)d)\), respectively.

To prove that they are a complete homology basis, take the free augmented \(T\)-resolution with one basis vector \(u_n\) at resolution degree \(2n\), internal degree \(npd\), and \(v_n\) at resolution degree \(2n+1\), internal degree \((np+1)d\). Its differential is
\[
 d v_n=e u_n,\qquad d u_n=e^{p-1}v_{n-1}\ (n\geq1),
 \qquad Tu_0\longrightarrow k.
\]
The kernels are exactly \(\ker(e:T\to T)=ke^{p-1}\) and \(\ker(e^{p-1}:T\to T)=eT\). These are the images of the preceding differentials, and the augmentation kernel is \(eT\). Hence the resolution is exact in every degree. The assignments \(u_n\mapsto1\otimes U_n\), \(v_n\mapsto1\otimes V_n\) give a map to the free bar resolution: its first face contributes precisely the displayed coefficient, while all interior products vanish. Its augmentation is the identity of \(k\). The free-resolution comparison and both inductively constructed homotopies in the [actual degree-eight companion, Section 3](the-actual-mod-two-cooperation-comparison-through-degree-eight.md#actual-eight-exterior-bar), therefore show that, after tensoring with \(k\), the original words \(U_n,V_n\) are a complete independent homology basis. This retains the full bar complex on every letter \(e^i\); letters other than \(e,e^{p-1}\) have not been omitted from that comparison.

The multiplication can be proved on the words themselves, before taking homology. Write \(a=e^{p-1}\), \(b=e\) for this paragraph only; their suspended degrees are both odd, and they are distinct since \(p>2\). In a shuffle of the alternating words \((ab)^m,(ab)^n\), pair every term whose output has two consecutive equal letters with the term obtained by exchanging the sources of the first such pair. Those letters come from different inputs because each input alternates. Their exchange is an allowed shuffle, changes its sign by \(-1\), preserves its entire output word, and is an involution without a fixed point. Thus these terms cancel with their full original signs. Every remaining word alternates, starts with \(a\), and ends with \(b\). Its first \(b\) must come from the input that supplied its first \(a\), because neither input has supplied another \(a\). Remove this complete pair and repeat. Hence each remaining shuffle interleaves the \(m+n\) whole pairs. There are exactly \(\binom{m+n}{m}\) such shuffles, and exchanging two whole pairs has four odd crossings, with sign \(+1\). Therefore
\[
 U_m U_n=\binom{m+n}{m}U_{m+n}
\]
in the full reduced bar, with the original integer coefficient mapped to \(k\).

Likewise shuffle \([b]\) with \((ab)^n\). Inserting \(b\) immediately before and immediately after each existing \(b\) gives the same output with opposite signs. These \(2n\) placements cancel in pairs; the sole remaining placement is before the first \(a\), with sign \(+1\). Thus \([e]U_n=V_n\). The two shuffles in \([e]^2\) have opposite signs, so \([e]^2=0\). Associativity of the full shuffle now gives all products, including
\[
 V_m U_n=\binom{m+n}{m}V_{m+n},\qquad
 U_m V_n=\binom{m+n}{m}V_{m+n},\qquad V_m V_n=0.
\]
Consequently the complete homology algebra is
\[
 H_*(B(T))=E_k(\sigma e)\otimes\Gamma_k(\varphi e),
 \qquad |\sigma e|=d+1,\qquad |\varphi e|=pd+2,
\]
with \(\sigma e\) represented by \(V_0\), \(\gamma_n(\varphi e)\) by \(U_n\), and \(\sigma e\gamma_n(\varphi e)\) by \(V_n\). All products and every original internal degree are explicit. The original one-letter suspension sends \(e\) to the nonzero indecomposable \(V_0\); it sends \(e^i\), \(2\leq i<p\), to zero, since
\[
 d[e^{i-1}|e]=(-1)^{(i-1)d+1}[e^i]=-[e^i].
\]
Both augmentation endpoints vanish and the internal differential is zero. Thus its kernel on the positive augmentation ideal is exactly the span of its decomposable powers.

## 2. The original odd-prime chains and the actual suspension {#odd-original-chains}

Use the original simplicial cocycle groups \(K^q\), with coefficient \(k=\mathbb F_p\), and put \(L_q=|K^q|\). These are the actual models of [Sections 8–11 of the included Adams-tower companion](the-adams-tower-and-exact-inverse-limits.md#adams-original-cocycles), which were constructed for every prime. In particular \(L_0\) is the discrete additive group \(k\); the actual group addition, original cochain quotient bundles and positive suspension maps are fixed there.

For any simplicial abelian group \(G\), the full signed shuffle followed by its addition gives the augmented graded-commutative differential algebra \(C(G;k)\). The [degenerate-chain contraction (1.1)](the-actual-mod-two-cooperation-comparison-through-degree-eight.md#actual-eight-chain-models) was proved with integer signs before passing to the field, so it applies here unchanged. A homogeneous odd chain \(a\) has \(a\ast a=-a\ast a\), whence \(a\ast a=0\), since multiplication by the actual nonzero coefficient two is invertible in \(k\).

A positive even chain has zero \(p\)-th power. First take a single simplex of positive even degree \(d\). Its \(p\)-fold product is the sum of all labelled \((d,\ldots,d)\)-shuffle paths, each with its original permutation sign. Rotate the \(p\) input labels cyclically. No nonidentity rotation fixes a path: the label of its first step changes. Thus each orbit has exactly \(p\) terms. The corresponding simplices have the same image under addition in \(G\), and their signs agree: moving one whole degree-\(d\) block past the other \(p-1\) blocks has sign \((-1)^{(p-1)d^2}=+1\). Each orbit therefore has coefficient \(p\), whose image in \(k\) is zero. For a linear combination of such simplices, its summands commute because their degrees are even. The full multinomial expansion has every mixed coefficient divisible by \(p\): in a partition of the prime \(p\) with at least two nonzero entries, each entry is less than \(p\), so \(p!/\prod n_i!\) has exactly one factor of \(p\). The pure powers already vanish by the orbit argument. Consequently
\[
 a^{\ast2}=0\quad (|a|\text{ odd}),\qquad
 b^{\ast p}=0\quad (|b|>0\text{ even}).
 \tag{2.1}
\]
No degree-zero chain identity is inferred from the second statement.

The [full multiplicative bar/prism comparison](the-actual-mod-two-cooperation-comparison-through-degree-eight.md#actual-eight-bar-comparison) applies over this coefficient field. In detail, use the same bisimplicial object \(\mathcal B_{s,t}G=G_t^s\), the same oriented product prism, and the sign
\[
 (-1)^{\epsilon_s},\qquad
 \epsilon_s=\sum_{i=1}^s(s-i)|a_i|.
 \tag{2.2}
\]
The difference of the internal exponents in (2.6) there is the integer \(2j-2s\); the two interior-face exponents in (2.7) are equal as integers. Hence those full signs agree over \(k\), without setting minus one to plus one. The two augmentation endpoints vanish for exactly the same reasons: a projected positive simplex becomes degenerate, and an augmentation-ideal degree-zero chain has coefficient sum zero. The signed product-prism subdivision enumerates the same paths in both orders and gives the suspended-letter Koszul sign. The degenerate quotients, front/back comparisons and finite length-filtration cone argument use only vector-space exactness and the original signed boundary identities. They therefore prove the actual multiplicative isomorphism
\[
 H_*(B(C(G;k)))\xrightarrow{\cong}H_*(|BG|;k).
 \tag{2.3}
\]
The characteristic-two assertion about all bar-chain squares is not used in this argument. The length-one word still represents the original positively oriented interval times its input, with connecting value the original group element.

The homogeneous group bundle \(K^q\to EK^q\to BK^q\) has contractible middle realization by insertion of the zero vertex. The [original quotient-bundle and homotopy exact-sequence proofs](the-adams-tower-and-exact-inverse-limits.md#adams-original-spectrum) give the sole nonzero homotopy group \(k\) in degree \(q+1\). The cellular cohomology-representing map
\[
 j_q:|BK^q|\longrightarrow L_{q+1}
 \tag{2.4}
\]
sends the actual connecting element to itself. The first extension is the [cellular construction with its explicit obstruction cocycle](the-actual-mod-two-cooperation-comparison-through-degree-eight.md#actual-eight-original-suspension): the signed attaching-sphere sum is zero exactly because the chosen cochain is a cocycle. Every higher obstruction lies in a zero homotopy group. It is consequently a homotopy equivalence by the included CW comparison. It preserves group addition up to homotopy: in degree \(q+1\), the product has no mixed positive cohomology classes, since both factors are \(q\)-connected. Its two restrictions agree with \(j_q\), so the two maps in the group-addition identity represent the same cohomology class.

For \(q\geq1\), the suspension comparison follows from the common positive connecting value and
\([\Sigma L_q,L_{q+1}]=\widetilde H^q(L_q;k)=k\). At \(q=0\), the reduced degree-zero cohomology of the \(p\)-point set has dimension \(p-1\), so checking one value alone would be insufficient. Instead check every original element \(g\in k\): the one-letter bar path lifts in the homogeneous bundle from zero to \(g\), and the original cochain contraction defining \(\sigma_0\) has that same endpoint \(g\). Both maps therefore have the same cohomology value on every nonbasepoint component. This proves the complete original suspension comparison also at \(q=0\).

## 3. The full homology-algebra induction, retaining all coefficients {#odd-full-induction}

For an odd-degree generator \(a\), the algebra \(E_k(a)\) has a bar with zero multiplication differential and basis the words \([a|\cdots|a]_n\). Every suspended letter has even degree, so every shuffle sign is plus. The full product coefficient is the integer \(\binom{m+n}{m}\) mapped into \(k\). Thus its bar homology is \(\Gamma_k(\sigma a)\), with original degree \(|a|+1\). For an even-degree truncated generator, Section 1 gives precisely \(E_k(\sigma e)\otimes\Gamma_k(\varphi e)\), with degrees \(|e|+1\) and \(p|e|+2\).

Retain the complete comparison of a divided-power algebra with its truncated generators. If \(z\) has even degree, let \(z_j=\gamma_{p^j}(z)\). For \(N=\sum_j n_jp^j\), with \(0\leq n_j<p\), the original product is
\[
 \prod_j z_j^{n_j}
 =c_N\gamma_N(z),\qquad
 c_N=\frac{N!}{\prod_j(p^j!)^{n_j}}.
 \tag{3.1}
\]
This is the actual integer multinomial coefficient; it has not been absorbed into a new divided-power generator. Counting the multiples of \(p,p^2,\ldots\) in a factorial gives
\(v_p(N!)=\sum_{r\geq1}\lfloor N/p^r\rfloor=(N-\sum_j n_j)/(p-1)\). Subtracting \(\sum_j n_jv_p(p^j!)\) proves \(v_p(c_N)=0\). Thus its residue in \(k\) is invertible. In contrast, the coefficient of \(z_j^p\) is \((p^{j+1})!/(p^j!)^p\), whose valuation is exactly one, so that power is zero. It follows that the actual algebra map
\[
 \bigotimes_{j\geq0}k[Z_j]/(Z_j^p)\longrightarrow\Gamma_k(z),
 \quad Z_j\longmapsto\gamma_{p^j}(z)
 \tag{3.2}
\]
is an isomorphism. Its inverse on the original basis is explicitly
\(\gamma_N(z)\mapsto(c_N\bmod p)^{-1}\prod_jZ_j^{n_j}\). Both products and every coefficient of this inverse are retained.

For a tensor product of odd exterior factors and even truncated factors, tensor the original free resolutions from Section 1 and the one-generator exterior resolution. They are exact free resolutions because every augmented exact complex over the field splits, and the full signed tensor homotopies contract every summand containing an acyclic factor. Shuffle their maps into the full free bar. This is a chain map lifting the identity, with its tensor Koszul signs; the inductively lifted reverse map and both homotopies prove that it induces a homology isomorphism. The shuffle map is multiplicative since both orders enumerate the same signed multi-input shuffles. Thus the bar homology is the tensor product of the two explicitly computed kinds of factors above. Infinite families are handled by their directed union: each chain and each bounding chain involves only finitely many factors.

This algebraic calculation applies to the actual spaces. If \(H_*(L_q;k)\) has this tensor-algebra form with positive generators, choose cycle representatives for its specified generators. Relations (2.1) make their assignment a well-defined differential-algebra map from that zero-differential tensor algebra to \(C(K^q;k)\), retaining all original products. It induces the given homology isomorphism. Bar length has finite range in every total degree, so the tensor comparisons and the finite filtered-cone argument prove that applying the full bar preserves this homology isomorphism. Composing with (2.3) and (2.4) calculates the original homology algebra of \(L_{q+1}\). The one-letter suspension sends every old algebra generator to the specified generator of degree one greater. Every product of two positive cycles maps to a boundary by the complete two-letter bar differential, with its original sign. The tensor-resolution bases show that the one-letter images are independent indecomposables. Hence the suspension kernel is exactly the decomposable subspace, and its map on indecomposables is injective.

The base of this induction is also exact. In degree zero the chains of the discrete original group \(k\) form its group algebra. For \(g=[1]\), with unit \([0]\), set \(e=g-[0]\). Then \((g-[0])^p=g^p-[0]=0\). The map \(k[e]/(e^p)\to k[k]\) is bijective: the expansions of \((g-[0])^i\), \(0\leq i<p\), in the ordered basis \([0],g,\ldots,g^{p-1}\) form a triangular matrix with diagonal one and all original binomial coefficients. Section 1 at internal degree zero, followed by the actual comparison (2.3)–(2.4), therefore proves
\[
 H_*(L_1;k)=E_k(a_1)\otimes\Gamma_k(b_2),
 \quad a_1\leftrightarrow[e],\quad b_2\leftrightarrow[e^{p-1}|e].
 \tag{3.3}
\]
The subscripts are the original degrees. Formula (3.2) supplies the even truncated generators \(\gamma_{p^j}(b_2)\) of degrees \(2p^j\), with their full coefficient comparison.

## 4. The exact stable cooperation degrees needed by the original stem six {#odd-stable-cooperations}

A generator of \(H_*(L_q;k)\) of degree \(d\) has excess \(r=d-q\). The induction retains each generator by the original suspension, with degree increasing by one and excess unchanged. Every generator has nonnegative excess, starting with (3.3). All additional generators at the next stage are exactly the following, with multiplicities retained:

- From an odd exterior generator of degree \(d=q+r\), the extra divided powers have degree \(p^j(d+1)\), \(j\geq1\), and excess
  \[(p^j-1)(q+1)+p^jr.\]
- From an even truncated generator of degree \(d=q+r\), the extra divided powers of its new two-letter generator have degree \(p^j(pd+2)\), \(j\geq0\), and excess
  \[(p^{j+1}-1)q+p^{j+1}r+2p^j-1.\]

These are direct substitutions into the full degrees in Section 3. For \(q\geq4\), \(p\geq3\), \(r\geq0\), every first kind has excess at least \(2(q+1)\geq10\), and every second kind at least \(2q+1\geq9\). Thus after stage four no new generator of excess at most seven appears. The original suspension is bijective on the generator bases in that range, including their specified representatives.

Here are all retained generators for \(p=3\) through stage four, restricted only after computing their full degrees. Each entry records (type, degree, excess), with \(E\) denoting odd exterior and \(T\) even truncated:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
q&\text{all generators with excess at most seven}\\\hline
1&(E,1,0),\ (T,2,1),\ (T,6,5)\\
2&(T,2,0),\ (T,6,4),\ (E,3,1),\ (T,8,6),\ (E,7,5)\\
3&(E,3,0),\ (T,8,5),\ (E,7,4),\ (T,4,1),\ (E,9,6),\ (T,8,5)\\
4&(T,4,0),\ (E,5,1),\ (T,8,4),\ (E,9,5),\ (E,9,5),\ (T,10,6).
\end{array}
\tag{4.1}
\]
The repeated entries at excess five are two different generators. Their original origins at stage three are, respectively, the new two-letter class from the degree-two truncated generator and the suspension of the degree-seven exterior generator. They are retained separately in (4.1). No excluded larger-excess generator can later contribute in this range: suspension preserves excess, and each extra-generator formula is at least the old excess and increases it for positive \(q\).

For \(p\geq5\), the complete stage-one list in this range is only \((E,1,0),(T,2,1)\). The next possible initial excess is \(2p-1\geq9\). At the first transition, the smallest extra generator from the odd class has excess \(2(p-1)\geq8\), and the smallest from the even class has excess \(2p\geq10\). At a later transition \(q\geq2\), every extra odd-source generator has excess at least \((p-1)(q+1)\geq12\), and every extra even-source generator has excess at least \((p-1)q+1\geq9\). Thus the two suspended generators of excess zero and one are the entire list for every stage.

The [actual stable homology comparison](the-adams-tower-and-exact-inverse-limits.md#adams-stable-homology) is the original one
\[
 \Gamma_r^{(p)}=\pi_r(Hk\wedge Hk)
 =\operatorname*{colim}_q\widetilde H_{q+r}(L_q;k).
 \tag{4.2}
\]
All generators at stage \(q\) have degree at least \(q\); consequently a product of two positive generators has degree at least \(2q\). For \(q\geq8\) and \(0\leq r\leq7\), the degree \(q+r<2q\) contains only individual generators. Formulas (4.1)–(4.2) and the exact suspension now prove the full dimensions
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (\dim\Gamma^{(3)}_0,\ldots,\dim\Gamma^{(3)}_7)
  &=(1,1,0,0,1,2,1,0),\\
 (\dim\Gamma^{(p)}_0,\ldots,\dim\Gamma^{(p)}_7)
  &=(1,1,0,0,0,0,0,0)\quad(p\geq5).
\end{aligned}
 \tag{4.3}
\]
This is an actual stable vector-space calculation, with the original maps and no operation-algebra classification assumed.

## 5. Vanishing in the actual odd-prime cooperation cobar {#odd-actual-cobar}

Use the [actual cooperation unit, multiplication and coproduct](the-actual-mod-two-adams-resolution-and-cooperation-maps.md#cooperation-original-factors) defined by the original coefficient spectrum and its ordered factors; Section 6 below supplies their graded comparison at every odd prime. Their cross-product construction and counit identities are the full graded ones. They are valid over \(k\): the shuffle cross product has its integer Koszul sign, the coefficient multiplication is associative and graded-commutative, and insertion of the original unit gives the coproduct. These maps give a connected graded-commutative bialgebra \(\Gamma^{(p)}\); the coproduct is an algebra map with the original tensor sign. The construction does not require a polynomial presentation.

At \(p\geq5\), every nonzero positive cooperation of degree at most seven has degree one, by (4.3). Every letter in a cobar word of stem six would have degree at most seven; the degree-one letters all have excess zero, so such a word cannot have stem six. The actual cochain group is zero in every length.

At \(p=3\), fix the actual class \(t\in\Gamma_1^{(3)}\) supplied by the stable image of the original \(b_2\) in (3.3), and the actual class \(x\in\Gamma_4^{(3)}\) supplied at stage two by the index-three divided power of the suspension of \(a_1\). Their nonzero and independent values follow from the complete bar bases and the injective suspension on indecomposables. These are specified representatives from the original spaces, rather than rescaled generators. The coproduct of each is primitive. For \(t\), positive bidegrees cannot sum to one. For \(x\), all possible reduced bidegrees are \((1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\), and (4.3) makes each corresponding tensor group zero. The original endpoints are fixed by the counit. Thus
\[
 \Delta t=t\otimes1+1\otimes t,\qquad
 \Delta x=x\otimes1+1\otimes x.
 \tag{5.1}
\]
Here \(|t|=1\), \(|x|=4\). The entire coproducts of the actual products are therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Delta(tx)&=tx\otimes1+t\otimes x+x\otimes t+1\otimes tx,\\
 \Delta(x^2)&=x^2\otimes1+2x\otimes x+1\otimes x^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.2}
\]
The two tensor terms in the first reduced coproduct lie in distinct bidegrees and are nonzero, and the second has its original nonzero coefficient two. Hence the actual products \(tx\) and \(x^2\) are nonzero, proved by these actual morphisms. No separate degree-eight dimension count or projective classification is needed to establish them.

Use the full signed cobar convention
\[
 d[a]=\sum_{\bar\Delta a=\sum b\otimes c}(-1)^{|b|}[b|c],
 \qquad d(UV)=d(U)V+(-1)^{|U|_{\rm tot}}U d(V),
 \quad |[a]|_{\rm tot}=|a|-1.
 \tag{5.3}
\]
Coassociativity cancels the two orders of each double split, with opposite signs; splits in different slots cancel by the displayed Leibniz rule. Thus this is the actual cooperation cobar differential. From (5.2), retaining exactly the two endpoints in the full coproduct before projecting them away, we get
\[
 d[tx]=-[t|x]+[x|t],\qquad d[x^2]=2[x|x].
 \tag{5.4}
\]
Formula (4.3) lists all positive single-letter degrees at most seven as one, four, five and six. Their slot excesses are zero, three, four and five. A sum of these excesses can equal six only by taking exactly two of excess three and otherwise excess zero. Therefore every stem-six word is exactly
\[
 [t]^a[x][t]^b[x][t]^c,\qquad a,b,c\geq0.
 \tag{5.5}
\]
The actual degrees-five and six spaces, including both degree-five generators, cannot contribute to such a word; all their excesses have been considered. The primitive equations (5.1) show that every word (5.5) is a cocycle.

For any cocycle words \(U,V\), (5.3)–(5.4) give the exact signed interchange
\[
 U[x][t]V-U[t][x]V=(-1)^{|U|_{\rm tot}}d(U[tx]V).
 \tag{5.6}
\]
Apply this identity to each adjacent pair with an \(x\) to the left of a \(t\), retaining the displayed signed preimage at each step. The number of such inverted pairs decreases strictly, so this process ends after finitely many steps at \([t]^{a+b+c}[x|x]\). Its actual preimage is
\[
 d\bigl(2[t]^{a+b+c}[x^2]\bigr)=[t]^{a+b+c}[x|x]
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb F_3,
 \tag{5.7}
\]
since \(2\cdot2=1\) in the original field and the prefix has total degree zero. Adding every signed preimage from (5.6) to the one in (5.7) gives an actual preimage of the original word (5.5). Linear extension covers every cocycle, at every length. Hence
\[
 H^{s,s+6}(C^*(\Gamma^{(p)}))=0
 \qquad\text{for every odd prime }p\text{ and every }s\geq0.
 \tag{5.8}
\]
This proves the vanishing in the actual cooperation cobar. The next section constructs its receiving comparison with the original odd-prime Adams tower, including the full sign change. The [original geometric framing proof](the-original-six-dimensional-framing-invariant.md#framed-six-original-nullbordism) constructs the full quadratic invariant, proves framed bordism invariance and gives value zero for the original framed homotopy six-sphere, with an actual framed nullbordism. The [sphere-twist and smooth-recognition proof](sphere-twists-and-the-original-smooth-six-sphere-comparison.md#twist-original-smooth-map) now constructs the new interior gluing with its full frame defect, cancels every actual handle and gives the orientation-preserving diffeomorphism to the original six-sphere, homotopic to its original degree-one map.
