## 6. The actual odd-prime Adams resolution, with both sign comparisons {#odd-actual-adams}

Use the [original ordered tower](the-adams-tower-and-exact-inverse-limits.md#adams-original-tower). Write \(H=Hk\), \(M(Y)=\pi_*(H\wedge Y)\), and retain the ordered original tower factors \(F_s=B^{\wedge s}\), \(W_s=H\wedge F_s\). The actual cross-product map \(Q_Y\) uses
\[
 (H_1\wedge H_2)\wedge(H_3\wedge Y)
 \longrightarrow H_1\wedge\mu(H_2,H_3)\wedge Y.
 \tag{6.1}
\]
It is an isomorphism on the field homology factors by the original signed field cross-product comparison. The unit-insertion definitions are
\[
 \Delta=Q_H^{-1}\pi_*(1_H\wedge\eta\wedge1_H),
 \qquad \rho_Y=Q_Y^{-1}M(\eta\wedge1_Y),
 \qquad \epsilon=\pi_*\mu.
 \tag{6.2}
\]
The counit is a left inverse to the coaction. Inserting two successive units proves coassociativity: under the iterated version of (6.1), both composites multiply the same neighboring factors in the same order. Multiplication of the two inside factors proves that \(Q_Y\) identifies the coaction on \(M(H\wedge Y)\) with the cofree coaction. All these maps retain their original symmetry maps; graded tensor products use \((-1)^{|b||c|}\) when crossing the middle homogeneous factors \(b,c\). Associativity and the graded commutativity of \(\mu\) consequently prove the graded algebra compatibility used in (5.2).

The suspension signs in the resolution must also be retained. Define the shifted comodules by actual suspended spectra,
\[
 V^s=M(\Sigma^sF_s),\qquad I^s=M(\Sigma^sW_s),
 \qquad V^s_t=M(F_s)_{t-s},\quad I^s_t=M(W_s)_{t-s}.
 \tag{6.3}
\]
Their coactions are those of (6.2), not unsigned copies of a shifted grading. The actual symmetry
\[
 \kappa_s:\Sigma^s(H\wedge F_s)\longrightarrow H\wedge\Sigma^sF_s
 \tag{6.4}
\]
moves the original \(s\) ordered suspension coordinates past the displayed \(H\)-factor. On a homogeneous degree-\(j\) coefficient its Koszul contribution is \((-1)^{sj}\). We use (6.4) itself, so that this sign is retained at every stage. Equations (6.1)–(6.4) make \(I^s\) cofree, isomorphic to \(\Gamma^{(p)}\otimes V^s\).

Suspend the original fibre/cofibre sequence
\(F_{s+1}\to F_s\to W_s\to\Sigma F_{s+1}\) by precisely these \(s\) ordered coordinates. The counit splitting in (6.2) makes its first homology unit map injective. Its full long exact sequence therefore gives the exact sequence of actual comodules
\[
 0\longrightarrow V^s\xrightarrow{v_s}I^s
 \xrightarrow{b_s}V^{s+1}\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{6.5}
\]
Here \(b_s\) is induced by the actual map \(\Sigma^s(\partial\wedge1_{F_s})\), with the appended suspension coordinate in its original order. Put \(D^s=v_{s+1}b_s\). Then \(D^{s+1}D^s=0\), since \(b_{s+1}v_{s+1}=0\), and exactness of (6.5) proves
\[
 0\longrightarrow k\longrightarrow I^0\xrightarrow{D^0}I^1
 \xrightarrow{D^1}I^2\longrightarrow\cdots
 \tag{6.6}
\]
exact, with cofree terms. No minus sign has been discarded in forming this sequence.

The first-page differential is the same connecting composite, with sign plus for the original cone coordinate. To verify this precisely, use the cones for
\(F_{s+1}\xrightarrow{a_s}F_s\xrightarrow{q_s}\mathbb S\).
The map \(W_s=\operatorname{cofib}(a_s)\to C_s=\operatorname{cofib}(q_sa_s)\) sends the base \(F_s\) by \(q_s\) and sends its cone on \(F_{s+1}\) by the identity of that cone. The connecting map from \(C_s\) to \(\Sigma F_{s+1}\) collapses the base sphere and retains the same increasing cone coordinate. Its composite with \(W_s\to C_s\) therefore collapses the original base \(F_s\) and retains that same cone coordinate; this is exactly \(\partial\wedge1_{F_s}\), with sign plus. The following map to \(\Sigma W_{s+1}\) is the suspension of the unit inclusion of \(F_{s+1}\). The connecting map in the cofibres-of-composable-maps sequence is this composite: on the middle cone coordinate it is the suspension of that inclusion, and on the sphere base it is zero. For the cellular cone convention this is also a direct signed chain calculation. If \(f:A\to B\) and \(g:B\to C\), retain
\[
 \operatorname{Cone}(f)_n=B_n\oplus A_{n-1},\qquad
 d(b,a)=(d_Bb+f(a),-d_Aa).
\]
The first map of the three-cone sequence is \((b,a)\mapsto(gb,a)\). Its connecting map from \(\operatorname{Cone}(g)=C\oplus\Sigma B\) to \(\Sigma\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) is \((c,b)\mapsto(b,0)\): applying either differential gives \((-d_Bb,0)\), retaining the negative differential of the suspension. Applying this formula at the next tower index to the preceding map gives \((b,a)\mapsto(a,0)\), with coefficient plus one. These are the same increasing cone coordinates used above. Hence
\[
 d_1=(\Sigma(\eta\wedge1_{F_{s+1}}))_*
        (\partial\wedge1_{F_s})_*:
 \pi_{t-s}W_s\longrightarrow\pi_{t-s-1}W_{s+1}.
 \tag{6.7}
\]
This verifies the orientation with the original mapping cones, rather than cancelling a possible minus sign by the coefficient characteristic.

The original unit gives
\(\lambda_s:\pi_t(\Sigma^sW_s)\to I^s_t\).
Under \(M(\kappa_s)\) and the cofree comparison, it is \(z\mapsto1\otimes(\kappa_s)_*z\). The primitive part of a cofree comodule is exactly its subspace \(1\otimes V\): applying its first-factor counit to the primitive identity proves both inclusions. Thus \(\lambda_s\) is an isomorphism onto \(\operatorname{Prim}(I^s)_t\), with inverse obtained by \(M(\kappa_s)\), the first-factor counit, and \((\kappa_s)_*^{-1}\). Unit naturality for the actual suspended map (6.7) gives
\[
 D^s\lambda_s=\lambda_{s+1}d_1.
 \tag{6.8}
\]
This identifies the actual first-page complex with primitives of (6.6), including the suspension symmetry of (6.4).

For its second exact resolution put \(q=1-u\epsilon\), \(\bar\Gamma=\ker\epsilon\), and
\(J^s=\Gamma\otimes\bar\Gamma^{\otimes s}\), with cofree first factor. Retain the full coproduct and both endpoints before projecting. The differential is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 d_J(g\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s])
 &=\sum g_{(1)}\otimes[q(g_{(2)})|a_1|\cdots|a_s]\\
 &\quad+\sum_{i=1}^s(-1)^i\sum
 g\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_i'|a_i''|\cdots|a_s].
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.9}
\]
Every adjacent double splitting has opposite signs in its two orders; coassociativity identifies its two tensor terms. Splitting different positions has the same cancellation. The leading two splittings cancel the leading-then-first-bar split by coassociativity and the projection \(q\). This proves \(d_J^2=0\), and the same identities prove that it preserves the coaction.

Define \(h_0(g)=\epsilon(g)\) and
\(h_s(g\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s])=\epsilon(g)a_1\otimes[a_2|\cdots|a_s]\).
In degree zero, \(h_1d_J=q\), so \(u h_0+h_1d_J=1\). In positive degrees, the leading term of \(h_{s+1}d_J\) is \(q(g)\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]\). The leading term of \(d_Jh_s\) has the unit contribution \(u\epsilon(g)\otimes[a_1|\cdots|a_s]\) and the reduced coproduct of \(a_1\). The latter cancels the position-one splitting from \(h_{s+1}d_J\), whose coefficient is \((-1)^1=-1\). A later position \(i\) has coefficient \((-1)^{i-1}\) after applying \(h_s\), and coefficient \((-1)^i\) before it, so every such pair cancels as well. The two retained terms sum to the original input. This proves \(d_Jh+h d_J=1\), with its full augmented interpretation, and exactness of the cofree resolution \(k\to J^\bullet\).

Here are the comparison maps and inverse homotopies. For a cofree target the mutually inverse assignments are
\[
 f\longmapsto(\epsilon\otimes1)f,
 \qquad g\longmapsto(1\otimes g)\rho.
 \tag{6.10}
\]
Thus a comodule map on a subcomodule extends: extend its first assignment as a degree-preserving linear map on a complementary basis, then apply the second. Start \(A^0=B^0=1_\Gamma\). If \(A^n\) is already defined, prescribe
\(A^{n+1}(D^nx)=d_JA^nx\) on \(\operatorname{im}D^n\). Exactness and the preceding chain identity make this well defined; extend it by (6.10). The same construction with the resolutions exchanged gives \(B\). These are actual cochain maps lifting the augmentation identity.

For \(E=BA-1\), set \(H^0=0\). Having defined through \(H^n\), the map \(R^n=E^n-D^{n-1}H^n\) vanishes on \(\ker D^n=\operatorname{im}D^{n-1}\), by the preceding homotopy identity and \(D^2=0\). Therefore prescribe \(H^{n+1}(D^nx)=R^nx\) and extend by (6.10). This gives \(BA-1=DH+HD\). Apply the same construction to \(AB-1\), giving \(AB-1=d_JK+Kd_J\). Every extension preserves the coaction, so applying primitives gives both inverse homotopies between the actual first page (6.8) and the primitive complex of (6.9).

That primitive complex has differential \(d_{\rm alt}\) given by the second sum of (6.9). It remains to identify its signs with (5.3). For a homogeneous original word define
\[
 T_s[a_1|\cdots|a_s]
  =(-1)^{s+\sum_{j=1}^s(s-j)|a_j|}[a_1|\cdots|a_s].
 \tag{6.11}
\]
It is its own inverse. If the letter at position \(i\) splits into \(b,c\), the change in the exponent in (6.11) is exactly
\(1+\sum_{j<i}|a_j|+|b|\).
Including the alternating coefficient \((-1)^i\), the total exponent of \(T_{s+1}d_{\rm alt}\) is
\[
 \epsilon_s+i+1+\sum_{j<i}|a_j|+|b|,
 \qquad \epsilon_s=s+\sum_{j=1}^s(s-j)|a_j|.
\]
The exponent of \(dT_s\), using precisely (5.3), is
\(\epsilon_s+\sum_{j<i}|a_j|-(i-1)+|b|\).
Their difference is the even integer \(2i\). Thus \(T_{s+1}d_{\rm alt}=dT_s\) on every original coproduct term. This proves the full chain isomorphism, without changing the underlying cooperation or absorbing any coefficient into its generators. Combining it with (6.8) and both resolution homotopies gives
\[
 E_2^{s,t}(\text{original mod-}p\text{ tower})
 \xrightarrow{\cong}H^{s,t}(C^*(\Gamma^{(p)}),d).
 \tag{6.12}
\]
All prime-dependent signs in this comparison are explicit in (6.4), (6.7), (6.9) and (6.11).

Equations (5.8) and (6.12) make every degree-six \(E_2\)-group zero for every odd prime. Every later group on that line is zero as well. The [complete separated convergence for the original finite sphere tower](the-adams-tower-and-exact-inverse-limits.md#adams-actual-convergence), together with its [unit-preserving arithmetic comparison](the-original-adams-tower-and-arithmetic-completion.md#arithmetic-adams-equivalence), therefore gives
\[
 \pi_6(\mathbb S^{\wedge}_p)=0\qquad(p\text{ odd}).
 \tag{6.13}
\]
Indeed all successive quotients of its Adams filtration vanish, so the filtration is constant; its intersection is zero by separatedness, forcing the original filtered group to be zero. This conclusion concerns the specified arithmetic completion. It does not infer an integral stable homotopy result without its further comparison.

### Exercise 7.1. The divided-power coefficient that cannot be discarded

Work with \(p=3\), the original algebra \(T=\mathbb F_3[e]/(e^3)\), and \(|e|=2\). In the full bar use \(U_n=[e^2|e|\cdots|e^2|e]\), with exactly \(n\) pairs. Calculate \(U_1U_3^2\) with its original integer coefficient, recover the inverse coordinate for \(U_7\), and calculate \(U_3^3\). Give every bidegree involved.

**Solution.** A pair has length two and internal degree six, so \(U_n\) has bidegree \((2n,6n)\) and total degree \(8n\). The complete signed-shuffle calculation of Section 1 gives
\[
 U_3^2=\binom63U_6=20U_6,
 \qquad U_1U_6=\binom71U_7=7U_7.
\]
Consequently
\[
 U_1U_3^2=140U_7=2U_7\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_3.
 \tag{7.1}
\]
Both sides have bidegree \((14,42)\), total degree \(56\). The base-three digits of seven are \(n_0=1,n_1=2\), so (3.1) gives the very same integer coefficient \(7!/(1!(3!)^2)=140\). For the map (3.2), \(Z_0\mapsto U_1\), \(Z_1\mapsto U_3\), the exact inverse value is
\[
 U_7\longmapsto 2Z_0Z_1^2,
 \tag{7.2}
\]
since the original coefficient two is its own inverse in \(\mathbb F_3\). Neither generator nor product has been rescaled.

The next complete product is
\[
 U_3^3=\binom63\binom93U_9
 =20\cdot84\,U_9=1680U_9=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_3.
 \tag{7.3}
\]
Its bidegree is \((18,54)\), total degree \(72\). The valuation of the integer coefficient is exactly one: \(1680=3\cdot560\), and \(560\) is not divisible by three. Thus (7.3) is precisely the retained relation \(Z_1^3=0\) under the original coordinate map. The vector \(U_9\) itself remains nonzero by the complete free-resolution basis; the zero product does not make that homology class zero.

statement_as_printed: ### Exercise 7.2. An explicit actual stem-six boundary with every sign
complete_source_text:
### Exercise 7.2. An explicit actual stem-six boundary with every sign

At \(p=3\), use the actual classes \(t,x\) of Section 5. Find a full preimage of the original word \([x|t|x|t]\) under the actual cobar differential (5.3), and expand every contribution.

**Solution.** The required word has length four, internal degree ten and stem six. Take the original length-three, internal-degree-ten cochain
\[
 Q=[tx|x|t]-[t|x|tx]+[t|tx|x]+2[t|t|x^2].
 \tag{7.4}
\]
Its four terms have ordered degree triples \((5,4,1),(1,4,5),(1,5,4),(1,1,8)\). All original coefficients are displayed. By (5.4) and the full Leibniz signs,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 d[tx|x|t]&=-[t|x|x|t]+[x|t|x|t],\\
 -d[t|x|tx]&=-[t|x|t|x]+[t|x|x|t],\\
 d[t|tx|x]&=-[t|t|x|x]+[t|x|t|x],\\
 2d[t|t|x^2]&=4[t|t|x|x].
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.5}
\]
The minus sign in the second line also retains the odd total degree three of the prefix letter \([x]\); the \([t]\) letters have total degree zero. The first two copies of \([t|x|x|t]\) cancel with coefficients minus one and plus one. The copies of \([t|x|t|x]\) do the same. The remaining coefficient of \([t|t|x|x]\) is \(-1+4=3\), whose image in the original field is zero. Thus
\[
 dQ=[x|t|x|t].
 \tag{7.6}
\]
This is an actual incoming boundary using the original degree-eight product \(x^2\), whose nonvanishing was proved from its full coproduct in (5.2). All four bounding terms and every coefficient are necessary to the displayed cancellation.

title: 1. The original coefficient algebra and its full maps
intended_section: Classical prerequisites appendix, in the dependency order of the retained course
statement_as_printed: ## 1. The original coefficient algebra and its full maps
complete_source_text: ## 1. The original coefficient algebra and its full maps The original-author source for this algebraic presentation is Isaksen–Wang–Xu, arXiv:2001.04247v1, original author ms.tex, lines 586–810, especially 629–661. The source gives the motivic dual algebra and then describes its relationship to the classical generators after inverting its coefficient. Its sentence at 652–654 says that tau_i and xi_{i+1} correspond to zeta_i and zeta_i squared. The classical indexing earlier in that same source starts with zeta_1 of degree one. The exact map must therefore display the shift and the coefficient powers. An informal correspondence is not a coefficient-preserving Hopf-algebra formula. Retain the source coefficient \(\tau\). Define \(R_0=\mathbb F_2[\tau]\), \(R=\mathbb F_2[\tau,\tau^{-1}]\), and the two explicit algebras \[ B_0=R_0[\tau_0,\tau_1,\ldots,\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots]/ (\tau_j^2-\tau\xi_{j+1}:j\geq0),\qquad B=R\otimes_{R_0}B_0. \tag{1.1} \] These are the source's displayed algebraic presentations. Their identification with all motivic operations is not proved by this chapter. Let \(\xi_0=1\). Retain the full coproducts over the coefficient ring: \[ \Delta\xi_i=\sum_{k=0}^{i}\xi_{i-k}^{2^k}\otimes\xi_k,\qquad \Delta\tau_j=\tau_j\otimes1+ \sum_{k=0}^{j}\xi_{j-k}^{2^k}\otimes\tau_k. \tag{1.2} \] The tensor product in (1.2) is over the displayed coefficient ring. In particular \(\tau\otimes1=1\otimes\tau\); it is not replaced by the formula for a group-like element. Write \[ C=R[\zeta_1,\zeta_2,\ldots],\qquad \zeta_0=1,\qquad \Delta\zeta_i=\sum_{\ell=0}^{i} \zeta_{i-\ell}^{2^\ell}\otimes\zeta_\ell . \tag{1.3} \] The exact \(R\)-algebra maps are \[ \begin{aligned} \Phi:C\longrightarrow B,\qquad &\Phi(\zeta_i)=\tau^{\,2^{i-1}-1}\tau_{i-1}\quad(i\geq1),\\ \Psi:B\longrightarrow C,\qquad &\Psi(\tau_j)=\tau^{\,1-2^j}\zeta_{j+1}\quad(j\geq0),\\ &\Psi(\xi_i)=\tau^{\,1-2^i}\zeta_i^2\quad(i\geq1). \end{aligned} \tag{1.4} \] Both maps fix every coefficient in \(R\). The defining relation of \(B\) is respected, since \[ \Psi(\tau_j)^2 =\tau^{\,2-2^{j+1}}\zeta_{j+1}^2 =\tau\,\Psi(\xi_{j+1}). \tag{1.5} \] The composite \(\Psi\Phi\) is the identity on \(\zeta_i\), as its exponent is \((2^{i-1}-1)+(1-2^{i-1})=0\). The other composite is the identity on \(\tau_j\) by the same equality, and on \(\xi_i\) because \[ \Phi\Psi(\xi_i) =\tau^{\,1-2^i+2(2^{i-1}-1)}\tau_{i-1}^2 =\tau^{-1}\tau_{i-1}^2=\xi_i. \tag{1.6} \] Thus they are inverse algebra isomorphisms. Here is the full coproduct comparison. The two endpoint terms of \(\Delta\Phi(\zeta_i)\) are exactly \(\Phi(\zeta_i)\otimes1\) and \(1\otimes\Phi(\zeta_i)\). For an interior term put \(\ell=k+1\), so \(1\leq\ell\leq i-1\). Applying \(\Psi\otimes\Psi\) to this term gives \[ \tau^{\,2^{i-1}-1} \bigl(\tau^{\,1-2^{i-\ell}}\zeta_{i-\ell}^2\bigr)^{2^{\ell-1}} \otimes \tau^{\,1-2^{\ell-1}}\zeta_\ell =\zeta_{i-\ell}^{2^\ell}\otimes\zeta_\ell, \tag{1.7} \] because its complete coefficient exponent is \[ (2^{i-1}-1)+2^{\ell-1}(1-2^{i-\ell}) +(1-2^{\ell-1})=0. \tag{1.8} \] This proves compatibility on all the \(\zeta_i\). Equivalently, direct use of \(\Psi(\xi_i)\) in (1.2) gives the common exponent \(1-2^i\) in every summand, since \[ 2^k(1-2^{i-k})+(1-2^k)=1-2^i \quad(0\leq k\leq i). \tag{1.9} \] The convention at \(k=0\) or \(k=i\) retains \(\xi_0=\zeta_0=1\) and its exponent zero. Counits send every positive-index \(\zeta_i,\xi_i\), and every \(\tau_j\), to zero and fix the coefficient ring, so they agree too. The maps (1.4) are consequently an exact isomorphism of the displayed coefficient Hopf algebras. The coproducts and coassociativity in (1.3) have already been proved in the course's full cobar companion. Transport by (1.4) also verifies coassociativity of (1.2) after the coefficient inversion. The first three generators, without suppressed powers, are \[ \zeta_1=\tau_0,\qquad \zeta_2=\tau\tau_1,\qquad \zeta_3=\tau^3\tau_2. \tag{1.10} \] For example \[ \Delta(\tau\tau_1)= \tau\tau_1\otimes1+\tau\xi_1\otimes\tau_0+1\otimes\tau\tau_1 =\zeta_2\otimes1+\zeta_1^2\otimes\zeta_1+1\otimes\zeta_2. \tag{1.11} \] The coefficient \(\tau\) in the middle source term is essential: \(\xi_1=\tau^{-1}\zeta_1^2\). Only after the separate coefficient specialization \(\tau\mapsto1\) do the generator formulas reduce to \(\tau_j\mapsto\zeta_{j+1}\), \(\xi_i\mapsto\zeta_i^2\). That specialization and the localization in (1.1) are different maps. No original algebra was silently replaced in obtaining (1.4). In fact \(B_0\) injects into \(B\). To prove this, apply polynomial division by the monic quadratic relation in each \(\tau_j\), involving only finitely many variables at a time. The reductions in different \(\tau_j\) commute, and give the unique coefficient expansion in monomials \[ \prod_{i\geq1}\xi_i^{a_i}\prod_{j\geq0}\tau_j^{e_j}, \qquad a_i\geq0,\quad e_j\in\{0,1\}, \tag{1.12} \] with finite support. Iterated division proves that these monomials form a free \(R_0\)-basis; uniqueness can also be checked successively as division by a monic polynomial over the preceding coefficient ring. Thus multiplication by \(\tau\) is injective, proving the localization injection. Its exact image under \(\Psi\) is the \(R_0\)-subalgebra of \(C\) generated by \[ \tau^{\,1-2^j}\zeta_{j+1}\ (j\geq0),\qquad \tau^{\,1-2^i}\zeta_i^2\ (i\geq1). \tag{1.13} \] Although these generators are written in the larger ring \(R\), (1.13) records the entire original subalgebra. This is the proved relation between the original coefficient algebra and the classical polynomial presentation. For any later cobar comparison, apply \(\Phi\) or \(\Psi\) to every slot. They preserve the augmentation ideals by the counit calculation, preserve the full reduced coproducts by (1.7)–(1.9), and therefore commute term by term with the complete cobar differential. Their tensor powers are inverse cochain isomorphisms over \(R\). This is an algebraic conclusion; it does not establish topological Adams convergence or a framed-manifold value.

statement_as_printed: ## 2. Cohomological and homological coefficient rings
complete_source_text: ## 2. Cohomological and homological coefficient rings Use two separately named rings \[ R_{\mathrm c,0}=\mathbb F_2[t_{\mathrm c}], \quad |t_{\mathrm c}|=(0,1), \qquad R_{\mathrm h,0}=\mathbb F_2[t_{\mathrm h}], \quad |t_{\mathrm h}|=(0,-1), \tag{2.1} \] and their Laurent extensions \(R_{\mathrm c}\) and \(R_{\mathrm h}\). Thus the coefficient symbol in the source cohomology ring at lines 699–701 and that in its dual-algebra description at lines 763–765 have opposite weights. The explicit degree-preserving coefficient-ring isomorphism after inversion is \[ \iota:R_{\mathrm c}\longrightarrow R_{\mathrm h}, \qquad t_{\mathrm c}\longmapsto t_{\mathrm h}^{-1}, \qquad \iota^{-1}(t_{\mathrm h})=t_{\mathrm c}^{-1}. \tag{2.2} \] The two composites fix the generators and their inverses, hence are the identity. Equation (2.2) is an algebraic comparison of the coefficient rings; it does not itself identify cohomology and homology functors. Before inversion it does not take values in the polynomial ring \(R_{\mathrm h,0}\). This domain restriction is essential. The coefficient \(\tau\) in Section 1 has its own source name. The precise coefficient change used below is the isomorphism \[ j:\mathbb F_2[\tau,\tau^{-1}]\longrightarrow R_{\mathrm h}, \qquad j(\tau)=t_{\mathrm h},\qquad j^{-1}(t_{\mathrm h})=\tau. \tag{2.3} \] It restricts to an isomorphism of the two original polynomial coefficient rings. On the presented algebras it sends every \(\tau_j\) and \(\xi_i\) to the generator with the same index and sends the original relation \(\tau_j^2-\tau\xi_{j+1}\) to \(\tau_j^2-t_{\mathrm h}\xi_{j+1}\). Its inverse reverses these assignments, so both composites are the identity. On the classical polynomial presentation the map sends \(\zeta_i\) to the generator named \(z_i\) below; its inverse sends \(z_i\) to \(\zeta_i\). Substitution in every summand of (1.2)–(1.3) proves the coproduct comparison, and the counits agree on all generators. These explicit maps relate the two retained coefficient notations; they are different from the Laurent comparison (2.2), which sends \(t_{\mathrm c}\) to \(t_{\mathrm h}^{-1}\).

statement_as_printed: ## 4. The homological dual presentation and every weight
complete_source_text: ## 4. The homological dual presentation and every weight Keep the original algebra of Section 1: \[ B_0=R_{\mathrm h,0}[\tau_0,\tau_1,\ldots,\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots]/ (\tau_j^2-t_{\mathrm h}\xi_{j+1}), \qquad B=R_{\mathrm h}\otimes_{R_{\mathrm h,0}}B_0. \tag{4.1} \] Its full coproducts are (1.2), transported by the exact coefficient map (2.3), including both endpoints. The homological weights are \[ |\tau_j|=(2^{j+1}-1,2^j-1), \qquad |\xi_i|=(2^{i+1}-2,2^i-1). \tag{4.2} \] The full coproduct really is defined on the original quotient \(B_0\), before any localization. On its quadratic relation it gives \[ \begin{aligned} (\Delta\tau_j)^2 &=\tau_j^2\otimes1+ \sum_{k=0}^j\xi_{j-k}^{2^{k+1}}\otimes\tau_k^2\\ &=t_{\mathrm h}\xi_{j+1}\otimes1+ t_{\mathrm h}\sum_{k=0}^j \xi_{j-k}^{2^{k+1}}\otimes\xi_{k+1} =t_{\mathrm h}\Delta\xi_{j+1}. \end{aligned} \tag{4.2a} \] The last equality reindexes by \(k+1\) and includes both endpoints. The original monomial-basis proof makes every tensor power of \(B_0\) free over \(R_{\mathrm h,0}\), so its localization map is injective. The coassociativity equality, proved after localization by the exact map to the classical coproduct, therefore holds in \(B_0^{\otimes3}\) itself. The same endpoint calculation proves the original counit identities. This justifies the original, unlocalized cobar differential used below. The antipodes are also fixed by these original formulas. With convolution \(f*g=\mu(f\otimes g)\Delta\), let \(u\epsilon\) be the convolution unit and put \(h=u\epsilon-\mathrm{id}\). On an element \(x\) of internal degree \(d\geq0\), define \[ S(x)=\sum_{m=0}^{d}h^{*m}(x),\qquad h^{*0}=u\epsilon. \tag{4.2b} \] Every tensor factor surviving \(h\) has positive internal degree, so an iterated coproduct of \(x\) cannot have more than \(d\) such factors. Thus \(h^{*(d+1)}(x)=0\). The two geometric-series products with \(\mathrm{id}=u\epsilon-h\) give \(S*\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}*S=u\epsilon\). This proves both antipode identities, including degree zero, where \(S\) fixes the coefficient ring. An isomorphism preserving multiplication, coproduct and counit preserves every term of this formula, and hence the antipode. No unlisted Hopf-structure choice is needed. Degrees (4.2) follow from the source's degree of its generator \(\zeta_i\) at lines 764–765 by the exact index comparison \[ \zeta_i^{\mathrm{DI}}=\tau_{i-1},\qquad t_{\mathrm h}^{-1}(\zeta_i^{\mathrm{DI}})^2=\xi_i \quad(i\geq1). \tag{4.3} \] Indeed the first formula has degree \((2^i-1,2^{i-1}-1)\). The second has degree \((2^{i+1}-2,1+2(2^{i-1}-1))\), giving (4.2). The source's lines 770–771 attach indices \(\tau_i,\xi_{i+1}\); with its preceding degree formula the consistent indices are those in (4.3). The later source arXiv:2001.04247v1, lines 633–645, uses the presentation (4.1) and its full coproducts. The map (4.3) gives the actual relation between the presentations. Let \(C=R_{\mathrm h}[z_1,z_2,\ldots]\), \(|z_i|=(2^i-1,0)\), and \(z_0=1\). The already proved inverse Hopf-algebra maps are \[ \Phi(z_i)=t_{\mathrm h}^{\,2^{i-1}-1}\tau_{i-1}, \quad \Psi(\tau_j)=t_{\mathrm h}^{\,1-2^j}z_{j+1}, \quad \Psi(\xi_i)=t_{\mathrm h}^{\,1-2^i}z_i^2. \tag{4.4} \] They are now verified to preserve both degrees. The weight of \(\Phi(z_i)\) is \(-(2^{i-1}-1)+(2^{i-1}-1)=0\). The weights of the last two expressions are \(2^j-1\) and \(2^i-1\); their internal degrees are \(2^{j+1}-1\) and \(2(2^i-1)\). The relation in (4.1) has bidegree \((2^{j+2}-2,2^{j+1}-2)\) on both sides, since its right weight is \(-1+(2^{j+1}-1)\). This retains the coefficient contribution. More generally the image under \(\Psi\) of any original monomial is \[ t_{\mathrm h}^{\ell}\prod_{i\geq1}\xi_i^{a_i} \prod_{j\geq0}\tau_j^{e_j} \longmapsto t_{\mathrm h}^{L}\prod_{i\geq1}z_i^{\,2a_i+e_{i-1}}, \quad L=\ell+\sum_{i\geq1}a_i(1-2^i) +\sum_{j\geq0}e_j(1-2^j), \tag{4.5} \] where the sums have finite support. Its original weight is exactly \(-L\), and its original internal degree is exactly \(\sum_i(2a_i+e_{i-1})(2^i-1)\). Hence (4.5) proves the grading comparison for every original coefficient and monomial, including the polynomial subalgebra \(B_0\) whose exact image was proved in Section 1. It does not replace \(B_0\) by its localization. For completeness the full coproduct in the source's \(\zeta^{\mathrm{DI}}\) coordinates is \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta\zeta_k^{\mathrm{DI}} ={}&\zeta_k^{\mathrm{DI}}\otimes1+ 1\otimes\zeta_k^{\mathrm{DI}}\\ &+\sum_{i=1}^{k-1} t_{\mathrm h}^{-2^{i-1}} (\zeta_{k-i}^{\mathrm{DI}})^{2^i} \otimes\zeta_i^{\mathrm{DI}} . \end{aligned} \tag{4.6} \] Although displayed in Laurent coordinates, every interior left factor is the original polynomial-algebra element \[ t_{\mathrm h}^{-2^{i-1}} (\zeta_{k-i}^{\mathrm{DI}})^{2^i} =\bigl(t_{\mathrm h}^{-1} (\zeta_{k-i}^{\mathrm{DI}})^2\bigr)^{2^{i-1}} =\xi_{k-i}^{2^{i-1}}\in B_0. \tag{4.7} \] Substitution of (4.3) in (4.6), with \(j=k-1\) and the summation index \(i-1\), gives the full original \(\Delta\tau_j\) term for term. Its weight balance also follows from \[ 2^i(2^{k-i-1}-1)+(2^{i-1}-1) -(2^{k-1}-1)=-2^{i-1}. \tag{4.8} \] The coefficient of weight \(+2^{i-1}\) in (4.6) compensates exactly this difference. The endpoint coefficients are one and are kept separate because \(\zeta_0=1\) has degree zero. The source's integral monomial basis is retained as well: \[ b_R=t_{\mathrm h}^{-\sum_i\lfloor r_i/2\rfloor} \prod_i(\zeta_i^{\mathrm{DI}})^{r_i}. \tag{4.9} \] Writing \(r_i=2a_i+e_{i-1}\), \(e_{i-1}\in\{0,1\}\), turns (4.9) into precisely \(\prod_i\xi_i^{a_i}\prod_j\tau_j^{e_j}\). The free \(R_{\mathrm h,0}\)-basis proof in Section 1 therefore applies to every such monomial. Its weight is \[ \sum_i\left(r_i(2^{i-1}-1)+\left\lfloor\frac{r_i}{2}\right\rfloor\right) =\sum_i\left\lfloor\frac{r_i(2^i-1)}2\right\rfloor . \tag{4.10} \] This proves the exact source basis-degree formula at lines 794–798 by evaluating all coefficient powers, rather than suppressing them. The tensor powers of (4.4) preserve length, internal degree and total weight in the augmentation-ideal cobar complexes, since the coproduct and counit comparisons were proved in Section 1 and the tensor products are over the stated coefficient ring. Thus the corresponding cochain isomorphism preserves \((s,f,w)=(t-f,f,w)\), with \(f\) the number of slots. The coefficient class \(t_{\mathrm h}\) has \((s,f,w)=(0,0,-1)\), exactly the convention explicitly stated in Isaksen, arXiv:1407.8418v2, May chapter lines 361–364. These are complete algebraic comparisons, including the original polynomial subalgebra, both localizations, all weights, every coefficient and the source index corrections. They do not supply the still-required proof that the chosen topological operation object realizes the presented algebra, nor the convergence and geometric detection needed for the original six-manifold.

complete_source_text: ## 5. The exact degree-six receiving calculation over the original coefficient ring The preceding comparison has a concrete consequence over the original coefficient ring. Write \[ C_0^{f,t}=(\overline B_0^{\otimes_{R_{\mathrm h,0}}f})^t, \qquad \overline B_0=\ker(\epsilon:B_0\longrightarrow R_{\mathrm h,0}), \tag{5.1} \] with \(C_0^{0,0}=R_{\mathrm h,0}\) and \(C_0^{0,t}=0\) for \(t\ne0\). The differential inserts each full reduced coproduct in turn; since the characteristic is two, every alternating sign is \(+1\). Coassociativity makes its square zero: insertions into two different slots occur twice, and the two insertions into the same original slot agree by coassociativity. Denote its cohomology by \(\mathcal H_0^{f,t}\). No topological interpretation is included in this definition. Localization gives an isomorphism of complete cochain complexes \[ R_{\mathrm h}\otimes_{R_{\mathrm h,0}} C_0^{\bullet,*} \xrightarrow{\ \Psi^{\otimes\bullet}\ } R_{\mathrm h}\otimes_{\mathbb F_2} C^{\bullet,*}(H_{\mathrm{cl}}), \quad H_{\mathrm{cl}}=\mathbb F_2[z_1,z_2,\ldots], \tag{5.2} \] where \(H_{\mathrm{cl}}\) has its full classical coproduct \(\Delta z_i=\sum_{k=0}^i z_{i-k}^{2^k}\otimes z_k\). The coefficient tensor in each degree on the left identifies with \(\overline B^{\otimes f}\): the split counit decomposition \(B_0=R_{\mathrm h,0}\oplus\overline B_0\) is retained by localization, and the tensor-product universal property gives the identification on every slot. Formula (4.4) then proves (5.2) term for term. Here is the full comparison with cohomology, including its exact kernel. For any \(R_{\mathrm h,0}\)-cochain complex \(D\), the natural map \[ R_{\mathrm h}\otimes_{R_{\mathrm h,0}}H^f(D) \longrightarrow H^f(R_{\mathrm h}\otimes_{R_{\mathrm h,0}}D), \qquad [a]/t_{\mathrm h}^k\longmapsto[a/t_{\mathrm h}^k], \tag{5.3} \] is an isomorphism. A localized cycle \(a/t_{\mathrm h}^k\) satisfies \(t_{\mathrm h}^m da=0\) for some \(m\geq0\), so it is the image of the genuine cycle \(t_{\mathrm h}^m a\), divided by \(t_{\mathrm h}^{k+m}\). This proves surjectivity. If a localized genuine cycle \(a/t_{\mathrm h}^k\) equals \(db/t_{\mathrm h}^{\ell}\), then for some \(m\geq0\), \[ t_{\mathrm h}^{m+\ell}a=t_{\mathrm h}^{m+k}db. \tag{5.4} \] Thus its cohomology class becomes zero in the localization of \(H^f(D)\), proving injectivity. In particular, the kernel of the original map \(H^f(D)\to H^f(D[t_{\mathrm h}^{-1}])\) is exactly the set of classes killed by some power of \(t_{\mathrm h}\); no other class is lost. Tensoring the classical complex over \(\mathbb F_2\) with \(R_{\mathrm h}\) likewise commutes with cohomology: a vector-space decomposition into boundaries, chosen cohomology representatives and a complement on which the differential is an isomorphism gives the same direct decomposition after tensoring. This proves the comparison without an unverified interchange of a Hom functor and localization. Apply the [complete all-length classical cobar calculation](https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/46785fdb4bbf7c7ba22e5238561451e54d6cdf9a/docs/courses/CG-S6/src/the-degree-six-milnor-cobar-calculation.md), equation (1.8) and Sections 2–5. Its degree-six result gives \[ \mathcal H_0^{f,f+6}[t_{\mathrm h}^{-1}] \cong \begin{cases} R_{\mathrm h}\{[z_1^4|z_1^4]\},&f=2,\\ 0,&f\ne2. \end{cases} \tag{5.5} \] The cited proof is available in the private repository and is part of the course's full included source. It covers every length \(f\), not a finite truncation. All coefficient factors in the surviving original cycle are explicit. Since \(\xi_1\) is primitive, \(\xi_1^2\) is primitive over \(\mathbb F_2\), so \[ e=[\xi_1^2|\xi_1^2]\in C_0^{2,8} \quad\text{is a cycle of weight }4. \tag{5.6} \] The original relation \(\tau_0^2=t_{\mathrm h}\xi_1\) and the balanced tensor product give \[ [\tau_0^4|\tau_0^4] =[t_{\mathrm h}^2\xi_1^2|t_{\mathrm h}^2\xi_1^2] =t_{\mathrm h}^4 e, \qquad \Psi^{\otimes2}(e) =t_{\mathrm h}^{-4}[z_1^4|z_1^4]. \tag{5.7} \] Thus \(e\) is not a boundary and no nonzero polynomial in \(t_{\mathrm h}\) annihilates its class. Indeed either assertion would contradict the free rank-one Laurent module in (5.5), since a nonzero polynomial remains nonzero in \(R_{\mathrm h}\). We can recover the entire free summand in the original polynomial coefficient ring and give a uniform bound on all remaining coefficient torsion. A monomial of the original \(R_{\mathrm h,0}\)-basis (1.12) has internal degree \(d\) and weight \(v\) satisfying \[ 0\leq v\leq\left\lfloor\frac d2\right\rfloor . \tag{5.8} \] For \(\xi_i\), twice its weight equals its internal degree; for \(\tau_j\), twice its weight is its internal degree minus one. Add these exact identities with the monomial multiplicities to prove (5.8). Consequently every tensor-basis vector of \(C_0^{f,t}\) has weight between zero and \(\lfloor t/2\rfloor\). Multiplication by \(t_{\mathrm h}\) lowers weight by one, so \(C_0^{f,t,w}=0\) when \(w>\lfloor t/2\rfloor\). Moreover, for every integer \(w\leq0\), multiplication is a cochain isomorphism \[ t_{\mathrm h}:C_0^{\bullet,t,w} \xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }C_0^{\bullet,t,w-1}. \tag{5.9} \] A tensor-basis vector of original weight \(v\geq0\) occurs in the first vector space with coefficient exactly \(t_{\mathrm h}^{v-w}\), and in the second with coefficient \(t_{\mathrm h}^{v-w+1}\). This gives a bijection on the full bases. The inverse removes one factor only in this stated range, where its exponent is positive; it is not a division map on the entire original complex. Coefficient linearity of the differential proves that (5.9) and its inverse are cochain maps. Therefore (5.9) also induces an isomorphism on cohomology. Let \(T^{f,t}\) be the kernel of localization on \(\mathcal H_0^{f,t}\). By (5.3) it is precisely the \(t_{\mathrm h}\)-power torsion. It satisfies the explicit bound \[ t_{\mathrm h}^{\lfloor t/2\rfloor}T^{f,t}=0. \tag{5.10} \] To prove this, decompose a class into its finitely many homogeneous weight components. Every component has weight \(w\leq\lfloor t/2\rfloor\). After the displayed power its weight is at most zero. If the original class is coefficient torsion, so is this image. But (5.9) is injective in every subsequent weight at most zero, so the image must already be zero. This proves (5.10) for each component and hence for the class. For \(f=2,t=8\), (5.5) and the grading determine a canonical coefficient-module retraction onto the full original free class. Every homogeneous \(h\in\mathcal H_0^{2,8,w}\) maps after localization either to zero or to \[ t_{\mathrm h}^{4-w}e. \tag{5.11} \] The exponent is nonnegative because \(w\leq4\); thus every localization image already belongs to the polynomial submodule \(R_{\mathrm h,0}e\). The unique coefficient in this submodule defines an \(R_{\mathrm h,0}\)-linear map \(\rho:\mathcal H_0^{2,8}\to R_{\mathrm h,0}\) with \(\rho(e)=1\). It is well-defined on sums by the uniqueness of Laurent coefficients, and its kernel is exactly \(T^{2,8}\). The map \[ R_{\mathrm h,0}\{e\}\oplus T^{2,8} \longrightarrow\mathcal H_0^{2,8}, \quad (ae,h)\longmapsto ae+h \tag{5.12} \] has inverse \(x\mapsto(\rho(x)e,x-\rho(x)e)\). This proves both composites and the exact direct-sum decomposition. In characteristic two the subtraction equals addition, but the displayed map specifies its role. Combining (5.5), (5.10) and (5.12), the original coefficient calculation is \[ \begin{gathered} \mathcal H_0^{2,8} =R_{\mathrm h,0}\{[\xi_1^2|\xi_1^2]\}\oplus T^{2,8}, \qquad t_{\mathrm h}^{4}T^{2,8}=0,\\ t_{\mathrm h}^{\lfloor(f+6)/2\rfloor} \mathcal H_0^{f,f+6}=0\qquad(f\ne2). \end{gathered} \tag{5.13} \] Here \(T^{2,8}\) is the exactly defined kernel of the displayed localization map; its internal presentation is not being asserted to be zero. Equation (5.13) proves the entire free summand, the exact original cycle receiving the classical class, and a specified annihilating power for every other class at every length. No coefficient-torsion contribution has been removed from the original object.

complete_source_text: ## 6. The remaining torsion in bidegree \((2,8)\) is zero We now compute the kernel left in (5.13), over the original polynomial coefficient ring. The complete finite calculation is retained in [calculate_original_coefficient_h28.py](../checks/calculate_original_coefficient_h28.py) and its [full matrix certificate](../checks/ORIGINAL_COEFFICIENT_H28_CERTIFICATE.json). Both files are included with this proof. The certificate includes every original basis word, every coefficient power in both differentials, all matrix columns, and explicit nonzero minors. No row or column of the original complexes is omitted from the retained data. Here is the construction and the proof of why this finite calculation covers the entire original bidegree. In internal degrees at most eight the only generators that can occur are, in this fixed order, \[ (\tau_0,\tau_1,\tau_2,\xi_1,\xi_2), \quad (d_0,d_1,d_2,d_3,d_4)=(1,3,7,2,6), \quad (v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4)=(0,1,3,1,3). \tag{6.1} \] Their original monomial basis is indexed by \[ m=(e_0,e_1,e_2,a_1,a_2),\quad e_i\in\{0,1\},\quad a_1,a_2\geq0,\quad \sum_i d_i m_i\leq8. \tag{6.2} \] Multiplication of two basis vectors first adds their exponents, then uses the exact original relations \(\tau_0^2=t_{\mathrm h}\xi_1\) and \(\tau_1^2=t_{\mathrm h}\xi_2\), retaining each resulting coefficient power. A square of \(\tau_2\) has internal degree fourteen and hence cannot occur in this degree-eight calculation. The full generator coproducts, before removing the two unit endpoints to form the differential, are \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta\tau_0&=\tau_0\otimes1+1\otimes\tau_0,\\ \Delta\tau_1&=\tau_1\otimes1+\xi_1\otimes\tau_0+1\otimes\tau_1,\\ \Delta\tau_2&=\tau_2\otimes1+\xi_2\otimes\tau_0+ \xi_1^2\otimes\tau_1+1\otimes\tau_2,\\ \Delta\xi_1&=\xi_1\otimes1+1\otimes\xi_1,\\ \Delta\xi_2&=\xi_2\otimes1+\xi_1^2\otimes\xi_1+1\otimes\xi_2. \end{aligned} \tag{6.3} \] Multiplying (6.3) with the exact multiplication rule proves every coproduct column in the certificate. For length \(f=1,2,3\), enumerate all ordered lists of nonunit monomials (6.2) whose internal degrees sum to eight. Sort individual monomials lexicographically by (6.2); enumerate words recursively by the first internal degree \(1,\ldots,8\) in ascending order, then that monomial order, then the same order on the remaining word. This specifies every basis index used in the certificate without an arbitrary basis change. In weight \(w\), a word of original weight \(v\) appears exactly as \(t_{\mathrm h}^{v-w}\) times that word, and appears if and only if \(v\geq w\). If its differential contains \(t_{\mathrm h}^k\) times a target word of weight \(v'\), homogeneity gives \(v'=v+k\). Therefore the entry in the weight-\(w\) matrix is exactly the coefficient of that target word, because \[ t_{\mathrm h}^{v-w}t_{\mathrm h}^k =t_{\mathrm h}^{v'-w}. \tag{6.4} \] This is a proved conversion from the original polynomial differential to a particular homogeneous \(\mathbb F_2\)-matrix. The certificate also retains \(k\) itself; (6.4) does not discard that coefficient in the original complex. The resulting exact matrix dimensions and ranks are: ::: {.coefficient-rank-table style="overflow-x:auto"} | Weight \(w\) | \(\dim C_0^{1,8,w}\) | \(\dim C_0^{2,8,w}\) | \(\dim C_0^{3,8,w}\) | \(\operatorname{rank}d_1\) | \(\operatorname{rank}d_2\) | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 0 | 4 | 26 | 63 | 3 | 22 | | 1 | 4 | 26 | 63 | 3 | 22 | | 2 | 4 | 26 | 63 | 3 | 22 | | 3 | 4 | 25 | 48 | 3 | 21 | | 4 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 1 | 3 | ::: For an exact verification of each rank lower bound, the certificate names row and column indices of a square submatrix with determinant one in \(\mathbb F_2\). Its rows are also included explicitly as binary integers: bit \(j\) is column \(j\). The algorithm for this determinant proceeds from column zero upward, exchanges the first row with a one in that column into the pivot position, then adds it to every later row with a one in that column. If no such row exists, the determinant is zero. Each exchange and row addition preserves the determinant in characteristic two. A successful step leaves a one at that diagonal position and zeros below it; induction gives an upper triangular matrix with every diagonal entry one. This proves that a successful certificate has determinant one and hence supplies the stated rank lower bound. The executable calculation checks every named minor by precisely this algorithm. The ranks are then forced to be exact without an assumed upper-bound computation. The full matrix composition \(d_2d_1=0\) is checked on every column and also follows from the proved coassociativity. In every table row the two lower bounds sum to \(\dim C_0^{2,8,w}-1\). The cycle \(t_{\mathrm h}^{4-w}e\) is nonzero in cohomology by (5.7). Independently, the certificate gives a row functional on \(C_0^{2,8,w}\) that annihilates every \(d_1\)-column and takes value one on this cycle's column; its pairings are explicitly checked. Thus cohomology has dimension at least one, while the two rank lower bounds make it at most one. Both ranks and the single stated cohomology generator follow. For \(w>4\), all degree-eight cochains are zero by (5.8). For every \(w\leq0\), (5.9) transports the weight-zero result by the original coefficient multiplication. Consequently every integer weight is covered, and multiplication by \(t_{\mathrm h}\) carries the displayed nonzero generator at each weight \(w\leq4\) to the displayed generator at weight \(w-1\). There is no coefficient-torsion class. We obtain the complete result \[ \boxed{\displaystyle \mathcal H_0^{2,8} =\mathbb F_2[t_{\mathrm h}] \{[\xi_1^2|\xi_1^2]\}, \qquad |[\xi_1^2|\xi_1^2]|=(f,t,w)=(2,8,4).} \tag{6.5} \] Its precise receiving map is still (5.7): the weight-zero original class \([\tau_0^4|\tau_0^4]\) is \(t_{\mathrm h}^4\) times this generator, and after localization it maps to the original classical class \([z_1^4|z_1^4]\). Equations (5.10) and (5.13) continue to retain every other length's coefficient torsion; (6.5) makes no unsupported assertion that those other groups vanish. ![The original coefficient generator and each of its first four coefficient multiples, with the full localized comparison.](../assets/original-coefficient-degree-six-class.svg) The vertical arrows are multiplication by the original coefficient of weight minus one, not a change of the underlying object. Both horizontal arrows use the same tensor-square map (4.4) and retain the powers in (5.7). The five displayed weights, together with the cochain isomorphism (5.9) in every lower weight, account for the entire module (6.5). The reproducible source is [draw_original_coefficient_class.py](../checks/draw_original_coefficient_class.py); its rendered output was inspected.

complete_source_text:
### Exercise 7.1. Every coefficient in two Adem relations

Compute the original relations for \(Q^4Q^4\) and \(Q^3Q^2\) in the cohomological coefficient presentation. Retain even the zero binomial terms. Apply both maps (3.5), keeping every power of \(t_{\mathrm c}\). Finally determine the image of the generator \(Q^1\) and its coefficient.

**Solution.** For \(a=b=4\), the original sum has \(c=0,1,2\). It is
\[
 Q^4Q^4
  =\binom34 Q^8Q^0
    +\binom22 t_{\mathrm c}Q^7Q^1
    +\binom10 Q^6Q^2
  =0\cdot Q^8Q^0+t_{\mathrm c}Q^7Q^1+Q^6Q^2.
 \tag{7.1}
\]
The only coefficient power one occurs for the odd \(c=1\). Under \(\Theta\), the left side becomes
\(t_{\mathrm c}^2S^4\,t_{\mathrm c}^2S^4=t_{\mathrm c}^4S^4S^4\). The two nonzero terms on the right become
\[
 t_{\mathrm c}(t_{\mathrm c}^3S^7)S^1
          +(t_{\mathrm c}^3S^6)(t_{\mathrm c}S^2)
     =t_{\mathrm c}^4(S^7S^1+S^6S^2).
 \tag{7.2}
\]
Their full coefficient powers agree. Applying \(\Lambda\) to the classical relation gives
\[
 (t_{\mathrm c}^{-2}Q^4)(t_{\mathrm c}^{-2}Q^4)
   =(t_{\mathrm c}^{-3}Q^7)Q^1
           +(t_{\mathrm c}^{-3}Q^6)(t_{\mathrm c}^{-1}Q^2).
 \tag{7.3}
\]
Multiplication by \(t_{\mathrm c}^4\) recovers exactly (7.1), including its one coefficient factor.

For \(a=3,b=2\), the only terms are
\[
 Q^3Q^2=\binom13 Q^5Q^0+\binom01 Q^4Q^1
                    =0\cdot Q^5Q^0+0\cdot Q^4Q^1=0.
 \tag{7.4}
\]
Its image under \(\Theta\) is \(t_{\mathrm c}^2S^3S^2=0\); applying \(\Lambda\) to \(S^3S^2=0\) gives \(t_{\mathrm c}^{-2}Q^3Q^2=0\). Finally \(w(1)=0\), so \(\Theta(Q^1)=S^1\). A coefficient \(t_{\mathrm c}^{-1}\) in this last formula would change weight zero to weight minus one and would not be the degree-preserving map in the stated convention.

statement_as_printed: ### Exercise 7.2. The surviving original class in a complete small matrix
complete_source_text: ### Exercise 7.2. The surviving original class in a complete small matrix Work in internal degree eight and weight four in the original coefficient cobar complex. For this exercise use the original elements \(x=\xi_1\) and \(y=\xi_2\), with internal degrees \(2,6\) and weights \(1,3\). Specify the complete bases in lengths one, two and three, calculate both differential matrices, and prove that the cohomology is generated by \([x^2|x^2]\). Relate the result back to \([\tau_0^4|\tau_0^4]\). **Solution.** Every word in this weight must have twice its weight equal to its internal degree. The exact degree formula in (5.8) therefore excludes every \(\tau_j\) factor: each would lower twice the weight by one. It also excludes positive powers of \(t_{\mathrm h}\), which lower the weight. Only the stated \(\xi\) generators can occur in internal degree at most eight. The complete ordered bases are \[ \begin{aligned} C_0^{1,8,4}:&\quad [xy],\ [x^4],\\ C_0^{2,8,4}:&\quad [x|y],\ [x|x^3],\ [x^2|x^2],\ [y|x],\ [x^3|x],\\ C_0^{3,8,4}:&\quad [x|x|x^2],\ [x|x^2|x],\ [x^2|x|x]. \end{aligned} \tag{7.5} \] These are the same original monomial and word orders as in Section 6. The full coproducts are \(\Delta x=x\otimes1+1\otimes x\) and \(\Delta y=y\otimes1+x^2\otimes x+1\otimes y\). Multiplying them gives \[ \Delta(xy) =xy\otimes1+x^3\otimes x+x\otimes y +y\otimes x+x^2\otimes x^2+1\otimes xy. \tag{7.6} \] Thus \(d[xy]=[x^3|x]+[x|y]+[y|x]+[x^2|x^2]\). The element \(x^4\) is primitive in characteristic two, so \(d[x^4]=0\). The first matrix, with every zero entry retained, is \[ D_1= \begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\0&0\\1&0\\1&0\\1&0 \end{pmatrix}. \tag{7.7} \] The reduced coproduct of \(x^3\) is \(x\otimes x^2+x^2\otimes x\), and that of \(x^2\) is zero. Inserting these and the reduced coproduct of \(y\) into each of the five words gives \[ \begin{aligned} d[x|y]&=[x|x^2|x],\\ d[x|x^3]&=[x|x|x^2]+[x|x^2|x],\\ d[x^2|x^2]&=0,\\ d[y|x]&=[x^2|x|x],\\ d[x^3|x]&=[x|x^2|x]+[x^2|x|x]. \end{aligned} \tag{7.8} \] Hence the second matrix is exactly \[ D_2= \begin{pmatrix} 0&1&0&0&0\\ 1&1&0&0&1\\ 0&0&0&1&1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad D_2D_1=0. \tag{7.9} \] The first matrix has rank one. Columns one, two and four of the second matrix are linearly independent: the first coordinate forces the coefficient of column two to vanish; the second then forces the coefficient of column one to vanish, and the third forces the coefficient of column four to vanish. Thus the second matrix has rank three and its kernel has dimension two. The vectors \[ (1,0,1,1,1)^{\mathsf T}, \qquad (0,0,1,0,0)^{\mathsf T} \tag{7.10} \] belong to that kernel and are independent. The first spans the image of \(D_1\); the second is the cycle \(e=[x^2|x^2]\). This proves the one-dimensional cohomology and its precise generator. Equivalently, the functional with coefficients \((1,0,1,0,0)\) annihilates both \(D_1\)-columns and evaluates to one on \(e\), giving an explicit nonboundary witness. Finally the original quadratic relation gives \[ [\tau_0^4|\tau_0^4] =[t_{\mathrm h}^2x^2|t_{\mathrm h}^2x^2] =t_{\mathrm h}^4[x^2|x^2]. \tag{7.11} \] This is the weight-zero class, whereas \(e\) has weight four. The exact tensor-square comparison sends \(e\) to \(t_{\mathrm h}^{-4}[z_1^4|z_1^4]\), so it sends (7.11) to the full original classical class. Section 6 supplies all other weights and proves that the resulting original module is the entire polynomial module, without coefficient torsion.
